#6438. The 6 Best Laptops You Can Buy

From wallet-friendly buys to big-money AI and content-creation powerhouses, we ranked today’s best portable computers.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Whether you're in the mood for a movie night, want to keep your social media game strong, plan an online grocery run, or settle in for a marathon gaming session, a good laptop is a trusty sidekick. Choosing one, however, is not a quick or simple decision. You’ll need to find the right machine to supercharge your productivity or fuel your passion for gaming. Just beware: Picking the wrong machine could get in the way of your passions instead of enhancing them.

Luckily, the laptop market offers options for every need and budget, and we've handpicked the best for you. Still, before you whip out that credit card, you first need to choose sides in the age-old Mac vs. Windows debate. Apple's MacBooks shine with top-tier build quality and a rock-solid platform. They're a dream come true for those who don't rely on Windows-specific software.

However, some folks think that Apple's ecosystem feels a bit like the Hotel California—you can check out anytime you like, but you can never leave. Separately, despite Apple's best efforts, the Mac ecosystem still has some software limitations, especially for avid PC gamers.

Now, let's talk style. Do you want a traditional laptop or one that can transform into a superhero? If you desire a laptop that moonlights as a tablet, a 2-in-1 device is your new BFF. These nifty gadgets come with a keyboard that vanishes when you don't need it, making them perfect for streaming, unleashing your inner artist on the touchscreen, and more. But here's the catch: touchscreens can sometimes make you miss the crystal-clear clarity of a traditional screen, especially when you're knee-deep in an epic writing session.

We pored over the specs and reviews of dozens of the latest laptops to assemble this list of the best notebooks you can buy today. We looked for laptops we would be happy to use ourselves, while also finding models that fit a range of budgets and preferences. Our tech staff personally own and use several of these machines at home, including the MacBook Pro, the Microsoft Surface lineup, and MacBook Neo, and can vouch for long-term quality and durability.

Apple’s current MacBook Pro is a bit of a lame duck, with a new and improved version coming out very soon with upgraded M6 silicon, but the current M5 model is still my favorite laptop, pound for pound. The M5 MacBook Pro offers an unbeatable mix of timelessly elegant design, top-tier craftsmanship, outstanding performance, and long battery life in a compact package.

On the performance front, the entry-level MacBook Pro handled everything we threw at it—from toggling between multiple apps to running blockbuster games like Cyberpunk 2077. Best of all, unlike PC rivals with similar hardware capabilities, the notebook can deliver a full day of mixed use on a single charge.

The M5 MacBook Pro is only available with a 14.2-inch display. Much more powerful variants with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips are available in two screen sizes—14.2- and 16.2-inch. With more CPU and GPU cores and significantly higher memory bandwidth, the M5 Pro and Max can handle heavy workflows—from AI-related tasks to high-resolution video editing projects—anytime, anywhere.

True to its “Pro” moniker, even the base MacBook Pro is powerful, made for users who need more than basic compute power for creative projects like image or video editing, audio production, or local AI workflows. If you’re using your Mac for email, Google Docs, and web browsing, you may be better off with a MacBook Air or even my budget pick, the MacBook Neo.

MApple genuinely shook up the entire computing world when it launched the Macbook Neo, a budget-tier Mac built around an iPhone processor that starts at less than $700. Up to this point, the cheapest new Mac was traditionally the Macbook Air, which cost just over a $1,000, which forced Mac users to spend a pretty penny to gain access to their preferred operating system, even if they didn’t need the power it offered.

You’d think that a “budget” Mac would somehow feel less than to justify the higher spend for an Air, but the truth is that the Neo is realistically more than enough machine for folks who just need the basic. Compared to similarly priced Windows machines, the Neo offers stellar all-around performance and great battery life, making it kind of a no-brainer for a lot of folks. It’s a bit thicker than an Air, but makes up for it on the style front with a small array of iMac-esque colorways.

Make no mistake, this is not a powerhouse, though: the Neo runs on the A18 Pro chip, which is not the newest mobile processor, and only features 8GB of RAM in the base configuration, which is enough for browsing and email, but will likely slow down and struggle with anything complex. While it drives the price up a bit, I would urge most folks to go with the slightly pricier 512GB version, which also adds a TouchID fingerprint sensor. Even with the base model, though, the Neo is cooler, and a better buy than just about any other machine under $1,000 you’ll find on this side of a Black Friday sale.

The Microsoft Surface Laptop is a formidable PC alternative to our top Apple pick, pairing beautiful design and craftsmanship with top-tier Qualcomm silicon that delivers stellar performance at a similar price. Weighing either just under or slightly over three pounds, depending on the screen size, this metal-clad notebook is impressively light and slim, given its hardware specs and performance.

Hardware-wise, the Microsoft Surface Laptop impresses with a sharp PixelSense touchscreen, the latest Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Plus or X2 Elite chip, plenty of memory, and a comprehensive set of futureproof wired and wireless connectivity features. In my experience, both the entry-level and top-spec versions delivered excellent all-around performance and long battery life.

The Microsoft Surface Laptop comes in three screen sizes—13-, 13.8-, and 15-inch — unlike the MacBook Air or Pro and any PC laptop rival. The 13-inch version with a six-core Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 chip is the most affordable. Upping your budget for a 13.8- or 15-inch model, alongside a more powerful chip, will get you a sharper and brighter display panel with a higher refresh rate and Dolby Vision HDR support.

The recently launched Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra with the brand-new Nvidia RTX Spark chip is the PC laptop to get if you are a PC power user with a big upgrade budget. The notebook’s first-of-its-kind silicon makes it great for demanding workflows—from AI-related tasks to AAA gameplay.

The Asus ROG Strix G16 is an upgrade-worthy gaming laptop for players looking to balance serious gaming specs with portability. With gaming laptops, there’s often a fine line between making an underpowered machine that lacks the specs to keep up with even a budget-tier desktop, and a huge “desktop replacement” that’s too heavy to carry on a daily basis. The Strix G16 walks that line well, delivering strong performance while keeping things relatively light.

Gaming laptops generally run heavier than performance machines, so while six pounds may sound like a lot, it's not that bad when you factor in the power at your disposal. The configuration we tested, with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti GPU, an Intel Core Ultra 9 processor, and 32 GB of RAM, will handle new games on high or ultra settings with ease. They'll also look great on a 2.5K G-Sync display that maxes out at 240Hz, ensuring smooth, lifelike gameplay.

Depending on your budget, you can scale this laptop's hardware up or down to meet your needs. If you can live with slightly less performance, there's a more budget-friendly sub-$1,500 version with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 GPU. On the other end, this monstrously powerful config costs nearly $4,000, but your games will look absolutely incredible.

Chromebooks are historically known for being a cheap, basic notebook option, which have been widely adopted for young students who need a school-only machine. But with tech prices going the way they’ve been going and Google releasing a new, more powerful class of AI-focused Googlebooks starting at $899, that price advantage has largely evaporated. Given that, we’re only inclined to recommend high-performance Chromebooks, rather than the cheapest models.

For $750, Lenovo’s Chromebook Plus 14 is a high-end Chromebook, but still feels fairly budget-friendly compared to the wider world of laptops. It features a MediaTek chip and 16 GB of RAM, which gives you pretty snappy responsiveness for basic email and web browsing, and across ChromeOS-friendly Android apps.

The best part, I think, is its display: A sharp, 14-inch OLED touchscreen that makes streams look great. For work and school, it also has a surprisingly good high-resolution webcam and Dolby Atmos-capable speakers. And it can run up to 17 hours on a single charge, which should easily get it through a workday of mixed use.

If you want a lightweight machine that looks and feels ready for hard work using Google’s vast suite of productivity apps and Gemini, this is a very reasonable option that can save you a few hundred bucks.

The Microsoft Surface Pro has been a stellar laptop-caliber tablet experience for a long time, and this year is no different. This Windows-powered slate is sleek, capable, and supremely versatile. Yes, you’ll need to buy a keyboard case to complete its transformation to full-blown laptop, but I think it’s absolutely worth it to do so.

Getting the laptop option mentioned above requires spending more on a Surface Pro keyboard and Slim Pen 2 bundle, but the investment is well worth it. The essential accessories, along with the Pro’s adjustable viewing stand, are instrumental in giving it such commendable versatility.

Equipped with Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Series silicon, the Microsoft Surface Pro balances abundant power, stellar multitasking, and long battery life. We prefer the higher-end version, which features a stunning OLED screen. Lower-priced iterations use an IPS panel, down to a 12-inch display panel in the starter model.

You'll want a laptop that cuts through every task you throw at it while also lasting as long as you do. The selections below are packed with the latest processing and graphics technology to rise to the occasion.

If you travel frequently or commute with your computer, look for thin, light designs like the MacBook Air—the 13-inch model weighs in at just 2.7 pounds and the 15-inch at 3.3 pounds.

Gamers or content creators will want higher-end processors and graphics cards as well as bright, detailed screens. Students, and those who will spend most of their time logging into classes and watching the occasional movie or surfing the web, might want to consider a convertible laptop that also functions as a tablet.

More to Consider: MacBook Air vs. MacBook Pro • Best Laptop Docking Stations • Best Wireless Mouse • Best Gaming Keyboards

With the latest laptops, battery life keeps improving. The reason newer laptops last longer on the same size battery is because modern processors are getting more energy efficient. Today’s laptops will run between 8 and 20 hours on a single charge. Look for a battery that lasts at least 10 hours.

There are more than a dozen types of ports, including HDMI for video out and USB-C, which can be for almost anything with the right adaptor, such as charging, but most users will only need a USB-C port. That’s because it’s possible to connect almost any type of peripheral to USB-C by itself or using an adaptor.

If you don’t want to pack an adapter, consider a laptop with HDMI ports that can output video and audio from your laptop to a TV, monitor, or projector. They can support high-definition resolutions up to 4K and surround sound formats. Another handy option is ethernet ports that can connect your laptop to a wired network for faster and more reliable internet access.

The fastest processors on the market now offer blistering speeds and are great for gaming or video editing. But quicker speeds can sometimes make for a pricier laptop that has less battery life.

In laptop chips, Intel’s most popular lineup is its Core series, while Apple’s is its proprietary M-series processors (starting with the base M1). The middle ground in the Core and Ryzen lineups offers the best mix of performance and value. The most expensive laptops offer Intel Core i9 H-Series processors while mid-range models tend to have Core i5 processors that offer a good balance between price and performance.

Screen quality is also crucial to a satisfying experience. Buy the best screen you can afford; your eyes will thank you later. Higher-resolution screens allow for greater image detail, though fonts on high-resolution displays can be small and difficult to read.

The most suitable screen size for most people ranges from 13- to 15-inches—the sweet spot between portability and enough real estate to get things done. The most common resolutions on laptops and 2-in-1 PCs currently hover just above 1920 x 1080 (also known as 1080p or Full HD). This keeps panel prices relatively low and fonts still large enough to view comfortably.

Pick a keyboard with a broad enough design and widely spaced keys if you’ll be doing a lot of typing. Also consider key travel (how far a key needs to be depressed until the keystroke is recognized), which can vary widely between models. Larger laptops tend to have better keyboards since the dimensions don't have be downsized for smaller frames.

The more money you spend on your laptop, the longer you can expect it to last. In general, Macs have a reputation for lasting longer than Windows laptops. I have an eight-year-old MacBook Air that’s still going strong.

One factor to consider is that operating system updates that are released regularly tend to take up hard drive space, so if you buy a model with a larger drive, your laptop may last longer. To make the most of your laptop’s lifespan, keep the laptop clean, cool, updated, and backed up.

The weak spots of inexpensive laptops tend to be the keyboard, trackpad, and display. Manufacturers may skimp on these items hoping that potential buyers will focus more on processor speed. For starters, even if your funds are limited, look for a screen with at least Full HD (1920-by-1080) resolution.

It pays to be fussy when it comes to a laptop keyboard as that’s the component you’ll be interacting with the most. Buying a laptop with keyboard backlighting can help you see the keys better and avoid typing mistakes.

Some keyboards have adjustable brightness and color options for backlighting. Another important feature is a laptop keyboard with a full-size layout instead of a compact or tenkeyless layout without a numeric keypad.

#6437. Common blood pressure drug may activate the body’s calorie-burning fat

Scientists discover that losartan, a common blood pressure drug, may activate calorie-burning brown fat and offer unexpected health benefits.

Doctors prescribe losartan to lower blood pressure, but new research suggests the medication may have another unexpected benefit.

In the medical records of more than 100,000 cancer patients, people on the drug were more likely to have active brown fat, the kind that burns calories to make heat.

In mice and in lab-grown fat cells, losartan switched that fat on through a pathway separate from the one that lowers blood pressure.

That makes losartan a candidate for a job no approved drug does today, turning up brown fat in people.

Active brown fat has been linked to lower rates of diabetes and heart disease. The new study also found associations with lower rates of anxiety and depression.

Paul Cohen, who heads the Laboratory of Molecular Metabolism at Rockefeller University, led the work.

First author Nicolás Gómez-Banoy is an endocrinologist in his lab who also holds posts at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and Weill Cornell Medicine.

The patient data can only show that losartan users had more brown fat, not that the drug caused it, and the direct tests were in mice and in cells.

Brown fat burns calories to make heat, so it takes up the sugar tracer used in PET scans. That makes it visible on the scans cancer patients get to track their disease.

The team pulled every such scan from Memorial Sloan Kettering between 2018 and 2024 and added them to an earlier set, for 101,243 patients in all.

Brown fat appeared on at least one scan in 8,897 of them, just under 9%. It was more common in women, in younger patients, and on colder days.

Each patient with brown fat was matched to roughly two without it, on age, sex, body mass index, and the outdoor temperature on the day of the scan.

The team then compared 511 diagnosis codes between the two groups. The cancer itself and its treatment were controlled for.

Of 98 diagnoses that differed between the groups, 92 were less common in people with brown fat.

The strongest were type 2 diabetes, at less than half the odds, and chronic ischemic heart disease, at about half.

Anxiety disorders and depression were on the list too, with odds about a fifth and a third lower.

“We know that metabolically healthy people tend to have lower incidence of psychiatric diseases, so it could be that having brown fat makes you more metabolically healthy, and this correlates with fewer psychiatric issues,” Gómez-Banoy said.

The six diagnoses more common with brown fat were mostly skin conditions, and people with brown fat also had slightly lower bone density in the spine.

The team listed both as possible downsides to study.

A machine learning tool measured how much brown fat each person had and where.

Brown fat in the armpits was tied to the lowest odds of high blood pressure. It was also associated with the least fat around the organs, the belly fat that carries the most risk.

The team then checked 125 medications the patients were taking a month before their scan. Thirty-nine lined up with brown fat one way or the other.

Two kinds of drugs already known to dampen brown fat, beta blockers and the antidepressants called SSRIs, came out on the negative side.

Losartan and its cousin valsartan came out on the positive side: 2.4% of patients with brown fat were on losartan, against 1.9% of those without.

“The scope of this new analysis is far more expansive,” Cohen said. “We doubled our number of patients and considered more than 500 codes, which allowed us to unearth many new insights.”

Losartan blocks a receptor for the hormone angiotensin, which is how it lowers blood pressure. In brown fat cells, it still worked after that receptor was knocked down, so the fat effect runs through something else.

The experiments pointed to a protein called PPAR-gamma, a master switch involved in regulating fat cells.

Losartan turned it on, and a chemical that blocks PPAR-gamma blunted losartan’s effect.

The version of losartan doing the work was a breakdown product that doesn’t touch the blood pressure receptor at all.

“The fact that its different effects are mediated by different molecular pathways is advantageous, since it means we could potentially isolate them in future therapies,” Gómez-Banoy said.

“That way you would be able to stimulate brown fat in people with normal blood pressure.”

In mice, 10 days of losartan in the drinking water raised energy use and oxygen consumption. That held at room temperature and in the cold, without changing body weight or activity.

After two weeks on the drug, the brown fat between a mouse’s shoulders made more heat when it was stimulated.

Everyone in the study had cancer. Brown fat tracked with some cancers and some treatments, so the team controlled for both but can’t rule them out.

The scans were taken without any cold exposure, which likely undercounted brown fat.

A PET scan measures sugar uptake, not heat, and the two don’t always agree. The mouse experiments were small, with five to 10 animals per group, and the direct tests of the drug stop at mice.

“There were plenty of other medications associated with brown fat activity in our large cohort,” Cohen said. “This is just a start.”

Whether losartan’s brown fat effect adds up to anything for a patient’s weight, blood sugar, or mood is the open question.

The researchers say prospective studies in people are needed to determine whether these effects translate into meaningful health benefits.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6435. Scientists uncover a troubling pattern beneath Earth’s frozen ground

A global study of 156 monitoring sites reveals widespread permafrost thaw, raising concerns about infrastructure, carbon emissions, and climate change.

Every summer for the past three decades, Anna Klene has driven north across Alaska’s Brooks Range, and pushed a metal rod into the ground.

She records the depth at which it hits frozen earth. Then she moves on to the next site, and the next. It’s not glamorous science.

“It’s not super sophisticated,” she said. “You push down on the probe, put your finger on the rod and you can measure how many centimeters into the ground it went.”

These simple, long-term measurements have now produced something significant: the first global assessment of long-term permafrost monitoring data.

The findings confirm what climate scientists have feared. Permafrost is thawing broadly, persistently, and in ways that matter far beyond the frozen ground itself.

The measurement Klene takes is called active layer thickness. It refers to the depth of the ground above permafrost that freezes and thaws each year.

In a stable system, that layer stays roughly constant from one decade to the next.

When it deepens over time, it can signal that the underlying permafrost is warming and becoming less stable.

Permafrost is not simply frozen dirt. It’s soil, rock, and sediment bound together by ice that has remained frozen for at least two consecutive years. In many places, that happened for thousands of years.

Permafrost underlies 15 percent of exposed land surface in the Northern Hemisphere and almost all of Antarctica’s ice-free areas.

And it holds something that makes its stability a matter of global consequence. Roughly 70 percent of the organic carbon stored in permafrost soils sits in just the top three meters.

As the ground thaws, microbes can break down previously frozen organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and methane into the atmosphere.

The study draws on data from 156 monitoring sites gathered between 2000 and 2024. The average record length per site is 20 years.

The pattern is consistent and troubling. Active layer thickness increased significantly at 55 percent of Arctic sites and 38 percent of Antarctic sites.

In mountain permafrost regions over 90 percent of sites showed significant increases. Several sites saw the active layer double in thickness over the study period.

At two Norwegian mountain sites, Juvvasshøe and Snøheim, the active layer increased by 8.45 centimeters per year. At Swiss Alpine sites, increases of 9 to 36 centimeters per year were recorded.

In the Arctic lowlands, sites with thick organic layers, including peatlands and densely vegetated areas, showed smaller increases.

That happens because the insulating properties of organic matter buffer the soil against air temperature swings.

It is the bare, sandy, and bedrock sites that are changing fastest. Alaska’s North Slope recorded active layer increases at most sites between 0.3 and 0.6 centimeters per year.

Sites previously impacted by wildfires showed larger increases, because fire removes the insulating vegetation layer, exposing frozen ground directly to summer warmth.

“One of Earth’s most important indicators of climate change is permafrost as it directly reacts to rising temperatures,” said lead author Dmitry Streletskiy, a geography professor at George Washington University.

“The significance of this study lies in the fact that we’re not just looking at isolated hotspots anymore.”

The regression analysis behind the study found that summer warmth is the dominant driver of active layer change in Arctic lowland permafrost.

Total liquid precipitation has a smaller but significant additional effect: wet summers deepen the thaw more than dry ones. Cold seasons, by contrast, have minimal influence once site-specific characteristics are controlled for.

Mountain permafrost behaves differently and is harder to model. The sites are highly heterogeneous and the available climate data at high elevations isn’t fine-grained enough to fully explain everything.

Some mountain sites, particularly in the Swiss Alps, are changing at rates that dwarf anything seen in the Arctic lowlands.

The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau in China deserves particular attention.

Active layer changes on the Third Pole – so called because it holds more ice than anywhere on Earth outside the polar regions – averaged 3.2 centimeters per year from 2000 to 2024.

That’s roughly four times the Arctic average for continuous permafrost.

The plateau is warming faster than almost anywhere else on the planet, and it sits beneath infrastructure that crosses some of the most challenging terrain in the world.

Permafrost degradation is not an abstract threat.

Roads, railways, airports, pipelines, and buildings across northern Alaska, Canada, Siberia, and the Tibetan Plateau are built on the assumption that the ground beneath them stays frozen.

When it doesn’t, foundations shift, roads buckle, and infrastructure built over decades requires expensive repair or abandonment.

Communities in northern Alaska have already been forced to consider relocation as coastlines destabilize and the ground under their homes subsides.

“It’s hard to see that the first frost and the first snow are shifting by a day or two a decade,” Klene said.

“It’s hard to see that kind of change and really appreciate that it will have a big impact over time. But with these long-term monitoring sites, we can see that this gradual change is happening, and it’s going to affect the whole system.”

That system includes the carbon cycle. Continued warming threatens to shrink the extent of permafrost worldwide, with consequences that could unfold for generations.

What that means in terms of carbon release remains one of the largest uncertainties in climate science.

The study is published in the journal Communications: Earth and Environment.

#6434. Volcanoes lurk behind the scenes of human history

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Cold spells after eruptions may have spurred famine, disease, revolt and religious changes

German artist Caspar David Friedrich painted Two Men by the Sea in 1817, two years after Mount Tambora’s eruption in present-day Indonesia. Though far away, the blast spread volcanic aerosols around the world and may have inspired the image’s dark sky.

Caspar David Friedrich (Wikimedia Commons)

“The bright sun was extinguish’d … and the icy earth swung blind and blackening in the moonless air.” These words from Lord Byron’s 1816 poem Darkness evoke a hellish apocalypse. But Byron may have been inspired by the fallout of a real cataclysm — one that happened half a world away.

Mount Tambora, in present-day Indonesia, blew its top in 1815. More than 71,000 people in the vicinity died. And climate-cooling aerosols from the eruption ushered in extreme weather the following years in far-flung places. Cold weather in the summer of 1816, sometimes with frosts and snow, destroyed corn in New England, rice and buckwheat in China and wheat, oats and potatoes in Ireland. In some places, the rising cost of bread sparked protests and riots. The circumstances may have helped spread typhus. Some called 1816 “the year without a summer,” others “the year of the beggars.”

Like Tambora, volcanoes, and the cooling they cause, may be an underappreciated geologic force at times moving behind the scenes of human history.

“These climatic impacts of the Tambora eruption were recorded without any knowledge that this had anything to do with an eruption,” says Clive Oppenheimer, a volcanologist at the University of Cambridge.

While Tambora is the most well-studied eruption in history, others have also rattled the planet. Oppenheimer and his colleagues analyzed 38 large eruptions in the 2026 Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences. Their work pulled together studies linking the geologic events and their effects on climate with their potential societal fallout in food systems, the economy, unrest, culture and religion. The locations and exact timing of the eruptions that spurred some notable cold spurts aren’t known. But understanding how the events impacted the climate, environment and society can offer clues to the past, including how people coped with climate stress.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“Volcanic eruptions, they are kind of this like hammer blow to the climate system,” says Heli Huhtamaa, a climate and environmental historian at the University of Bern in Switzerland. Volcanoes may offer lessons about resilience for modern societies in a warming world, she says.

Volcanoes spew sulfur-containing gases. Over weeks, those gases react in the atmosphere to form particles that block sunlight. The particles can stay aloft for many months, riding jet streams to encircle the globe. Paintings from years after eruptions show bloodred sunsets or landscapes shrouded by hazy skies.

Because no two eruptions are exactly alike, it takes work to grasp each one’s impacts on weather and climate. “If we understand the climate response of one [eruption], that does not mean that we understand the climate response of another,” says Ulf Büntgen, a paleoclimatologist at the University of Cambridge.

A volcano’s explosivity impacts how high it shoots its gases and where they travel. Over time, those gases form particles that block sunlight. The particles can stay aloft for many months, riding jet streams to encircle the globe. In this computer model of a 1991 eruption, colors represent how high particles are in the atmosphere. Red is high and blue is closer to Earth’s surface.

Researchers find the traces of past eruptions in ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica. Scientists try to nail down the date on a sulfur-loaded ice core layer and compare it with tree ring data, a logbook of sorts for summer growing conditions since temperatures impact how trees lay down their wood each year. Scientists can pull together tree ring records from far-flung places and use statistics to work out annual temperatures in a hemisphere.

Cold spells sometimes jump out from tree ring records. For years when cool summers impeded the final stages of wood formation, a chemical method used to estimate temperatures turns wood layers blue. Büntgen and colleagues saw two blue rings around 1345. “And that is very rare. We never saw that two years in a row,” he says. The rings coincided with the timing of the Black Death’s spread in Europe, the team reported in 2025 in Communications Earth & Environment. The researchers traced the connections between chilly summers, poor grain harvests in the Mediterranean and shipping records showing how Italian city states imported flea-ridden grain from the Caucasus.

Oppenheimer, Büntgen and their colleagues broadened the detective work for their 2026 review. The team studied Northern Hemisphere temperature responses to the 38 largest eruptions between A.D. 1 and 1900. On average, each volcano caused about 0.5 degrees Celsius of cooling in the year after the eruption. Recovery to normal temperatures was slower for eruptions that occurred in times that were already colder on average, Büntgen says. In some periods, large or successive eruptions may lead to an elevated amounts of particles in the atmosphere for a long time. The team’s calculations show that high aerosol levels concur with some of the past two millennia’s coldest spells, such as the one preceding the Black Death.

Those cold snaps often had dire consequences. Out of 17 large-scale famines in Europe from 1300 to 1800, 11 followed major eruptions. In addition to faltering crops and famines, the most frequently societal responses described in studies collected by the review authors were disease outbreaks, political turmoil and migration.

The societal circumstances surrounding eruptions are as important as the amount of cooling, Huhtamaa says. She and her colleagues studied crop failures and farmstead desertion in three different volcanic eruptions that impacted Ostrobothnia, in what is now Finland. During the 17th century, Ostrobothnia experienced cooling from three sets of eruptions at different time periods.Although the latest eruption event, in 1695, was the coldest of all, peasants fared better than they had after eruptions earlier in the century, Huhtamaa and colleagues reported in 2022 in Climate of the Past. Though people still starved, only around 7 percent of peasants lost their farmland, compared with 20 percent in the other periods. This was because the crown provided tax relief, Huhtamaa says. This wasn’t humanitarian aid, as it was meant to preserve the tax base and prevent possibly decades of lost revenue.“When there is a climatic shock, it doesn’t matter if it’s 0.5 or 1.5 degrees cooler, because what really matters is the societal vulnerability,” Huhtamaa says.

Studies like Huhtamaa’s reveal how societies can tick on in spite of climate disasters. But historians haven’t always been keen to look to climate for clues to explain history. Human agency has often been considered the only reasonable explanation for human affairs, Huhtamaa says. “And climate explanations sounded lazy.”

Investigating societies’ preconditions and responses to the climate change caused by volcanoes could help people prepare for a now warming world. A recent report from the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, noted that not enough research had been done on responses, Huhtamaa says. Researchers could examine one place’s response to different events, as in Huhtamaa’s work on Ostrobothnia, or parse different locales’ responses to the same event. Meanwhile, greater use of insights from ecology, agronomy and economics, for instance, can help with this detective work that reveals how humans respond to climatic events beyond their control.

Those responses appear in religion, too. For instance, lines in the famed 10th century poem Vǫluspá seem to reference the 939 eruption of Iceland’s Eldgjá volcano, with high-flying flames and blackened sun beams. “It’s like an eyewitness description of a phenomenal lava flood,” Oppenheimer says. The poem foretells a fiery end to pagan gods, such as Odin, who are replaced by one god. Vǫluspá, which explained the eruption in terms of divine displeasure,may have contributed to the island’s Christianization around 1000, Oppenheimer and colleagues suggest.

Famines, riots, disease, migration. The widespread climatic effects of volcanoes across the ages may be subtler than the hellscapes conjured by poets but more tangible in the marks they’ve left on history.

M. Bauch and U. Büntgen. Climate-driven changes in Mediterranean grain trade mitigated famine but introduced the Black Death to medieval Europe. Communications Earth & Environment. 2025. doi: 10.1038/s43247-025-02964-0

F.C. Ljungqvist, A. Seim and D. Collet. Famines in medieval and early modern Europe—connecting climate and society. WIREs Climate Change. 2023. doi: 10.1002/wcc.859

#6432. Astronomers found the first star that would look green to the human eye

Astronomers have identified the first known green star, a white dwarf tinted by sodium from planetary debris, alongside unusually colored stars.

A dead star called WD J1330+6435 is the first known star that would appear green to human eyes. Astronomers at the University of Warwick identified it while working out the true colors of nearby white dwarfs.

The star’s green tint comes from sodium in rocky material it has pulled in from its own planetary system. That sodium absorbs the orange part of the star’s light.

The same work flagged WD J1011+2845, just 48 light-years from Earth, as what may be the reddest star ever recorded.

White dwarfs are the dense remnants left behind when Sun-like stars reach the end of their lives. None is close enough for its color to be seen directly.

The researchers worked from each star’s spectrum, the pattern produced when starlight is split apart by wavelength, and ran those spectra through a model of human color vision.

The sample covered the 151 white dwarfs within 20 parsecs, or about 65 light-years, of Earth.

The results correct a common misconception in astronomy that white dwarfs are typically blue. Hotter, bluer white dwarfs are brighter, so surveys based on brightness alone over-represent them.

Dr. Mark Hollands, a Warwick Prize Fellow in the Astronomy and Astrophysics Group at the university, led the work.

“Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like ‘perfect radiators,’ so their colour is set almost entirely by temperature,” Hollands said.

“It turns out these incredibly dense stars can produce colours nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me,” he added.

WD J1330+6435 has a temperature of roughly 7,200°F (4,000°C). It has accreted rocky material from its planetary system, enriching its atmosphere with calcium, lithium and sodium.

The atmospheres of these stars can reach roughly the density of water, millions of times denser than the Sun’s visible surface, the university explained.

Because this star’s atmosphere is so dense, the sodium absorbs light across a broad range of yellow, orange and red wavelengths. What remains gives the star a chartreuse green appearance in the team’s models.

As far as the researchers are aware, no other star, living or dead, has ever been credibly reported as green. That makes WD J1330+6435 the first known genuinely green star in the Galaxy.

“Imagine standing on a planet and looking up at a green star,” Hollands noted. “It feels like something out of science fiction.”

White dwarfs that pull in the remains of planets carry elements such as lithium, sodium and calcium in their atmospheres, where astronomers can read them in starlight.

In 2021, Hollands and his colleagues reported lithium in four cool, old white dwarfs with cooling ages of five to ten billion years. WD J1330+6435, catalogued then as SDSS J1330+6435, was one of the four.

That work placed the star about 87 parsecs, or roughly 280 light-years, from Earth.

The amounts of lithium and potassium compared with sodium and calcium “strongly suggest that all four white dwarfs have accreted fragments of planetary crusts,” the authors wrote in Nature Astronomy.

Another star in that set, WD J2317+1830, also showed extra infrared light, a sign that it was still drawing material from a surrounding disk of dust and rock.

In the new color study, white dwarfs enriched with fragments of shattered asteroids and comets tend toward yellow. Carbon-rich white dwarfs are typically pink or purple.

In WD J0902+2010, the convection zone has reached the core and lifted interior carbon to the surface. There, carbon forms C2 molecules that absorb blue, green and yellow light, so the star would look pink to the human eye.

WD J1011+2845 goes further. Carbon molecules distort its light so heavily that almost all of it is squeezed into wavelengths beyond 600 nanometers, producing a deep salmon-pink glow.

Cooler white dwarfs with mixed hydrogen and helium atmospheres often take on a cyan or pale blue tinge. That color comes from hydrogen molecules colliding with helium atoms in their ultra-dense atmospheres.

Sirius B, the nearest white dwarf to the Solar System, has a hot hydrogen atmosphere that gives it a bluish color in the models.

Of the 151 nearby white dwarfs, five showed unusual coloring: two yellow and three pink. That suggests roughly one in 30 white dwarfs in the Universe shines with an unusually colored light.

For the remaining 146 stars, the median color temperature was about 6,800 kelvin, roughly 11,800°F (6,530°C), which people perceive as white.

Professor Boris Gänsicke of the Department of Physics at Warwick co-authored the study.

“One in thirty might not sound like a huge fraction, but across the entire population of white dwarfs in the Universe, that is still a lot of oddly coloured stars out there,” Gänsicke said.

“Yet if we take the median across a representative population of white dwarfs, we found that the average white dwarf really is white,” he explained.

The study was published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments.

Writer Olivia Maule spoke with biologist James O'Hanlon about his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats." In it, he explores deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it amounts to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most deception in nature happens without much awareness from the creature involved. From a moth that has evolved to look like a hornet to orchid mantises that mimic flowers to lure in pollinators, deception is part of these animals' nature. But in his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), biologist James O'Hanlon turns to tactical deception aimed at manipulating what another animal believes — and whether we can consider this as lying.

Live Science spoke with O'Hanlon about his book, and why so many scientists are reluctant to say "yes, animals can lie."

Read an excerpt: Can animals lie? This sneaky bird might be proof.

James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. He is the author of "Eight-Legged Wonders: The Surprising Lives of Spiders" (2024).

Olivia Maule: The chapter opens with a moment from a talk you gave, where a woman at a senior citizens' club asked you a question about orchid mantises that left you stumped: "How does the mantis know to look like a flower?" Why did that moment stick with you enough to open the chapter with it?

James O'Hanlon: Because it was such a simple, straightforward question that I couldn't give a simple, straightforward answer to. At the time, I was thinking about what's going on in the brains of the animals I was looking at — does a camouflaged animal actually know it's camouflaged? Does an insect that looks like a leaf know what a leaf even is?

And it got me thinking: they don't need to. This stuff just sort of works because it works. That's a completely different type of deception to the other things dealt with in this chapter, which is: Do animals actually know that they can lie? Can they intentionally deceive, like we can?

OM: So would you say you have an answer to that question now? And if so, what would it be?

JO: If I had to answer, it would be yes. It looks like it. But scientists are paid to be pedantic, so it's always going to be a "yes, but" or a "possibly." There's a ton of behaviors that look like animals can lie, and they're really good at it, but with any type of science, we're never going to know for certain what's going on in their brains. It's a best-guess situation.

The Pink Orchid Mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) is an insect that uses camouflage as a form of protection in the wild.

OM: How would you help readers hold those two ideas at once — that this is genuine deception in an evolutionary sense, but not necessarily lying in the way we mean it as humans?

JO: When we talk about lying in humans, there's a value judgment attached. We're judging each other on whether we're good or bad people, doing right or wrong things. We kind of have to relax that judgment a bit when we're talking about other animals.

I guess it becomes an ethical question — we look at deception as being right or wrong, morally good or bad, and that's a very human-centric way of thinking. Ethics and morals are things we've developed to help us get along in our own societies. Who knows what's going on in animal societies?

There's an example in the book of golden snub-nosed monkeys that use deceptive alarm calls to scare off other members of their group and steal their food. After a while, those monkeys start to get ignored, and the group stops responding to their calls. So maybe there is some sort of animal-society rules and regulations keeping lying in check. Maybe. We'll see.

OM: I do want to ask about the chimpanzee study, in which chimpanzees intentionally misled competitive handlers to boxes without food, and compare it to the 2017 dog study, where dogs learned to mislead handlers much faster than the chimps did. What did that result do to the assumption that big brains equal better lying?

JO: There's always been this idea that lying is a really cognitively complex task — you need the brains not just to realize what's going on in the real world but to imagine a false possibility, and then to describe that false possibility as if it were real. We talked that up as something you need big brains to do, and there was also a bit of patting ourselves on the back for being such smart animals — maybe we lie a lot because we're such smart animals. But the more we learn about animals and what they're capable of, the more we realize they can do so much more than we thought was possible with the brains they've got.

OM: Does that suggest lying is less about raw intelligence and more a byproduct of needing to survive in a group?

JO: As far as all the examples of tactical deception in the book that look like they're intentional, they all, or mostly all, come from social animals. We don't seem to see it in solitary animals. That's a big sign that maybe it's something that's evolved because individuals can exploit it in a social setting. But it's still such early days, so it's hard to say for definite how different levels of sociality, and how bonded individuals are within groups, correlate with more deception.

OM: Could you elaborate on the distinction between deception and something like the camouflage you introduce in the book with the tiger's stripes?

JO: Compared to the intentional deception we've been talking about, things like camouflage still work regardless of whether the animal doing it is aware of it or not. The idea behind lying and tactical deception is that it only works because it's intentional — there's some sort of choice to do it.

Whether the animals are aware of that choice is another question. Think about the way we do it as humans — are we always aware of it? Whenever your friend asks whether you like their new haircut and you just go, "Yeah, it's great," you don't really think about the fact that you're probably lying. It's just part of our social norms. So it becomes a very blurry gray area very quickly.

OM: It sort of boils down to the choice of it all — whether they can choose to do it or not, which raises the question of whether it's conscious or unconscious.

JO: It's tricky, because as soon as you start talking about it being a conscious decision these animals make, you start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches, giggling at how evil they are for pretending to hide nuts. And you start to think, maybe this isn't the right exact way to think about lying and deception.

OM: The drongo — a bird renowned for its ability to deceive meerkats — doesn't just have one trick, it cycles through different alarm calls and borrows calls from other bird species. Does that put it in a different category of liar than squirrels or monkeys, or is it the same trick with a different toolbox?

JO: It could just be the same trick with a different toolbox. It's essentially doing the same thing as the golden snub-nosed monkeys we were talking about before. But birds are incredible singers and have very flexible call structures, and there are tons of birds that can mimic other birds. Maybe you just pair that ability with this deception adaptation, and it looks a bit different, but it's the same kind of trick.

OM: Do you think these behaviors are inherited, or just innate characteristics of the drongos themselves?

JO: I don't know — I'd be interested to find out. The evolutionary aspect would be that the ones who can do it get more food and are better able to survive and reproduce. Whether they learn it from their parents, it's entirely possible. We know from birds in general that they learn calls from their parents and their social groups, and there are even studies showing birds will start learning calls while they're still in the egg, listening to their parents' calls. So it's entirely possible they learn this trick socially, as far as I know.

Male cuttlefish can change their body pattern to trick competing suitors.

OM: In writing this book, what did you find is the best way to approach understanding animal behavior as it relates to human traits like lying or deception?

JO: I think there's still a little bit of baggage from old-school thinking, that you need bigger brains to be deceptive and tricky in this way, and there are still people who think it must be things like the higher apes and great apes that are capable of this stuff.

As soon as you start studying that in something like an invertebrate, it's really hard to get the idea out there — other scientists will come back and say, "No, that couldn't be possible, this must be some other type of behavior, or it just looks like tactical deception, but it's not." This happened with the researchers who did the work on cuttlefish that change one side of their body to look like a male and the other to look like a female — there was a lot of resistance to that idea, seemingly just because it was a cuttlefish, this little invertebrate, so it couldn't possibly be capable of such cleverness. But as far as the actual evidence goes, and what we can see, it's really no different from what we see in these big-brained mammals, so why not assume the same thing is going on?

A lot of it comes down to the culture and practice of science, and the people doing the science. We're supposed to be as objective as possible, but we're still humans, we're still animals. It takes a while for ideas to change.

OM: Is there a risk that this caution has become its own kind of bias, where we assume human specialness by default until proven otherwise?

JO: Yeah, definitely. It's important, as part of scientific practice, to be as objective as possible, and as a general rule, to not anthropomorphize. But at the same time, we're just animals too — we're just another one of the great apes. We share characteristics with lots of different animals, so it's not a huge stretch to think that what's going on in our brains is also going to be similar to what's going on in other animal brains.

It's just a question of when we apply that kind of thinking, and when it's useful or not. Something similar happened in the field of understanding pain in animals — scientists studying this were always trying not to anthropomorphize, not to assume animals experienced pain the way we did. Then, the more we understood it, it became quite clear that they probably did, and it almost became an ethical question to stop with the anti-anthropomorphizing and instead go, no, we know what pain feels like, we can say that.

We're never going to be able to see what's going on in their brains, but that doesn't excuse us from recognizing what's going on. So I think it became okay not to anthropomorphize but to recognize the similarities between humans and other animals, as opposed to always hinging on the differences between us.

OM: At the end of the chapter, you say that if you buy a scientist a few drinks, they'll eventually admit that animals can lie. I obviously can't buy you a drink over email, so I'll just ask you directly — do you think animals can lie?

JO: Yeah. I'll give a straightforward yes, because I can.

You need to get scientists out of their professional mindset, where they're trained to give the most correct answer that they can. And yes is a bit of a broad-stroke answer for a scientist when they're in professional mode, which is why you need to get them out of the lab and out to a bar or a cafe, and get them talking in human terms again.

OM: What would you say is your favorite example in the book — what are you most excited for readers to walk away with?

JO: I'll go with the cuttlefish example — the one where a male cuttlefish will put male color patterns on one side of its body and female patterns on the other, to trick other male cuttlefish. It might be my favorite because, as a young student, I worked on this particular species of cuttlefish. We were studying them, watching all of their crazy color-changing abilities, and just wondering what on earth they must be talking about, what was going on there. Then, years later, seeing the aforementioned research come out was this sort of lightbulb moment — that's what I was watching them do all along. I think that has a personal connection for me. I spent so much time looking at these creatures, being mesmerized by what they were doing, with no idea what was going on. So it was great to see scientists come in and figure it out, and answer those questions.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

#6429. After the dinosaurs died, the massive ‘D. rex’ fungus ruled the woods

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Dianjunus rex’s mushrooms can be half a meter tall and weigh over two kilograms

Dianjunus rex (shown) grows in southwestern China and its yellowish, pillar and tentacle-shaped fruiting bodies may be the largest known among sac fungi.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A pineapple-sized fungus has quietly grown undetected in the forests of southwestern China – until now. The massive mushroom may set a size record for a major branch of the fungal family tree.

The fungus — named Dianjunus rex — may also represent a previously unknown family, researchers report September 28 in Frontiers in Fungal Biology. Fittingly, D. rex is part of a lineage that split off from other fungi right after the dinosaurs — like T. rex — went extinct.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In 2024, researchers in China were conducting a survey of fungal diversity in a tropical rainforest in Yunnan Province when local farmers tipped them off to an unusual fungus in the area. The farmers included photos, says Indunil Chinthani Senanayake, a mycologist at the Kunming Institute of Botany in China. Some of the farmers who’d made the discovery took a bite of the mystery fungus, Senanayake says, and the tipster “wanted to confirm whether it was edible or not.”When Senanayake and her colleagues went to the location, they found strange, yellowish, tentacle-like and spatula-like mushrooms growing out of decaying tree roots. These were some kind of ascomycete, or “sac fungi”. Sac fungi like morels, truffles and molds make their spores in microscopic bladderlike receptacles, unlike the bowling pin-shaped reproductive structures in club fungi, the group that includes most culinary mushrooms.The mushrooms we see growing out of the ground are called fruiting bodies and make the spore-producing cells for the often hidden or subterranean fungus. Most sac fungi have relatively small fruiting bodies. But the mushrooms growing off these mysterious Yunnan fungi were enormous, with some reaching 50 centimeters tall. The team took samples of the fungi back to the lab for further study and found that they weighed up to 2.2 kilograms. By their estimates, these are the largest spore-making fruiting bodies among all sac fungi.

Torda Varga — a mycologist at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew in Richmond, England who was not involved with the research — notes that some truffle species are known to get close to the bulk. D. rex appears to be the largest sac fungal fruiting body he’s aware of. “What I find particularly remarkable is that a fungus with such an enormous fruiting body appears to have remained scientifically undocumented until now,” says Varga, though he adds his experience has mostly been within Europe.

The researchers compared samples of the fungus’s DNA with those from other fungi to determine its evolutionary relationships. They found that it was a relative of species like candlesnuff fungus and dead-man’s-fingers, which make fruiting bodies only a few centimeters tall, but that it was probably in its own, unique family. The team gave the new species the name Dianjunus rex, referencing both the Latin “rex” for “king” and the ancient Dian kingdom of the region.

The team’s genetic analysis suggests D. rex’s family first evolved in the aftermath of the mass extinction at the end of the Cretaceous Period that wiped out the dinosaurs, some 65 million years ago. “During the dark, cold, postimpact years after the mass extinction, fungi that decompose dead organic matter could keep functioning better than light-dependent photosynthesizers,” Senanayake says.

Varga wonders if searching databases for bits of DNA shed into the environment could help uncover other members of D. rex’s royal family in the absence of physical specimens.

“Some of these [genetic] sequences might belong to previously undocumented relatives of Dianjunus rex,” he says. Finding these hidden species could tell researchers more about the biology and evolutionary history of this king of the sac fungi.

#6427. Researchers found a crushed Celtic helmet in Poland that proves wealthy southerners traveled along the Amber Route

A crushed Celtic helmet lay in a charred pit at Łysa Góra, Poland, with four iron adzes, a scythe and nearly 350 metal finds from the site.

Łysa Góra is a glacial sand dune between the Orzyc River and one of its oxbow lakes, near the village of Bagienice in northern Mazovia, Poland.

Inside its fortifications, archaeologists found a pit filled with charred remains that held a crushed bronze helmet, four iron adzes and an iron scythe.

The helmet is a Berru-type helmet of La Tène (Celtic) origin. Five authors, Kaczyński, Maciałowicz, Borkowski, Sobczak and Aniszewski, described the find in Antiquity on October 14, 2026.

They propose that people from the Celtic south may have been on the dune themselves. The idea has not been tested yet.

The name means Bald Hill. From the sixth to the fourth century BC, members of the West Balt Barrow Culture lived on the dune.

According to the paper, these communities built fortified sites, lived off rivers and lakes, and buried their dead together in urns.

Archaeologists logged the site in 1957 and dug it in short bursts between 1971 and 1992. Those digs recovered several La Tène imports. No full analysis was ever published, so the paper says the site’s importance went unnoticed.

In 2024 the State Archaeological Museum in Warsaw and the Faculty of Archaeology at the University of Warsaw resumed the work. Kaczyński, Borkowski, Sobczak and Aniszewski work at the museum. Maciałowicz is at the university.

The pit lay within the fortifications. The authors found the helmet crushed and fragmented, lying alongside several iron tools, including adzes and a scythe. They read the pit as one of the traces of ritual activity at the site.

The paper’s plan view of the pit, based on a photograph by Kaczyński, numbers the helmet, the scythe and four adzes marked 3a to 3d. The helmet closely parallels finds from Dürrnberg in Austria.

Two kinds of timber-and-earth defenses guarded the dune around the middle of the first millennium BC. In the south, a rampart with a palisade and an outer ditch was cut partly into the natural sediment. In the north, the team found a fortification built entirely of timber.

A second ritual zone lay in the marsh at the foot of the dune’s southwestern slope. Two deposits there held bronze ring ornaments and earrings with glass beads.

One deposit included a spiral armlet made of bronze ribbon and decorated with incised lines. The team found traces of repair on one end, where two rivets once sat and left circular holes. B. Karch drew a reconstruction of the armlet.

Nearly 350 metal objects have come out of the ground so far, among them ornaments, weapons and evidence of bronze working. Pottery, animal bones, cereal grains, seeds of cultivated plants and charred wood turned up as well.

Many of the bronze ornaments were broken into pieces and packed into tight bundles. The authors think they were prepared for remelting, and excavators had already recorded ceramic casting crucibles in the 1970s.

The site also yielded amber beads and an amber ring that was never finished. The authors say these finds suggest the people on the dune took part in long-distance amber exchange with regions south of the Carpathian Mountains.

Amber was prized in northern Europe long before: in Karelia, a 5,400-year-old grave held 140 amber ornaments.

The team also looked at the carbonized wood left in the socket of one iron adze. Under the microscope, a cross-section showed pores arranged in rings and both very wide and narrow wood rays, which are features of oak.

The dune has also given up 31 mostly broken Early La Tène brooches and ring ornaments, dated to around the middle of the fourth century BC.

According to the paper, helmets in the Early La Tène world symbolised “high social status and affiliation with the warrior elite.”

The authors consider that concept likely alien to the local societies, which were presumably without centralized leaders.

For that reason they argue the helmet may reflect “the physical presence of southern groups, including members of their elite.”

Trade from hand to hand is the alternative, since smaller La Tène ornaments did reach distant parts of Central and Eastern Europe.

The authors find that explanation less convincing, because the helmet was a prestige object and no comparable helmets are known outside the La Tène zone in the fourth century BC.

The dune lies close to the amber-rich Kurpie region, and the paper ties it to routes that led to the Sambian Peninsula on the Baltic coast.

Most Celtic sites of that age lie well to the south and west. Road surveyors in the Czech Republic found a lost Celtic town full of gold, silver and amber, and in central France, archaeologists dug up 2,300-year-old Celtic swords adorned with gems and symbols.

The authors say their hypothesis “will require verification through further research.” The ore source of the helmet’s metal is not yet known.

Lead isotope analyses are planned, and the results will be compared with similar objects from Bohemia, where a 2021 study of the Duchcov hoard examined Celtic movements in the fourth century BC.

The northern and southern defensive lines may or may not have stood at the same time. The team plans electrical resistivity tomography and magnetic surveys to check.

Money for the project came from the museum, the Chorzele commune authorities and the Faculty of Archaeology. The lead isotope results are still to come. Until then the helmet only points south, and nobody can say who put it in the pit.

The full study was published in the journal Antiquity.

#6426. What Happens If Your Passport Expires While You're Abroad?

Most countries don't allow international travelers to enter their territory unless they have at least six months left before their passport expires. That might sound like an unnecessary ask for a week-long vacation, but the rule is in place for good reason.

That's because if you do find yourself in a scenario when your passport expires while you're abroad—say due to an unexpected medical issue or trip delay, for example—you could be facing a major bureaucratic headache.

However, although it might feel like a crisis, having your passport lapse while traveling is not the end of the world. There are procedures that travelers can follow to obtain a renewed document and get their trip back on track. Here’s a look at what happens if your passport expires while you’re abroad.

Many countries do not allow international tourists to visit unless they have a certain amount of validity left on their passport. A common rule of thumb that many nations observe is the six month rule: there must be at least six months before your passport expires in order to enter the country.

In some countries, including many popular destinations in the EU, your passport is required to be valid for an additional three months after your intended departure date. Before you board an international flight, airlines will verify your passport expiration and usually will not let you board the plane if your passport doesn’t meet the validity requirements. It's important to note that some airlines and cruise lines might have their own passport validity policies that differ from the country's official requirements, so be sure to check both.

Sometimes, it’s possible to enter a different country and stay past your passport’s expiration date. If that's the case, the protocol you’ll need to follow is similar to when a passport is lost or stolen abroad.

First, you’ll need to contact the nearest US embassy or consulate for assistance. If you’re not sure where the nearest embassy or consulate might be, you can use the search tool on the State Department’s website. You’ll need to then visit the embassy or consulate location in person in order to have them issue you a new passport. Keep in mind this could mean you need to travel to a different city within the country you’re visiting.

When you arrive, you’ll essentially need to apply for a new passport. That means you’ll need to bring:

“Even if you cannot present all these documents, consular staff will do their best to help you get a new passport quickly,” the State Department’s site says.

US citizens abroad who have urgent travel plans are usually issued an emergency passport, which is valid for up to one year. However, it’s also possible to get a full-validity passport that doesn’t expire for 10 years. It will depend on the specifics of your situation.

Replacement passports are usually issued by the next business day, according to the State Department.

If you’re a US citizen living overseas for an extended period of time, you might qualify for routine passport renewal by mail through the nearest US embassy or consulate. Processing times for renewal by mail are usually about four to six weeks, not including shipping time. Visit the website of the local embassy or consulate in your area and follow their instructions for passport renewal.

#6424. A ranching couple took photos of rock spires carved from ancient ash and helped create Chiricahua National Park

A 27-million-year-old eruption left a caldera 12 miles wide in Arizona. Its rock spires, protected since 1924, are now Chiricahua National Park.

Around 1900, a teenager named Ed Riggs climbed Sugarloaf Mountain, in what is now Chiricahua National Park in southeastern Arizona. He was hiking with Ben Erickson, aged nine, the brother of the woman he would later marry. From the top they looked down on a canyon full of rock pinnacles.

Ed only got to explore it after World War I, when he came home from the Army. The pinnacles are what is left of ash from a volcano that erupted about 27 million years ago.

On October 20, 2026, President Donald J. Trump signed the Chiricahua National Park Act. It turned the monument that Ed and his wife Lillian pushed for into a national park.

NASA published a Landsat 9 image of it on October 28, but the change is to the name and status, not to the trails or the scenic drive.

Ed came from a ranching family in the Sulphur Springs Valley. He served in the war as an aerial photographer. The National Park Service page on Ed Riggs quotes him calling the canyon “some of the most wonderful country.”

Lillian was the daughter of Swedish homesteaders Neil and Emma Erickson. She taught school until about 1918. That year she and her sister Hildegard named the family place Faraway Ranch, the NPS profile of Lillian Erickson Riggs says.

In the summer of 1921 Lillian was in Los Angeles, trying to start a writing career. Ed helped out at the ranch and wrote to her about a big house in the upper garden “to take care of the tourist trade.” They married on February 26, 1923.

The couple cut trails into the rocks and took photographs. Some of the pictures went to the county fair in Douglas, where a Dr. J.J.P. Armstrong saw them and came out to look for himself.

He and Ed explored the side canyons together. The park service says they were probably among the first non-Indigenous people to see Natural Bridge and Echo Canyon.

In August 1923, Arizona Governor George W.P. Hunt rode out on horseback in pouring rain from Faraway Ranch into the Chiricahua National Forest. Ed wrote afterward that the party came back “a wet bunch I can tell you but well pleased with what they had seen.”

Hunt backed a monument on the Forest Service land. President Calvin Coolidge established Chiricahua National Monument on April 18, 1924. Ed and Lillian then advertised Faraway Ranch as the closest place to stay.

In the Depression, Ed took a job with the Civilian Conservation Corps as a local trail foreman, at $1,800 a year. Lillian kept running the cattle and the guests.

Ed built the Sugarloaf Trail, with a tunnel blasted through rock. Then he asked Frank Pinkley, superintendent of Southwestern National Monuments, to let him route a trail down to Echo Park.

Pinkley agreed, but told him that if he failed he should “just hand in your resignation.” The Echo Canyon Trail needed eleven switchbacks in one quarter-mile.

In 1934 the monument passed to the National Park Service. More than 6,000 people in about 1,000 cars came to the dedication at Massai Point, according to the NPS history of Massai Point.

A 1997 U.S. Geological Survey guide dates the eruption to 26.9 million years ago. Its authors were John S. Pallister and Edward A. du Bray of the USGS and Douglas B. Hall of the University of Arizona.

According to the guide, magma pooled a few miles down, just south of today’s park. The rock on top broke and gas escaped. The foaming magma swelled up to 50 times its volume in a series of explosions.

More than 100 cubic miles (over 400 cubic kilometers) of magma came out. Hot ash and pumice covered at least 1,200 square miles (3,100 square kilometers).

Mount St. Helens put out about a tenth of a cubic mile in 1980. The empty chamber’s roof caved in and left the Turkey Creek caldera, 12 miles (19 kilometers) wide and at least 5,000 feet (1,500 meters) deep.

Ash of a similar age elsewhere in the West kept other records. At John Day Fossil Beds in Oregon, 29-million-year-old ash holds paw tracks left by a cat with retractable claws.

Calderas can matter for other reasons too, and the McDermitt caldera on the Nevada-Oregon border may hold a large lithium deposit.

In the park area the ash filled an old valley at least 1,600 feet (490 meters) deep. It was hot enough to weld into solid rock. The layer is known as the Rhyolite Canyon Tuff, named for the canyon where it is best exposed.

The tuff cracked along vertical joints as it cooled. Water got in, froze and thawed, and pried the blocks apart, the NPS Geodiversity Atlas says.

What stayed standing became pinnacles, columns and balanced rocks. Mind you, the USGS guide thinks the columns we see today are less than three million years old, a fraction of the tuff’s age.

NASA’s satellite singles out Big Balanced Rock, where a large boulder sits perched on top. Civilian Conservation Corps crews named many of the formations in the 1930s, the park service says. The Chiricahua Apache, whose homeland this is, already called the area the Land of the Standing-Up Rocks.

The Operational Land Imager on Landsat 9 took the NASA picture on July 2, 2026. Lauren Dauphin of the NASA Earth Observatory processed it. The worn tuff looks gray, and Rhyolite Canyon and Bonita Canyon show up as green lines of trees.

The Chiricahua Mountains are one of the sky islands of southern Arizona, ranges that stand alone above the desert. Sky islands in other places have their own residents, like the four new chameleons described from Mozambique’s sky islands.

NASA’s write-up, by Adam Voiland, says four regions meet in the park, from the Sonoran Desert to the Sierra Madre. About 1,000 plant species grow there, from agaves and prickly pear to pine, fir and oak.

The Interior Department release describes a park of about 12,000 acres. Nowhere does it give figures for staff, money or expected visitors.

Jessica Bowron, who is exercising the authority of the National Park Service director, said that while the name is changing, the agency’s commitment stays the same.

From orbit, single spires are too small to pick out, NASA notes, so the gray patch in the image is the tuff as a whole.

Lillian Riggs went blind in 1942 and closed the guest ranch in 1970. She sold most of the Stafford land and cabin to the park service in 1968 and the rest of the homestead in 1974. She died in 1977, after moving to a nursing home in Willcox.

Ed died in 1950. His gravestone says he engineered the Echo Trail, and it adds, “He wished this to be his monument.” The trail still winds through the spires he first saw from Sugarloaf as a boy.

The information was obtained from NASA Earth Observatory.

In his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats," biologist James O'Hanlon surveys deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it adds up to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most trickery in nature happens without a shred of awareness behind it. An orchid mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) doesn't know it looks like a flower, and a moth with eyespots on its wings has no concept of the predator it's startling. These are adaptations shaped by natural selection over countless generations, not conscious choices. But a smaller set of animal behaviors look like something else entirely — deliberate tactical, and aimed at manipulating another individual's beliefs, the same way human lies do.

Figuring out which is which turns out to be one of the trickiest questions in animal behavior research, James O'Hanlon, zoologist and science communicator, told Live Science.

In this excerpt from his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), O'Hanlon explores camouflage, mimicry and misdirection throughout the natural world, building toward the book's central question: Can animals tell lies?

In it, O'Hanlon examines one of the strongest candidates for an animal that deliberately lies: the fork-tailed drongo (Dicrurus adsimilis), a small African bird whose ever-changing repertoire of false alarm calls has made it a favorite subject for scientists studying tactical deception.

James O'Hanlon interview: 'You start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches': A biologist on whether animals can lie

This is a Live Science Pro article that we're publishing for free to all our readers. If you'd like more exclusive book excerpts, as well as news analysis, scientist interviews and in-depth features, please consider subscribing.

Fork-tailed drongos are remarkable vocal mimics and can do an uncanny impression of a meerkat alarm call. The meerkats respond to it just as they would one of their own and scamper to safety. Meanwhile the drongo flies in once more to steal the meerkats' abandoned food.

They don't stop there; drongos mimic a whole range of other animals' signals, mimicking various avian neighbors like the caped glossy starling or the pied babbler. Those ever-watchful meerkats fall for the ruse once more, leaving their meals behind. Researchers have identified over fifty unique deceptive vocalizations in the drongo's arsenal.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By constantly rotating their "cry-wolf" tactics, these birds ensure their victims don't grow wise to the deception, allowing the theft to continue unabated. Yet, their cleverness isn't reserved solely for exploited meerkats.

This remarkable talent for mimicry extends to other creatures as well. Pied babblers and sociable weavers, who both forage in groups upon the earth, frequently find themselves bamboozled into fleeing their food by these false warnings. Had the legendary boy who cried wolf possessed such adaptive ingenuity, he might have successfully maintained his trickery.

It would, however, have resulted in a peculiar fable with an entirely different, perhaps darker, moral lesson.

It's early days in our understanding of whether animals can tell lies. Social group-living animals are likely candidates for finding animal tricksters in the wild, and we have only scratched the surface of what kinds of trickery goes on in these societies. Time will tell whether similar forms of deception are happening in the subsonic songs of whales and dolphins, the chemical mists of ants and termites, or the barks and howls of wild dogs.

Meerkats are tricked by fork-tailed drongos mimicking the alarm calls, so the birds can swoop in and steal their food.

Despite the growing list of evidence, scientists are still hesitant to conclude definitively that animals can intentionally deceive another, in a similar way to humans. This might have more to do with the professional conduct of scientists than it has to do with the reality of what goes on in animal societies.

Firstly, one of the most important rules in studying animal behaviour is to not anthropomorphise animals. In other words, don't project human-like qualities or emotions onto other species. Scientists must be completely objective and not assume that other animals think, behave or make decisions for the same reasons we do.

Since lying has always been perceived as a human behaviour, scientists are incredibly hesitant to conclude that it could be happening in other animals.

The second reason is that scientists are trained to never definitively conclude anything. There is an idea in science that you can disprove things, but never really prove things. This is why you will find scientific writing littered with phrases like "the evidence suggests," "it's probable that," or — my personal favourite — "the most parsimonious explanation is," and so on and so forth.

A professional scientist will often give a direct "No" answer but rarely a direct "Yes." It's like squeezing blood from a stone. But this is a good thing. What often sounds like indecisiveness or a lack of certainty is actually just good professional practice. It's part of a scientist's job description — to consider all possible explanations for the observations they have made and examine every possibility on its own merits.

Then the conclusions that are drawn come down to which of these possibilities is most likely. In a universe of infinite possibilities and scales of enquiry, it would take an impossible amount of overwhelming data for scientists to exclude all possibilities but one.
