To understand how these creatures swindle their way to survival, Liars, Cheats, and Copycats reveals the science behind camouflage, mimicry, and masquerade. Taking readers on a journey from tropical rainforests to the darkness of deep ocean trenches, James O’Hanlon explores how animals and plants use deception to avoid predators, lure in prey, and even reproduce.

James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. He is the author of "Eight-Legged Wonders: The Surprising Lives of Spiders" (2024).

#6421. Believing you’ll be remembered after death is linked to better mental health

Believing you'll be remembered after death is linked to better mental health and fewer addictive behaviors, according to new research.

When they think about death, some people picture heaven or another life after this one. Others simply hope to be remembered by family and friends, or through the work they leave behind.

In new research on adults living through a war, only that second hope was linked to better mental health.

Those who expected to live on in other people’s memories reported less depression, anxiety and trouble sleeping, while belief in an afterlife showed no link to those problems.

The associations were generally modest, but they appeared across all the mental health and addictive behavior measures examined.

Psychologists Uri Lifshin and Mario Mikulincer led the work at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Both are part of the university’s Israel Center for Addiction and Mental Health.

Lifshin’s team surveyed 2,912 Jewish adults in Israel in February 2025, during the country’s war with Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.

Everyone answered once, so the survey can show which feelings tend to appear together but not which one comes first.

“The feeling that our lives matter and will continue to matter to other people may be an important part of how we cope with uncertainty and the knowledge of our own mortality,” the researchers wrote.

In his 1973 book The Denial of Death, Ernest Becker wrote that much of human behavior is driven by a need to keep the terror of death out of mind. His ideas grew into terror management theory.

The theory holds that people manage that fear by feeling valued, loved and part of something that will continue after they’re gone.

In tests of the theory, reminders of death have made people more likely to choose alcohol over a nonalcoholic drink.

Similar reminders have raised cravings for tobacco and cannabis. They can also increase the urge to gamble in people who already have a gambling problem.

A 2024 review that pooled 104 studies found a moderate link between fear of death and a range of mental health symptoms.

Psychologists have a name for the opposite feeling, the sense that some part of a person will carry on through other people, a legacy or a group. They call it symbolic immortality.

In an earlier study, Lifshin and colleagues linked that feeling to higher self-esteem. Apart from depression, though, no study had tested whether it was linked to fewer mental health problems or addictive behaviors.

Lifshin’s team collected the answers online, in Hebrew, as the fifth round of a larger national study of mental health and addiction. Volunteers were 18 to 70 years old.

The team built the sample to match Jewish adults in Israel by gender, age, how religious they were and where they lived. Of 10,869 people invited, 4,731 agreed to take part.

The team then dropped incomplete, careless and duplicate answers, along with anyone beyond the sample’s quotas, leaving 2,912.

At the center of it all was a single question. “Do you think that you will be remembered by other people after you die (e.g., through your accomplishments or legacy)?”

Answers ran from 1, for certainly not, to 7, for certainly yes. Most people chose answers toward the yes end of the scale, and the average was 4.55.

Volunteers were also asked whether they believed in an afterlife, such as heaven or reincarnation.

Standard questionnaires covered depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, sleep and emotional control, plus nine kinds of addictive behavior, from problem drinking to social media.

A correlation measures how closely two things are related. Values range from -1 to 1, with zero indicating no linear relationship.

The team adjusted its figures for other differences between people, such as gender, education, politics, military service, relationships, parenthood and afterlife belief.

After that, the hope of being remembered was most closely tied to feeling that life has meaning, at 0.45.

Self-esteem and feeling supported by others each came in at 0.35.

People who expected to be remembered also reported fewer mental health problems. The correlations had magnitudes of 0.27 for trouble managing emotions and 0.26 for depression.

Links of that size reflect a tendency across thousands of people, not a rule for any one person.

Parents, and people in long-term relationships, were slightly more likely to expect to be remembered. Age made no difference.

People who expected to be remembered reported fewer signs of all nine problem habits the survey covered.

The associations were weakest for gambling (0.07) and alcohol (0.08). Internet addiction showed the strongest association (0.18), followed closely by pornography and social media.

“Our findings suggest that feeling connected to others, having meaning in life and believing that something of us will remain may go hand in hand with better mental health and fewer problematic addictive behaviors,” the researchers wrote.

The authors offered one possible reason for the overlap. Other animals can show addictive behaviors, they wrote, but don’t normally develop problem substance use in the wild.

Perhaps, they suggested, that’s because addictions are partly tied to problems only humans face, such as knowing they will die.

The two beliefs did overlap. People who expected to be remembered were also somewhat more likely to believe in an afterlife, with a link of 0.37.

Belief in an afterlife, though, was tied mostly to religion. It was most closely linked to belief in God or a higher power, at 0.79.

Afterlife belief showed no significant association with depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, sleep problems or emotional control.

It was associated with slightly less problem drinking, cannabis use, pornography use and compulsive sexual behavior, and slightly more problem internet use.

Even with afterlife belief taken into account, the hope of being remembered kept its links. The study doesn’t show that this hope adds anything beyond self-esteem, meaning or close relationships, though.

The authors describe it instead as a broad marker tied to several of those supports.

Which comes first is the biggest open question. Feeling remembered could help protect mental health, but depression or addiction could also weaken a person’s sense that their life will matter, and each may affect the other.

The hope of being remembered was also measured with one question. The authors wrote that a single item may be less accurate and less stable than a full set.

Timing may matter too. The authors suggested that wartime may have made the links stronger than they would be in peacetime or in other countries.

During a war, they wrote, threat, national identity and trauma are likely to be on many people’s minds.

Everyone in the survey came from the general public rather than from people being treated for addiction or mental illness.

Whether a stronger sense of legacy can actually ease depression or addiction is still unknown.

Answering that will take experiments and long-term studies that follow the same people over time, the authors wrote, along with fuller measures of legacy and repeat surveys in other countries.

The full study was published in the International Journal of Mental Health and Addiction.

#6420. Roller coaster safety is a matter of science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Extreme ride guidelines don't all reflect the latest findings

Current industry guidelines for roller coaster design don’t account for all the forces riders face on extreme coasters from previous decades. Hershey Park’s Fahrenheit, pictured here, briefly held the world record for steepness when it opened in 2008.

The first roller coaster in the United States to loop upside down tucked riders by twos into bench seats, secured them with a single seat belt and subjected them to an estimated 7.5 times the force of gravity (some say it was closer to 12 g). The Flip Flap Railway opened in New York City’s Sea Lion Park in 1895, where the roller coaster reportedly strained backs, wrenched necks and dazzled spectators until the park closed in 1902.

Now, roller coaster safety is in the news again. In September, three lawsuits were filed against Six Flags and ride manufacturer S&S Global, alleging that riders sustained “catastrophic” brain injuries on the roller coaster X2 at California’s Magic Mountain theme park. These are just the most recent cases related to the ride, filed after a CNN investigation found dozens of injuries on X2 leading to hospitalization, disability and death. On September 29, Six Flags announced X2 would shut down permanently even though it said the ride “consistently passed a multitude of safety tests.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Weeks later, the company said it would temporarily close another nine coasters across the United States and Canada after a man fell from his seat on the roller coaster Goliath and died at Six Flags Over Georgia. Six Flags announced Oct. 24 that it would add seat belts to Goliath and other coasters, and a spokesperson told Science News that the company is “committed to rigorous ride inspection, maintenance and safety procedures.” But the incidents and closures are prompting new questions about coaster design and safety — particularly when they are operating correctly — and whether guidelines overlook crucial factors.

Roller coasters are not regulated at the federal level in the United States; each state has its own approach to their management. But an international technical group comprising over 1,000 industry professionals, the ASTM Committee F24 on Amusement Rides and Devices, publishes recommendations that are considered industry standards.

The first ASTM standards for roller coaster design were released in 1982. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission had been stripped of authority to regulate fixed-site amusement rides the year before. In the wake of this newfound freedom, it was a “roller coaster arms race,” says Brian Avery, an event and tourism management researcher at the University of Florida in Gainesville who studies risk and amusement ride safety protocols. The period was characterized by attempts to “build it taller, faster, longer.”

When X2, originally called X, opened in 2002, it was the world’s first fourth-dimension coaster. It catapulted people 60 meters high, traveling 122 kilometers per hour while its seats rotated independently on their own tracks. In the 24 years since, only 20 or so other fourth-dimension coasters have been built, and several have closed.

As roller coasters grew more extreme, injuries increased and were more publicized, sparking calls for further research and regulation.

Generally, roller coasters are quite safe. Out of 1.7 billion annual amusement park rides across North America, just 652 roller coaster injuries were reported in 2024 by parks choosing to share data. Studies suggest that riding a roller coaster is very unlikely to cause a brain injury, although most research on roller coaster brain impacts is about a decade or more old.

In 2002, a study used reported g forces from three roller coasters in a mathematical model to determine that their acceleration levels were below those predicted to cause head injuries. A 2017 study found brain effects on three roller coasters that were low on average, but “comparable with mild sports impacts,” like those sustained by heading a soccer ball, at their peak.

“The limiting of g forces alone might be an insufficient design criterion for roller coaster rides,” wrote the authors of the 2017 study.

In 2020, David Eager, a biomechanical engineer at the University of Technology Sydney, coauthored a paper on under-acknowledged forces affecting roller coaster safety, including jerk (the rate at which acceleration changes), snap (the rate at which jerk changes) and vibration.

“Roller coaster passengers need time to sense acceleration changes and adjust their muscle tension or suffer conditions such as whiplash,” Eager wrote.

The ASTM standards are exacting in some ways. Research conducted during the space race led to a 6g recommended limit on roller coaster acceleration exposure. However, ASTM doesn’t make recommendations about other types of motion on a roller coaster that might impact the neck, head and brain. It disregards forces lasting less than 200 milliseconds, no matter how intense.

But each tiny imperfection and variation in the circumference of the track — especially plentiful in coasters built before modern manufacturing techniques — causes a jolt, says Jurnan Schilder, a mechanical engineer and researcher who teaches roller coaster design at the University of Twente in Enschede, the Netherlands. He studies ways to create smoother roller coaster rides.

Schilder’s research suggests that at each track imperfection, “theoretically, you experience infinite jerk.” On a fourth-dimension coaster, he says, two sets of tracks mean double the variations. “Not only is the train sometimes shaking, but also the tilting mechanism is shaking.”

Research beyond rides also suggests intense and repeated rattling, jostling and vibration could meaningfully impact the brain. The U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration recommends limiting the duration and intensity of whole-body vibration. In April, the Virginia Tech Helmet Lab, which studies the science of brain injuries, published an article suggesting some concussions experienced by baseball players may result from just milliseconds of vibration.

North Carolina high school student Kayleigh Bonner’s quest to understand her father’s death exposed similar risks. After her father, a retired U.S. Coast Guard surfman who captained boats through rough waves for 21 years, experienced symptoms of a brain injury and died by suicide, Kayleigh surveyed 77 other elite surfmen for a senior capstone project. She found that 89 percent of those she spoke to had some symptoms of brain injury likely caused by the intense, rapidly changing forces traveling through their bodies as their boats were tossed by waves. Her quest to understand her father’s death was written about in July in the New York Times, and soon after acknowledged by the Coast Guard.

Of course, professional baseball players and Coast Guard surfmen have more significant and prolonged exposure to these forces than occasional roller coasters riders. But as researchers discover more about how different kinds of motion impact the brain, safety standards seem to lag behind. Minimizing jerk and snap is “an important consideration,” Eager says.

The mounting roller coaster-related headlines have renewed scrutiny of both the existing coaster safety standards and the lack of federal regulation. U.S. Rep. André Carson, a Democrat from Indiana, has called to pass a bill he first introduced in 2025 that would create federal oversight of amusement rides. Since 1999, Democratic U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts has repeatedly introduced legislation to regulate fixed rides, but the bills have consistently stalled.

The amusement industry has long opposed federal oversight. In 2010, Avery coauthored a paper asserting that “the industry needs to find a collective voice and establish consistent self‐regulating policies in order to curb the incidents rates and avoid federal regulation.”

But Schilder says: “It makes you wonder: Are the current safety standards sufficient?”

For modern rides, Schilder says he believes they are. Modern manufacturing techniques mean roller coasters designed and built today are much smoother than predecessors. ASTM standards that filter out brief but intense forces, like vibration and jerk, are likely fine for rides that don’t vibrate and jerk very much. But at many parks, the ambitious and intense rides born of the roller coaster arms race are still in place.

Riders are “flirting, if you would, with danger when they experience rides and devices. They know that they’re more likely than not going to be safe,” Avery says. The point is to be “right on the cusp.”

#6419. Copenhagen is Opening a Stunning New Bathhouse Along Its Harbor This December—And It's Shockingly Affordable

Copenhagen is a swimmer’s city. "The cure for anything is salt water: sweat, tears, or the sea," Danish author Karen Blixen, who lived up the coast from Copenhagen, famously wrote in 1934. Locals and visitors alike have taken her words to heart ever since.

In the early 2000s, floating swimming pools were introduced to the Danish capital's harbor after the city's shipbuilding industry collapsed. These pools turned an unused space into a playground for swimmers, divers, water polo enthusiasts, and boaters, especially on hot summer days. In recent years, cold plunging has also risen in popularity as a way to help with mental and physical health—nowadays, you can expect winter swimming clubs with sauna access along the harbor to have lengthy waiting lists.

The new bathing house was designed by the Japanese architectural firm Kengo Kuma Associates and has been 8 years in the making.

The next time you visit Copenhagen, there's even more reason to pack a swimsuit. The city’s historic waterfront welcomes a long-awaited new addition on Saturday, December 5: a public swimming pool set to become a new landmark along the city's harbor.

Designed by the Japanese architectural firm Kengo Kuma Associates, Kai is the new 62,500 square-foot bathing house that has been eight years in the making. It promises ten pools in total, including an open-air rooftop pool and a heated onsen overlooking Copenhagen Harbor. Delayed due to the pandemic and its knock-on effects, the pool was originally slated to open in 2021 and now joins the list of architecturally distinct buildings lining Copenhagen Harbor, including the modern Opera House and the Royal Danish Playhouse.

This designer swimming experience comes with a surprisingly affordable price tag.

Pools will be spread across the several levels of the minimalist interior, with a 82-foot pool on the ground floor. The building also offers year-round access to the harbor with designated swimming and dipping zones in and around a timber boardwalk. While the harbor itself can get pretty chilly in winter, the outdoor first-floor pools benefit from a sustainable vertical ground-source heat pump system providing year-round heating.

This designer swimming experience comes with a surprisingly affordable price tag for visitors. Tickets are expected to be in line with other local city-run swimming pools—known as "water culture houses"—where entry is typically under 100kr (about $10). Capacity overall is capped at 380 swimmers. The 989 million DKK ($150 million) project was funded by the City of Copenhagen and Nordea Fonden.

Kai will open on Paper Island on December 5, 2026.

Swimmers all over the city are delighted with the news, including Copenhagen’s Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling. “I’m really excited about the opening of the Water Culture House,” she said. “Copenhagen needs more swimming facilities, so it’s incredibly important that we are now getting new pools for adults, as well as paddling pools for children. I hope it will become the city’s new gathering point for water-loving Copenhageners and visitors alike.”

The original idea for a new pool in the heart of the city came directly from Copenhageners. Surveys had pinpointed a desire for a new, central public swimming pool and the location on Paper Island could not be better. Once the site of a beloved food market, the area had stood empty for years, before being redeveloped to play home to restaurants, cafes and hospitality businesses. Directly across the harbor from the central tourist hub of Nyhavn and accessed by pedestrian and cycle bridge, the new pool brings renewed focus to the area, that links the old town with the rapidly gentrifying former military area of Holmen and the former shipbuilding area of Refshaleøen.

Copenhagen's harbor is the heart of the city's year-round swimming culture.

If you are keen to explore Copenhagen’s swimming cultures, the harbor is the place to start—but brace yourself for chilly waters. At Sandkaj in Nordhavn in the north of the city, a demarcated swim zone invites bathers directly into the deep harbor for lane swimming. It’s a great place for a chat with a fellow winter swimmer; changing room access is members-only, but there is space to change on the quay. Warm up with a sauna at Saunanor, where you can also try the distinctive Danish saunagus tradition.

Those seeking a more spa-like experience should head up the coast to Skodsborg Spa Hotel. The former sanatorium offers a superlative spa experience with 16 different bathing experiences, including saunas, steam rooms and access to a private swimming jetty on the beach. Alternative public swimming spots include Valby’s Water Culture House, a chic grey building a world away from typical leisure centre design with a slide, lane swimming and a hot pool area.

This article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller UK.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6418. Did viruses borrow their shells from bacteria? New evidence raises questions

Tiny viruses found in gut DNA carry a virus protein shell much like the boxes bacteria use for chemistry, and the design crossed both ways.

Many viruses have a remarkably simple design: a protein shell containing their genetic material.

Bacteria build almost the same shell and use it as a sealed container for chemical reactions, with enzymes inside instead of genes. For years the leading idea was that bacteria had borrowed the design from viruses.

Now a search through billions of DNA fragments has turned up tiny viruses whose shell proteins look more like the bacterial version.

The family tree they belong to runs in both directions. The researchers found evidence that the shell may have passed between viruses and cells at least three times, in both directions.

Abelardo Aguilar, a Ph.D. student in the Department of Biology at the University of Miami, led the search with Antoni Luque, an associate professor of biology there.

The team never grew a single virus. Everything came from DNA sequences in public databases, read from soil, seawater, wastewater, and the human gut.

“The majority of viruses cannot be grown in the lab,” Luque said.

“But now through sequencing, we have access to information on viruses for which we don’t know the host, that we can’t culture in the lab, but that are everywhere.”

The protein at the center of the story folds into a shape biologists call the HK97 fold, and copies of it assemble into hollow shells.

In a large family of viruses, that shell is the capsid, the case around the genome.

In bacteria and in archaea, a separate branch of single-celled life, the same fold builds a container called an encapsulin, which cells use to store iron and run other chemistry.

The two versions differ in size. Most encapsulins are built from 60 copies of the protein.

Many viral capsids are larger and have additional assembly machinery, including scaffolds, DNA-packaging portals, and sometimes tails.

The size gap is the problem with the old story. If encapsulins came from viruses, the simpler structure evolved from the more complex one, and that idea never said how.

Aguilar’s team reasoned that if the two shells were related, there might be viruses nobody had found yet, small enough to sit between them.

The smallest known tailed virus of this family has a genome 11,600 base pairs long, the paired letters that DNA is written in.

The team sifted more than 14.4 billion DNA fragments, including those in IMG/M, run by the Department of Energy’s Joint Genome Institute.

They kept only fragments that looked like complete viral genomes, carried this virus family’s hallmark genes, and fell below that line. That left 4,730 candidate genomes.

Each genome’s shell protein was then checked against the sequence signatures of encapsulins, with AlphaFold and other AI tools predicting the proteins’ shapes.

Among the genomes between 5,000 and 11,600 letters long, 93 of 491 shell proteins, nearly 19%, carried encapsulin signatures. In a control set of slightly larger viral genomes, 2.5% did.

The biggest cluster of these encapsulin-like viruses, 76 of the 93, came from human gut samples. Their genomes averaged about 8,750 letters.

None carried a portal, a tail, or the motor that known viruses of this family use to pack DNA into the shell.

Genes they did carry included ones for splicing themselves into a host bacterium’s chromosome and lying dormant there.

So how do these viruses copy themselves with no portal? The authors suggested they may depend on other viruses for the missing parts, or may carry single-stranded DNA and pack it through pores in the shell.

Several of their genes fit the second idea, though it remains untested, the team wrote.

The team built family trees of the HK97 fold three ways, from the proteins’ sequences, from their predicted shapes, and from which features they share.

All three methods produced groups in which viruses and encapsulins sat side by side.

In one group, a family of encapsulins clustered with viruses that infect soil bacteria.

In another, a virus that infects archaea clustered with an archaeal encapsulin rather than with other viruses.

At least three separate crossings, in the team’s reading, and not all in the same direction.

A capsid is built in stages. The shell proteins first assemble around the scaffold into a smaller, empty form called a procapsid.

As the genome is packaged, the procapsid expands and matures into the finished viral shell.

Aguilar’s team compared a bacterial encapsulin with a procapsid and finished capsid from a Staphylococcus aureus genetic element.

The two proteins share only 14% of their sequence. Yet the encapsulin and the procapsid are almost the same size inside, about 1.3 millionths of an inch (33 nanometers) across.

Inside an encapsulin sits an enzyme. Inside a procapsid sits the scaffold, and the two proteins turned out to share a similar helical structure.

So the authors proposed that whatever sits inside the shell decides what the shell becomes. An enzyme turns it into a reactor. A scaffold lets it expand and take on a genome.

“One implication of this research is the possibility that viral capsids could also facilitate biochemical reactions, which would open up the potential roles that capsids have in environments as a whole,” Aguilar explained.

The study doesn’t settle whether the first HK97 shell held genes or enzymes.

The deep branches of the family tree are too poorly supported to say, and the authors wrote that repeated crossings may have erased the signature of the earliest steps.

The authors’ best guess, which they labeled speculative, is that the earliest shells were built from 12 to 24 proteins, too small to hold any genome.

In their model, chemistry came first and genes later, once the shells grew to 60 proteins.

Whether procapsids in living bacteria run reactions during an infection is what no one has measured.

Infected cells often produce empty procapsids, the authors wrote, so a lab could test that directly.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6417. The 9 Best Portable Tire Inflators for Peace of Mind on Your Next Road Trip

These earned top spots after hands-on testing with real flats.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

There’s no polite way to say this. It stinks to get a flat tire and stinks even more when your spare is also flat. As a veteran road warrior who drives 4,000 miles round trip each year between the northern border of Oregon and the tip of Baja in search of waves, wind, and warm weather, I know firsthand that flats happen. I’ve experienced everything from a full-on blowout at highway speed to the inevitable nail-in-the-tire slow leak. I’ve also woken up to find that inexplicable flat tire which has a way of happening when the waves are pumping and I’m jonesing to get the beach—but thankfully I own a portable air pump.

For those times when you need to get air in your tire quickly and get back on the road, a portable tire inflator is ideal to have in your vehicle’s trunk and definitely a smart addition to any car emergency care kit.

A portable tire inflator is also handy to have when it’s not a worst-case scenario. I use one of these when I deflate my tires to drive my car on dirt and sand so I can access remote Baja beaches and then inflate the tires when back on pavement. I’ve owned several tire inflators over the years, everything from janky budgets jobs that take forever inflate a tire to my current favorite, the Viair 400P-RV.

Read on to find the right portable tire inflator for you.

There’s good reason why Milwaukee’s M18 Portable Tire Inflator earned inclusion in our prestigious 2025 Gear of the Year Awards and returns as the top choice among portable tire inflators: It’s the fastest to inflate a tire of any product that I tested. Its separate rechargeable 18-volt battery barely lost power while its detachable 36-inch inflator hose didn’t appreciably heat up like some of the others we tested.

Since it performs an automatic pressure check and shuts off once the target psi is reached, Wraight liked that he “could walk away without worrying about watching the inflation gauge.”

Also, it's the only one we tested that has four psi memory presets, an appreciated perk for Wraight, since he refills tires on various lifeguard vehicles at different pressures. The solid-brass screw-on Schrader chuck is another bonus (an inflation needle and nozzle and Presta chuck for bike tires are also included). Finally, at 5 years, the Milwaukee’s M18 Portable Tire Inflator has the longest warranty of any device tested.

This portable air inflator gets points for its simplicity. It has an LED display, physical + and - buttons to dial in a preset psi, and a toggle switch on one side to start inflation. It automatically stops after the preset pressure is reached.

Its 9.8-foot power cord was long enough to reach from the 12-volt outlet inside Wraight’s truck to all four tires while its 24.8-inch air inflator hose was adequate. While Wraight and I were impressed with this small, inexpensive device’s overall performance relative to its low price, thanks to its induction-magnet motor, it struggled with the truck’s large tires and took several minutes to go from 20 to 40 psi whereas the more powerful tire inflators we tested did this in under a minute. The hose and clamp-type Schrader chuck also got hotter than most other devices.

It also has an LED flashlight that turns on with the toggle switch and it comes with a Presta valve adapter for bicycle tires and an adaptor for sports balls and other inflatables. If you want ease of use and affordability, this is a solid option.

The Etenwolf Vortex S6 is the inflator to get if you’re filling up larger tires and don’t want to worry about running out of juice. Its 19,200 mAh battery is massive, and Etenwolf says it can top off 18 F-150 tires (from 30 to 35 psi) on a single charge. That’s a claim that should put range anxiety to rest for anyone who regularly airs up after a day on dirt roads or at the beach.

A dual-cylinder motor and active cooling system give the S6 a true 100 percent duty cycle, so you don’t have to wait between tires for the unit to cool down. At 1.5 cfm, it fills a 31-inch tire in about a minute and maxes out at 160 psi. Seven preset modes and automatic shutoff at the target pressure make the Vortex S6 easy to use, and the gauge is accurate to within ±1 psi. The air chuck includes a built-in deflation valve for real-time pressure adjustments, so you can dial in the exact pressure.

Beyond tires, the S6 doubles as a power bank with USB-C and USB-A ports—the USB-C handles 45-watt fast charging in both directions—and has a 1,000-lumen LED with SOS and strobe modes. It comes with both high-pressure and high-volume hoses, the latter of which helps for inflating air mattresses, pool floats, and other low-pressure items. A Presta valve adapter, ball needle, and carry bag round out the kit. At about 7.9 pounds, it’s heavier than pocket-size inflators but lighter than you’d expect given the battery and motor inside.

The Milwaukee M12 Compact Inflator filled the tires on Wraight’s truck almost as fast as its big brother and Best Overall and Gear of the Year pick, the Milwaukee M18.

The design of the M12 is smaller and lighter, weighing in at 3.45 pounds, than some of the other powerful devices we tested. It is intuitive to use with a digital gauge that shows the pressure reading, + and – buttons to set a target psi, a power button in between, and an inflation-start button underneath.

This device performs automatic pressure checks and shuts off once the target psi is reached and includes a brass Schrader chuck, Presta chuck, inflation needle, and two nozzles—like most of the other devices tested. But, like the Milwaukee’s M18 inflator, it requires buying a separate 18-volt battery and charger—and one that’s different from the one used with the Milwaukee M18 Compact Inflator—and this adds to its cost and weight.

For completists who want the best portable inflator not only for large vehicles but with all the trimmings, the Viair 400P-RV checks all the boxes.

In addition to the obligatory features such as preset psi and automatic shutoff. and standard accessories like a Presta valve adaptor, the Viair 400P-RV comes with an incredible list of accoutrements. These include a quick-connect Schrader chuck, a 45-degree extended-reach chuck designed for vehicles with rear-dually tires like many RVs, and an additional 30-foot inflator hose that attaches to the primary 30-foot hose, all of which fits in a heavy-duty storage bag. Whew!

This device has the same high 2.30-cubic-feet-per-minute (cfm) rating—and quick inflation—as the Milwaukee M18, but unlike that device, this one is powered by a car’s battery via a pair of heavy-duty alligator clamps at the end of an 8-foot cable, and doesn’t require a separate battery.

Of note: This inflator also has a feature not found on any of the other devices we tested—and one Wraight noticed immediately—a deflate button on the gas-station-style inflation gun that makes airing down tires a breeze.

Having tested the Battery Tender 800 AMP Jump Starter and Tire Inflator as part of a recent roundup of portable jump starters, and because I was so impressed with it, this became part of my family’s vehicle must-haves. Along with an emergency kit, something every motorist should carry, this is another trusted essential.

The jump starter can crank any 12-volt engine up to 6.0-liters gas and 3.0-liter diesel while the air compressor has an inflation pressure of up to 140 psi, and comes with adaptors for bikes and toys, a 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A outlet for charging devices such as phones, LED flashlight, and zippered soft-shell carrying case.

In addition to saving space by combining two devices into one small, lightweight package, I also like the Battery Tender 800’s intuitive interface. And I found that its built-in battery didn’t discharge as quickly as the Gooloo GT160 Dual that also uses a built-in rechargeable battery.

On the downside, this device has the shortest inflation cord of any units we tested and the inflation hose heated up, with the clamp-on chuck getting hot enough to burn Wraight’s finger when he disconnected it.

This device is small but mighty. It’s versatile, too, with preset modes for filling car, motorcycle, and bike tires as well as sports balls and other inflatables. There's a custom mode for anything else with a convenient auto shut off once a preset pressure is reached.

This inflator also has the only LED color display of any of the units tested, with 2000 nits of brightness, making it visible even in direct sunlight. A rotating indicator ring monitors tire pressure and tracks inflation in real-time. The device also has an LED flashlight and comes with adaptors like an inflation needle, Presta valve, and storage bag.

While its dual-chamber design and 160-psi rating quickly fill a tire, we noticed that going from 20 to 40 psi drained the built-in battery from 100 percent to 50 percent. That said, if you have more than one tire to fill, you’ll probably have to recharge the inflator using the supplied USB-A to USB-C adaptor. At just 20 inches, it also had the second-shortest inflation hose.

If you’re an off-roader, the Viair 88P is the perfect choice. It’s specifically designed for use with everything from large 4x4 trucks and other off-road vehicles like ATVs, side-by-sides, and dirt bikes, as well as average cars and SUVs, to balls, air mattresses, and inflatable SUPs. It is powered by a vehicle’s battery via alligator clips, so it is always ready if your vehicle has a good battery.

While priced slightly above some of the lower-cost inflators here, the Viair 88P doesn’t skimp on either quality or features. It comes with a heavy-duty gearless motor and brass twist-on Schrader chuck, and includes an LED flashlight, Presta-valve adaptor, and three other inflation tips. It also has 16-foot air hose, a 10-foot power cord, and comes with a carrying case.

The DeWalt 20V Max is the device to own if you frequently need to inflate items other than tires. It has both a high-pressure mode with automatic shutoff for inflating tires and a high-volume mode for inflating—and deflating—items like air mattresses.

It also has versatile power options using a supplied 12-volt cord that plugs into a car’s cigarette lighter outlet, a DeWalt rechargeable battery sold separately, or an available extra-cost 120-volt cord that plugs into a standard wall outlet. We also liked that the 12-volt power cord, at 13-feet long, still fit neatly into a side compartment.

In testing, we found that it was one of the fastest to inflate tires thanks to its larger battery. Like the Milwaukee M18, the DeWalt 20V Max’s rechargeable 20-volt battery lost little power, and its 36-inch inflator hose didn’t heat up appreciably. Another bonus: It's about 1.5 pounds lighter than the Milwaukee M18 and includes an LED flashlight for nighttime illumination.

I’ve been covering aftermarket automotive products as a journalist for more than three decades, and tested everything from radar detectors to dash cams to tire chains, not to mention more than a thousand new vehicles. I drive a 2015 Thor Majestic motorhome with six tires and tow a daily-driver 2007 Honda Element. Last season I hit a huge pothole at highway speeds and pulled the RV over to find a shredded back tire on the Element—and its temporary donut spare half inflated.

Fortunately, I had a portable tire inflator. I keep it on hand along with jumper cables, a portable jump starter, and an emergency kit. After inflating the spare, switching it out for the tattered tire and with daylight quickly fading on a deserted stretch of Mexico Highway 1, I limped 10 miles to a Pemex station where an attendant phoned his amigo to bring me a replacement tire.

Recently while I was in San Diego, I connected with my Baja surf buddy Adam Wraight, a lifeguard sergeant at Imperial Beach, California. Wraight helped me test these portable tire inflators since he and his crew regularly deflate and inflate the tires of their lifeguard vehicles to drive on the sand. He also shared valuable insights on each of the products I tested given his more than 25 years on duty at the beach and his daily deflate/inflate routine.

I met Adam on a weekday morning, and we ran the tire inflators through their paces by deflating the tires on his 2019 Chevrolet Colorado truck to 20 pounds per square inch (psi), and then inflating to 40 psi. Using the devices I brought with me for review, we evaluated how much time it took to inflate the tires, ease of use, useful features, and how hot the units and their inflation hoses and air chucks got. We also considered the length of each one’s power cables (where applicable) and inflation hoses, as these factors affected use.

In selecting the products to test, I considered how they would be used and who would use them. Consequently, I picked products that fit a range of applications and cover a variety of budgets—everything from the $30 Avid ACAP008 to the $365 Viair 400P-RV, and many in between. I also chose devices that use a variety of power sources with the idea that the average motorist only needs a relatively inexpensive device like the $75 Gooloo GT160 Dual with a built-in rechargeable battery.

Conversely, DIY Pop Mech Pro peeps who probably own portable power tools, and their separate rechargeable batteries, may lean toward the Milwaukee and DeWalt we tested. I also pored over online reviews to see what others had to say about portable tire inflators and read real users’ comments and reviews.

Portable tire inflators are simple devices, and there are two important interrelated, objective specs to be aware of—cfm and psi. Other subjective factors to think about are a portable air inflator’s power source and features like the air-valve connection, display type and memory settings. Here’s more detail below.

Cfm measures the volume of air that the compressor can deliver in one minute and indicates how much air a compressor can move. The higher the cfm spec, the faster a compressor can fill a tire; for portable inflators, a cfm of 1 works for most usage. However, if you are using the compressor often to fill all four tires or you drive a vehicle with large tires, then you might want a device with at least a 2 cfm spec.

Many people know the term psi from filling car and bike tires. It's a measure of the amount of pressure placed on one square inch of space. While cfm measures the amount of air a compressor can deliver in one minute, psi refers to the maximum amount of air it can deliver to an inflatable such as a tire or SUP.

While not a perfect analogy, think of cfm as relative to horsepower produced by a vehicle engine that determines the maximum amount of power it can deliver, while psi is analogous to the top speed the engine can deliver—and cfm and psi work hand in hand.

For most motorists, a portable tire inflator with a maximum capability of 120 psi is plenty. If you drive a bigger rig like my RV, you may want to consider a device with a psi of up to 150.

While cfm and psi are straightforward and easy to compare, how a portable tire inflator gets power depends on your needs, how often you’ll use the device, and if you have other portable devices that use compatible rechargeable batteries.

The portable tire inflators tested here rely on one of four power sources: a built-in rechargeable battery, 12 volts by plugging into a car’s cigarette lighter, 12.6-14.7 volts by connecting to a car’s battery via jumper cables, or 18 volts from a portable battery that’s the same used to power portable tools such as drills, saws, and sanders.

For the occasional roadside emergency, a low-cost portable tire inflator with a built-in rechargeable battery, or one that plugs into your car’s 12-volt cigarette lighter outlet, is adequate. The two Viair devices we tested that connect to a car’s battery both supplied impressive inflation power, but if you frequently air up tires—or are a gear guy or gal who owns a set of portable power tools—you may want to consider the higher power provided by a portable battery.

Keep in mind: With portable tire inflators that plug into a car’s cigarette lighter or connect directly to a car’s battery for power, you won't have to worry about not having a portable battery available or making sure a device with a built-in rechargeable battery is topped off. That is, unless you are unlucky enough to also have a flat tire and a dead battery, in which case a combo device like the Battery Tender 800 AMP Jump Starter and Tire Inflator is ideal.

While portable tire inflators are uncomplicated devices with few features, pay particular attention to the length of the power cables and inflation hose. With devices that plug into a car’s 12-volt outlet or connect to the battery, make sure the power cord is long enough to reach the rear tires.

Similar, although less critical, is the length of the air inflation hose. It can make the difference between easily filling a tire and wishing for a longer hose when dealing with a flat tire. The units we tested have hoses ranging from as short as just over 15 inches to as long as 30 feet.

Portable tire inflators also come with two types of Schrader chucks, the name for the connection that fits on the valve that’s standard on most car tires. A clamp-type (or push-on) chuck connects to a tire valve with a quick-release sleeve, and is faster and easier to use than screw-on chucks but can be less airtight.

Screw-on chucks that twist onto a tire’s valve stem provide a more secure, airtight connection that’s less prone to leaks, but take a bit longer to attach and remove. The Viair 400P-RV was an exception, with a convenient quick-disconnect Schrader chuck.

Finally, every portable tire inflator tested for this roundup has a digital display and the ability to dial in the desired tire pressure so you can set and forget it while filling a tire. All the portable tire inflators tested here can also be set for kPa and bar air-pressure measurements. In addition to a Schrader chuck, they all come with a Presta valve to fill a bike tire, an inflation needle for sports balls, and various other attachments.

Which of these is the best power source: a separate battery, a rechargeable battery, a 12-volt outlet plug, or battery clamps?

It depends how you intend to use your portable tire inflator along with other factors. For example, if you already own portable power tools that use a rechargeable battery, like the Milwaukee and DeWalt devices tested here, and/or want the maximum inflation power and use the devices frequently, that’s the way to go.

On the other hand, devices that connect to a car’s battery or 12-volt outlet for power or have an internal rechargeable battery are less powerful but also less expensive since you don’t need an extra battery. Devices like the DeWalt 20V MAX that run off a separate battery and have a 12-volt cord that plugs into a car’s cigarette lighter are the most versatile.

Do I need a separate inflator for tires and one for accessories?

Not really, since one inflator can serve dual duty for inflating a tire and, say, an air mattress. All the devices tested in this article except the DeWalt 20V MAX are designed mainly for high-pressure inflation.

They can fill things like air mattress and inflatable SUPs that require a large amount of air volume to fill quickly, but use low pressure. If you want to best of both worlds, go for a combo high-pressure/high-volume inflator like the DeWalt 20V MAX.

What is the difference between an air compressor and a tire inflator?

They both push air and can be used to fill a tire and other items. Here is the difference: An air compressor is a more powerful and expensive tool designed for tasks such as inflating large truck tires or running air tools, and usually used by tradesmen and mechanics, while a tire inflator is a smaller, portable, and less expensive device.

It is specifically for inflating car tires such as bike tires, sports equipment, and air mattress. Portable tire inflators are convenient since they are often run off a car's 12-volt power outlet, battery, or a rechargeable battery.

Depending on the quality of the device, frequency of use, and maintenance, a portable tire inflator can last anywhere from 5 to 20 years. My top pick, the Milwaukee M18 Portable Tire Inflator 2848-20, has a five year warranty.

Where is the best place to store this in my car?

I keep mine with my tool kit and emergency road kit in the cargo area of my Honda Element or with similar gear in the Thor Majestic RV. It can also easily be stored in a trunk. Just make sure that if your tire inflator has a rechargeable battery that you check in on it often.

#6416. Deep inside a Spanish cave, archaeologists found at least 120 Latin inscriptions, and five of them honor a goddess called ‘the Lady’

At least 120 Latin inscriptions in Cova Dones, Spain, name a goddess called Domina, the Lady, and point to women taking an active part in her cult.

One chamber of Cova Dones, a cave in Millares in Valencia province, now holds at least 120 Latin inscriptions. Teams from the universities of Alicante and Zaragoza recorded them during fieldwork in May and June 2026.

When the room was first explored in 2024, about 15 had been logged.

Five of the texts are vows to Domina, “the Lady,” a goddess the visitors addressed with reverence. Several of the names read so far are women’s. The team calls the results preliminary, and many texts are still being read.

The researchers call the room the Roman Sanctuary. It sits more than 650 feet (200 meters) from the entrance, according to the University of Alicante.

Most of the texts are believed to date to the 1st and 2nd centuries AD, and they cover the walls and the ceiling. Small natural pools on the floor, known as gours, catch water from the galleries, and visitors dropped offerings into them.

That first campaign also yielded a coin from the reign of Emperor Claudius. Someone had wedged it as an offering between a fissure and a stalactite in the ceiling, and in a team photo Xabier Garín Artázcoz points at the crack. Trinidad Pasíes Oviedo of the Valencia Museum of Prehistory recovered and conserved the coin.

The January 2025 announcement from the University of Alicante placed the room among the deepest known Roman inscription sites in Iberia, second only to Cueva del Puente in Burgos and possibly Cueva de Román de Clunia.

This year’s readings were done by two epigraphy specialists. Silvia Alfayé teaches ancient history at the University of Zaragoza, and Sergio García-Dils lectures at UNED in Seville. García-Dils also directs the Spanish School of Speleology.

According to Alfayé, five votive texts show that women “played an active role in her cult.” Three of them carry the word MALACI. In a release dated July 27, the University of Alicante called it an unpublished epithet for a goddess not known until now.

García-Dils noted that the texts are packed into one marked-off part of the cave, well away from the entrance. To him that “strongly suggests the existence of a well-organised and structured cult” with a named deity, not scattered visits.

The University of Southampton, where Aitor Ruiz-Redondo is also based, put out the English release on October 20. It says early readings suggest some women wrote their vows themselves, without a go-between.

Until now, the Roman cave sanctuary with the largest known set of inscriptions was La Griega, with 107. One of them names a woman.

The 2026 team logged objects on the chamber floor, among them two bronze rings found under the inscribed rock. There were two bronze rings, a bracelet, chalice-shaped cups, spindle whorls, bits of pottery and animal bones.

The whorls came up in numbers. Virginia Barciela co-leads the project with Ruiz-Redondo and teaches prehistory at Alicante. She said the whorls probably point to offerings of spindles, a textile tool tied to women in antiquity.

She also brought up the first written name of the site, Cova de les Dones, meaning Cave of the Women. That name may hold “the fossilised memory of a place long associated with women,” she said, or with female spirits.

Alfayé said the goddess’s title may have to do with water. Water shrines existed elsewhere in the ancient world, such as a circular water shrine at Pelusium in northern Sinai.

The inscriptions are extremely difficult to see with the naked eye. So the team photographed the surfaces for high-resolution photogrammetric models and read the texts on those.

That work turned up inscriptions no one had seen. It also split apart lines that earlier readers had taken as one text.

Jorge Angás and Carlos Valladares, from the IPH institute in Zaragoza and the DigHER project, ran the geomatics side. Javier Velaza Frías, a Latin professor in Barcelona, leads the study of the Roman inscriptions. Víctor Sabaté Vidal of the University of Valencia has also contributed to the project.

Latin wishes turn up on other Roman objects too, for instance openwork glass cups carved with drinking wishes in Greek or Latin.

In a Roman underground sanctuary, finding texts and offerings together in place is exceptionally rare, says the Southampton release.

Ruiz-Redondo, Barciela and archaeologist Ximo Martorell published the first results in 2023. In the journal Antiquity they described over 100 Paleolithic paintings and engravings. Some are older than 24,000 years.

Pottery from the Iron Age had already led archaeologists in the 1960s to class it as an Iberian sanctuary. In 2025 the team logged more than 100 stalagmites that people had modified on purpose.

For that kind of find, the University of Alicante ranks the cave second in the world, after Saint-Marcel in France.

Ruiz-Redondo said people may have kept returning for “its permanent water supply,” its landscape or its easy access.

At La Pasiega, Maltravieso and Ardales, red marks have been dated to more than 64,000 years ago.

Alfayé and her colleagues are still working on the goddess’s title. For now the team has not said who Domina was or what MALACI means. Many inscriptions are still being read, and much of the cave is unstudied, so 120 is a minimum.

The DONARQ project started in 2023 with money from the Generalitat Valenciana and the British Academy. In September 2026 the sanctuary was shortlisted for a National Geographic +Historia readers’ prize. Public voting closed on October 12.

This year the regional Pla Restaura program and the Millares town council are paying for more work. The money goes to the cave’s access and entrance, safety measures, a digital twin and a catalog of the Paleolithic images. The company Arquivolta Patrimoni i Societat is coordinating it, and virtual visits should follow.

Among those offerings, two bronze rings sat on the surface right below the inscribed rock.

The information was obtained from the University of Southampton , the University of Alicante and the University of Zaragoza.

#6415. The Best Islands in the World: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

Trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in New York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best cities in the world as voted by you, our readers.

View all of the the Readers’ Choice Awards winners for 2026 here.

The six islands of the Bazaruto Archipelago—Bazaruto, Benguerra, Magaruque, Santa Carolina, Bangue, and Shell—are a protected conservation area and national park off the eastern coast of Africa. Nicknamed the Pearl of the Indian Ocean, the islands have only seen the arrival of big-name resorts within the past decade, like the impeccable andBeyond Benguerra Island in 2015.

Pro tip: This is one of the few habitats of the endangered manatee-like dugong, which sailors sometimes mistook for mermaids.

Getting there: Fly to Vilanculos on the coast of Mozambique; from there, take a seaplane to your final destination.

Instagram and Pinterest have created renewed interest in this island in the Indian Ocean, thanks to its so-called underwater waterfall—a visually stunning runoff of sand and silt best viewed from above. Roughly 550 miles east of Madagascar, Mauritius may also be home to a lost continent hiding beneath the waves.

Pro tip: Don’t trust the scales on Mauritius: The island has a stronger gravitational field, causing things (and people) to weigh more.

Getting there: The island’s Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam International Airport is your link for flights to other cities in Africa, as well as to major cities in Europe, Asia, and Australia.

With its white coral sand beaches, turquoise waters, and laid-back island vibe, few destinations offer a sense of escapism quite like Zanzibar. Add to that plenty of sunshine and consistently pleasant temperatures, and it’s easy to see its appeal. For the history buffs among us, don't skip historic trade center Stone Town, famous for its meandering lanes, minarets-crowned buildings, and the 19th-century House of Wonders where the Sultan used to live.

Pro tip: Visit the island during the dry season from June to October, when temperatures average out at 77 degrees. This time range also overlaps with the high season for safari, should a two-for-one trip be of interest.

Getting there: To get to Zanzibar, fly directly to Abeid Amani Karume International Airport (ZNZ), or arrive by ferry from Dar es Salaam in Tanzania.

Our readers aren’t the only ones who consider this African nation one of the best islands in the world: Prince William and Kate Middleton and Victoria and David Beckham spent their honeymoons on the North Island of the Seychelles. Yet some stretches of sand are so deserted that parts of the movie Castaway were filmed here. The ultimate draw, however, is the nature—the white beaches here are so beautiful that visiting them borders on a religious experience.

Pro tip: Seychelles is one of the best spots in the Indian Ocean for snorkeling. Head to the islands of La Digue and Félicité for the best variety of sealife.

Getting there: Air France, Air Seychelles, and Turkish Airlines have regular flights that connect to Seychelles International Airport (SEZ), just south of the capital of Victoria.

A chain of 26 atolls and more than 1,000 islands in the Indian Ocean, the Republic of Maldives is one of the most sought-after tropical destinations in the world. It’s dense with villas and overwater bungalows, and the diving is unreal (though, sadly, some of the coral has been threatened by bleaching). Still, there’s a dive for all skill levels at Ari Atoll, where you can swim with rays and, deeper down, reef sharks.

Pro tip: Cheval Blanc Randheli, the number one resort in the Indian Ocean (per this year’s reader survey), has 45 luxe villas—some tucked among the coconut groves, some jutting out directly over the water.

Getting there: Fly into Malé’s international airport and transfer there to the appropriate resort or atoll.

If your idea of the perfect vacation involves three-day beach parties, Koh Pha Ngan is the Thai island for you. Famous for its full-moon parties at the Haad Rin peninsula's Sunrise Beach, this island is for hardcore partygoers and the anything-goes crowd. During peak season, the island can see upwards of 20,000 visitors dancing and cavorting on the white sands under a full moon. If you can't make it at the right time of month, don't worry—there are half-moon and black-moon parties in intervening weeks, too, and there's action every night of the week at the island's beach and cocktail bars.

Pro tip: There are secluded beaches far from the crowds (like local favorite Bottle Beach, arguably one of the best beaches in Thailand), and plenty of spas where you can check yourself in for an afternoon of recovery, from the basic to the deluxe (such as the Ayurvana Spa at Santhiya Resort on Thong Nai Pan Noi Beach in the north of the island).

Getting there: From Koh Samui, take the ferry or a high-speed boat from a nearby pier like Maenam or Bangrak to Thong Sala Pier or Haad Rin Pier.

India's Andaman Islands are chock-full of beaches for thrill seekers looking to snorkel among sea life and peer through shipwrecks, as well as relaxing sandy stretches for more meditative types who prefer their quiet strolls backgrounded by sherbet-hued sunsets alike. Whether you're enjoying Havelock Island's serene Radhanagar Beach or Elephant Beach, whose shores are a veritable water sports arena, these islands provide 365 days of sun, sand, and fun.

Pro tip: Beyond the beaches, hike through the Baratang Limestone Caves' striking natural corridors through one of the most renowned natural wonders of these islands.

Getting there: Direct flights to Port Blair's Veer Savarkar airport fly from Kolkata, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Delhi, and Vizag. Alternatively, travelers may also choose to arrive at Port Blair via ferry from Kolkata or Chennai.

The Phi Phi Islands lie in the cozy cradle between Phuket and the Straits of Malacca off Krabi Province. Each of the six islands—Ko Phi Phi Don, Ko Phi Phi Le, Bamboo Island, Mosquito Island, Bida Nai, and Bida Nok—have their own charms to offer. From silky soft white sand to dramatic limestone cliffs, the beaches found on these islands are among Southeast Asia's finest.

Pro tip: For a feel of local life, stop by Ko Phi Phi Don, the largest and most populated island of the group. If flopping in solace is more your speed, pop over to Ko Phi Phi Le, which lays claim to some of the island's most stunning vistas and coastal stretches.

Getting there: As there are no airports on any of the Phi Phi Islands, visitors will have to arrive via ferry from ports such as Phuket or Krabi.

Phuket is not exactly a hidden gem, but that's because it's such a magical place to vacation, whether you want a busy immersion in city life or a quieter experience. Since it’s the biggest island in Thailand, you’re sure to find something to fit your desired itinerary. In general, though, we recommend skipping the overcrowded west coast and heading to quiet corners like Cape Panwa, where you’ll find luxury accommodations and rum distilleries that feel a bit more removed from the oft-touristed track.

Pro tip: Phuket Town receives far fewer tourists than the western beach areas. Here you can sample colorful spices at markets, visit aging Taoist temples, and snap photos of the colorful street murals.

Getting there: There are more than a dozen daily flights from Bangkok to Phuket, with most trips clocking in at an hour and 20 minutes.

Nowhere on the planet offers the same combination of surfing, spirituality, and sun-kissed pleasure as Bali. The island has sadly become synonymous with the concept of overtourism, but there are still enclaves of hidden cultural treasures and undiscovered gems—if you know where to look. For a primer on everything Insta-famous and off-the-beaten-track, check out our list of the best things to do in Bali.

Pro tip: The shoulder months of April-May and September-October are the best times to visit Bali. Not only can you enjoy lower airfares and hotel rates during the low season, but you’ll also have the rare ability to see the island without its usual crowds.

Getting there: Many airlines fly directly from the United States to Bali, including Singapore Airlines, Delta, and American.

Thailand’s second-largest island is famous for its palm-lined beaches, buzzing nightlife scene, and luxurious hotels. AVANI+ Samui Resort was voted one of the best resorts in Thailand by our readers, though the hillside villas at Four Seasons Resort Koh Samui and floor-to-ceiling bookshelves at The Library are also worth checking out. In terms of beaches, be sure to visit the five-mile Chaweng Beach, lined with coconut trees and surrounded by a natural reef. Just note that the northern end of the beach is party central.

Pro tip: If you are looking for parties, check out Green Mango, one of Koh Samui’s oldest and most famous clubs.

Getting there: You can fly directly from Bangkok to Koh Samui. A more budget-friendly option may be to fly to Surat Thani and then catch a ferry to Koh Samui—it will add a couple of hours to your travel time, but the views are pretty spectacular.

Located off the northwestern coast of Malaysia, the Langkawi archipelago has pristine beaches, coral reefs, and lush mountains—plus that famous Sky Bridge you’ve definitely seen pictures of. This collection of 99 islands is also a foodie wonderland (eating is the unofficial national sport here), with spicy peanut satay skewers and macheted coconuts sold everywhere from high-end hotels to sidewalk stands.

Pro tip: The Ritz-Carlton, Langkawi was voted the best resort in Asia by our readers this year—chalk it up to a world-class spa, multiple beachfront restaurants, and a location in a 10 million-year-old rainforest.

Getting there: Take a one-hour flight from the Malay capital of Kuala Lumpur.

This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.
