#6414. How brain implants turn thoughts into speech

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Casey Harrell, here at home in the summer of 2026, uses a brain-computer interface to communicate with his family.

Regents of the University of California, Davis

Casey Harrell lost his voice to ALS or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. As a volunteer in a clinical trial, he’s helping scientists test a brain-computer interface. Electrode arrays that are implanted in Casey’s brain send signals to nearby computers, where those signals are translated into words he intended to say.

Casey uses this system every day to talk with his wife, daughter, friends and work colleagues. The moment he realized that it worked was “pure joy,” Casey says. Even though the researchers scripted his words for that first test, “it was a profound moment,” he says. “The possibilities for the near future for me and the rest of humanity were overwhelming to realize.”

This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me follows Casey and the fast-moving neuroscience that enables him to speak.

Patients paralyzed from the neck down can manipulate robotic arms with their thoughts. The woman in this video is controlling a robot with her mind. The so-called BrainGate system relies on a sensor of electrodes implanted in the motor cortex of the brain. Researchers hope by implanting electrodes in the brain it can read the brain signals meant to move the muscles involved in speaking, and translate the person’s intention to speak into comprehensive speech produced by a computer.

Laura Sanders: Controlling things with your mind. It sounds like science fiction, but it’s definitely real. Today, we’re going to explore what it’s like to communicate with a brain implant that decodes your thoughts and turns them into words.

[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? The voice is absolutely an integral part of your identity. Hello? That added layer of it being you. Do you want to talk? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.

Sanders: From Science News, I’m Laura Sanders, and this is The Deep End, Talk to Me. Okay, so what is BrainGate? It’s an experimental system that connects electrodes that are implanted in a person’s brain to a nearby computer. It’s called a brain-computer interface, or BCI. The goal here is big: to help people with paralysis or brain injuries or missing limbs regain control over their world.

Leigh Hochberg: BrainGate clinical trials have now been going on for nearly 22 years. It’s 21 point something at the moment.

Sanders: Leigh Hochberg is the director of the BrainGate Consortium and Clinical Trials. He also has a job at Massachusetts General Hospital, Brown University and the VA.

Hochberg: People who may have had a brainstem stroke and suddenly lost the ability both to move and to speak, or for somebody with ALS who is progressively losing the ability to move or to speak, there’s long been a hope that particularly implantable brain-computer interfaces could restore communication and could restore mobility.

Sanders: In 2004, a BrainGate device was implanted into a person’s brain for the very first time. That person was a man named Matthew Nagle, and he had been paralyzed in an accident. With BrainGate, he could control a computer cursor with his thoughts. Here’s a 2008 report from IT World.

Technology gave him hope. He was one of four testing BrainGate, a new technology where a chip is implanted in the brain that picks up electrical impulses. A computer then interprets those impulses as actions.

Hochberg: Those early studies have been really encouraging, and I think speaks to the potential for the field.

Sanders: Over the years, there’s been amazing examples of people using BrainGate. People have used it to click around on the internet, play video games, one woman who was paralyzed was even able to drink a cinnamon latte with a robotic arm.

Hochberg: And she was able to think about using her own arm and reach out with a robotic arm and pick up that thermos and bring it to her mouth, and tip it towards her mouth, and then put the straw in her mouth and then to take that sip. And while it wasn’t the first time in nearly 15 years that she had had something to drink, it was the first time that she was really able to do so solely of her own volition. I remember the smile on her face when she did that.

Sanders: Over the decades, BrainGate has had a lot of research success in a lot of ways. But what about talking? Hochberg says that when it comes to decoding speech, the science here is still very, very young.

Hochberg: We are at early days, just to be super clear. This is the very beginning of this field. There are only a small handful of people in the world who have had any type of implantable BCI that has been decoding speech.

Sanders: Where does the science stand when it comes to decoding the intention to talk? In the past few episodes, we’ve heard the stories of people who have lost their ability to speak. One of those people was Casey Harrell, and Casey also happens to have a BrainGate device implanted in his brain.

Casey Harrell: My name is Casey Harrell and I am 47 years old.

Sanders: Casey wakes up in the morning, and plugs in.

Casey: The first thing I will usually do after getting out of bed is to plug into the Matrix, so to speak.

Sanders: By that, he means attaching two wires to two pedestals that come out of the top of his head. These two black wires then snake down to nearby computers. Collectively, these electrodes in Casey’s brain, wires from his head, and computers are called the BrainGate 2 neural interface system. So Casey gets it all fired up and then he’s off.

Casey: Unless I have a medical appointment or something that will move me out of the house, I will sit in this position for most of the day, with specifically small breaks in between.

Sanders: All the while, Casey is generating brain signals as he thinks about saying words. These are small, precise electrical pulses made by Casey’s neurons, specifically the cells in his speech motor cortex. Remember how we learned there are over 100 muscles that are involved in speech? These are the parts of the brain that control those muscles.

Casey: I am using a decoder for about ten to 14 hours a day, seven days a week, for the past almost two years, making me the world’s biggest power user of the brain-to-computer interface known to man.

Sanders: Like Jules, Casey has ALS. The disease has slowly taken away his ability to move and to talk.

Casey: I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020. Then it became a slow motion car crash of multiple years before almost no one would be able to understand me.

By the time of my surgery, only my assistant and my wife, Levana, could really understand me fully. A few other friends who were around often would be able to understand some of what I was saying. I relied upon my assistant and my wife to basically serve as my translators to other people. I did not go anywhere, even a video call without them, either one or both.

Sanders: In July of 2023, Casey volunteered for a clinical trial called BrainGate 2. A UC Davis neurosurgeon put four small electrical arrays onto the left side of Casey’s brain. I wanted to know more about how these arrays worked, so I talked to the neurosurgeon who put Casey’s devices into his brain.

David Brandman: My name is David Brandman, and I am the co-director of the UC Davis neuroprosthetics lab, developing next-generation neurotechnology to help people with paralysis. A brain-computer interface is a device that records brain signals from people that are paralyzed and then translates those brain signals to allow people to control objects in their environment using their minds.

Sanders: Casey’s implant is made of four arrays. Each of them are square and they’re about as wide as a peppercorn. Each array has a bunch of pointy ends that go down into his brain. They look a little like those metal cat brushes. Altogether, the four arrays contain 256 electrodes. These electrodes are all listening to Casey’s brain activity when he thinks about saying a word.

Brandman: The way this device works is by recording the electrical activity of the brain as he tries to speak.

Sanders: The wires from Casey’s head carry those neural signals to nearby computers. That’s where machine learning algorithms attempt to do a very complex sort of matching. The algorithms match Casey’s brain activity patterns to the patterns that predictably occur with certain sounds called phonemes.

Brandman: We translate his brain signals into one of 39 different English phonemes. Now, a phoneme is a building block of language. So if I say the word hello, the word hello can be broken down into ha, uh, uhl, and oh. Hello.Sanders: Next up, those algorithms assembles these phonemes into words by making its best guess about what Casey wants to say.

Brandman: So I translate this brain activity into a phoneme and then, using artificial intelligence, turn phonemes into words, words into sentences, and sentences into paragraphs.Sanders: So that’s the process, and it allows Casey to type messages on Slack, text his friends, and send emails. Sometimes in his emails to me, he includes a tagline at the bottom: “Sent from my brain,” with that cute little pink brain emoji. His setup also lets him convert these typed messages into spoken words. These words show up on a screen for him where Casey proofreads them. If everything looks good, Casey gives the go-ahead and the system speaks the words out loud. Brandman tells me that when Casey tries to speak naturally, he can say about six understandable words per minute. That’s pretty slow.

Brandman: Using this prosthesis, he’s in the ballpark of 50 words per minute. Now, as I’m speaking to you right now, I’m speaking on the order of 120 to 150 words per minute, depending on how excited I am, right? So we’ve got him back to about a third of how quickly he spoke as an able-bodied person.

Sanders: I had emailed Casey some questions a few days before our talk. But he didn’t answer them by email. He used his brain-computer interface to answer my questions in real time just by thinking about the words he wanted to say to me. As we introduced ourselves, I saw how the timescale had stretched.

Casey: It’s a challenge because we can have this conversation, but I am slower than the average Joe, even where we grew up.Sanders: Casey and I both grew up in the south, Casey in the Atlanta area and me in middle Tennessee. But he’s lived in the Bay Area for over 20 years now. And like me, his accent had faded.

Casey: And yes, I do not have much of a Southern accent anymore. But I love my roots, and I would love to show my daughter where and how I grew up. But it is exceedingly difficult to travel when you cannot move.

Sanders: Before his mobility was limited, Casey did a lot of cool things.

Casey: I spent most of my professional career as a climate campaigner and have went all over the globe, fighting companies who are destroying the Earth and trying to bring some justice to our planet and the people who inhabit it. I am very fortunate because I have been able to do something that I love and also develop some deep friendships and relations with other phenomenal people.

Sanders: My interview with Casey was unlike any I’ve ever had. I’m used to being flexible for interviews. There’s time zone problems, language barriers, mathematicians who sometimes answer my questions in symbols and formulas. But when I logged on to Zoom to talk with Casey, I quickly realized this conversation would be different. I was self-conscious at the beginning of our talk. I fumbled around too much. I’d ask Casey a question and then another one before he had a chance to answer. I accidentally interrupted him a few times. Sometimes I wasn’t sure if he was composing an answer or just waiting for me to say something else. This poor performance on my part wasn’t unusual for Casey at all.

Casey: It is hard for people in your position to stay focused because you were not used to the cadence of a conversation this slowly.

Sanders: He’s right. I was not used to it. And timing, in conversations and in life, is everything. Here’s Greg Bryant of UCLA.

Bryant: Turns, conversational turns, happen at the level of hundreds of milliseconds at the longest. Two hundred milliseconds is a long turn. That’s a fifth of a second. I mean, that’s really fast. So if you are slow at all, it’s noticeable. We have to coordinate our talk so our terms make sense. I can’t take too long or be too quick to respond to your questions. I have to know when to stop and start. We get into this flow, kind of a dynamic, and that is hugely consequential for how we feel about the conversation, the other person, ourselves. You know, it’s all timing.

Sanders: Let’s turn to Jules. His words start in his brain too, but then they take a different route. He types them by looking at letters on a screen, then his voice clone says them. It’s also a slow process and one that takes a lot of mental power, too. At one point in our conversation, MA describes the effort this requires of Jules.

MA: And in his brain, you know, you can imagine he’s doing all these mental gymnastics, to, right now, he’s listening to us. He’s writing something with his eyes, like letter by letter to contribute to the conversation. Plus, he has the answers that he pre-wrote, of the questions that you asked. So it really is like, there’s a whole lot happening behind the scenes that of course anybody who doesn’t have to think about their voice takes for granted. So I’ll pause to let him complete what he’s saying.Sanders: MA and I wait here for Jules to weigh in. So far you’ve heard ten seconds of the pause. The full length of the pause was a minute and 18 seconds.

Jules: It is a challenge to communicate with people who don’t interact with me on a daily basis. I have a major bottleneck from my thoughts to actually speaking.

Sandes: And as with Casey, these pauses can introduce difficulties. Here’s speech pathologist Jessica Pietrowski with more on that.

Pietrowski: Humans are not very comfortable with silence, especially communication. And when we’re talking to one another, we fill in the silences, it’s less awkward. And so, someone who’s communicating with a device is probably very used to those latency periods and some more silence and they’re comfortable with it. Whereas the person they’re communicating with is like, let’s keep it going, like this is, I want to help, I want to fill in the blanks, I don’t want this to feel awkward, but in turn, might make it a little more awkward than they think.

Sanders: Jules hates when people read his screen before he’s ready to say what he wants. This particular hate inspired a joke in his stand-up routine.

[Jules audio]: People read off my screen while I’m typing and try to finish what I am saying. It’s like having to constantly deal with an over-competitive charades partner.

Sanders: Jules and Casey encounter other people’s impatience constantly. Not that it isn’t well-intentioned but still, it does not help. Even worse, they face other people’s misconceptions about what they’re capable of. Casey is an interesting, funny and compelling conversationalist. That might not be apparent to everyone who doesn’t slow down to hear him. And that’s an assumption that really bothers him.

Casey: It is incredibly undignified and a terrible consequence of the health care system to treat me like this very quickly.

Sanders: Brandman has seen this dismissal, this mistreatment too. It happens with some of the volunteers he works with on the BrainGate 2 project I mentioned earlier. That’s the same trial Casey’s in.

Brandman: I think as healthcare professionals, we conflate the inability to communicate with the lack of understanding. And I’ve witnessed this firsthand as I’ve watched doctors and nurses interact with my BrainGate participants and then treat them as if they are invalid. Or they’re not there because they’re unable to express themselves. And in fact, I go out of my way in the intensive care unit on the wards and dealing with anyone who’s dealing with my participants to say, look, you know, they’re inside. They’re there. They can understand everything that’s happening. They just happen to not be able to speak. And so please treat them with the respect and dignity that they deserve. And it’s a constant challenge for the participants that I work with. And it’s the reality of which we face and it’s the bias that we have against people that can’t speak for themselves.

Sanders: Casey and the other people with ALS are not alone. Many people who have trouble talking or who just need more time can be judged this way. Here’s Karina Nagin from Bridging Voice.

Nagin: It’s how people see you. And so when you have ALS and you cannot move and you don’t even have facial expressions and you’re hooked up to machines, people assume you’re not there. And we see this every day where people either don’t talk to the person with ALS, assuming that they can’t respond. They speak really loudly and slow. Their mind is completely working.

Sanders: For now, Casey’s words may be slow. But despite all the drawbacks, they are still an absolute marvel. Remember Hochberg from the start of this episode? He’s one of the neuroscientists who works with Casey, and he told me a story from the first few days of testing after Casey’s BCI was implanted.

Hochberg: We gave him a 50-word vocabulary on day one. And even on day one, he was able to say some key sentences from those 50 high-value words.

Sanders: At this point in the testing, Casey was asked to say some pre-specified sentences so researchers could test their system out.

Casey: Most of the sentences were what we called closed loops.

Sanders: That means that the researchers already knew what brain activity patterns should go with the words Casey thought about saying. It was a test to see if the system was working.

Casey: The decoder would be able to verify whether I was right or wrong, giving me short preloaded sentences to say. I was asked to say, “What good is that?”

Sanders: “What good is that?” is not the most poignant sentence ever uttered, but it had a big effect both in the room and for researchers joining remotely by video.Casey: “What good is that?” Everyone is crying after I am successful.

Sanders: Later on, there was time for Casey to actually express himself.

Sanders: Things only got better from there. To set the scene here, during this session, Hochberg was in his office and Casey was at his home, sitting in his living room. Hochberg was watching Casey on a screen.

Hochberg: On the second session, came back and gave him the full 125,000 plus word English dictionary to be able to select from. That is, the decoders and the AI and the machine learning language models would be able to select from basically a full dictionary. And the first thing that he said was something along the lines of, “Is this thing on?” Kind of a funny statement.

The next thing that he said on the second day of using brain-computer interface, or the second thing that we decoded was, “I’m looking for a cheetah.” And it’s the second day. We know there’s all kinds of opportunities for decoding errors. And when I saw that, I said, you know, there’s no way that the second sentence on the second day of using an implanted brain-computer interface is going to say anything about a cheetah. You know, that’s obviously a decoding error and that’s fine.

Sanders: Hochberg could see Casey on the screen, but he couldn’t see something really important that had just happened in the room.

Hochberg: His four-year-old daughter had just walked into the room dressed as a cheetah.

Sanders: Here’s Casey remembering the same moment.

Casey: Yes, I remember this time very well. It was the second session of talking that I experienced early in August 2024. My daughter was incredibly cute in her cheetah outfit. This was one of her favorite animals. They were going through a phase where everything they did was super fast, running from thing to thing. Hochberg: And she was born around the time that he was diagnosed with ALS. And one could imagine that because the voice that was coming out of the computer was a version of his own voice, and then the rest of the interaction was between dad and daughter. And it was between parent and child.

Sanders: At the beginning of the experiment, the research team had told Casey and his wife that they’d be able to try using the BCI for casual chats just a few hours a week. Brandman: As we kept coming to his house two or three times a week, things kept getting better and better. Sanders: That’s a far cry from a few hours a week. Those numbers in this very bare-bones science kind of way are dry, if we’re being honest. But when you stop to think about it, each sentence, each of those nearly two million words, is a tether that connects Casey to his life. Okay, so no A, but we got an E. M-I. O. M-I. Good job, team. We are almost there.

Sanders: We’ve talked a lot about words here and the fundamental ways that Casey’s BCI has restored his ability to say them. But Casey’s BCI goes a little bit farther than that. It gives him the ability to add some extras. #6413. Scientists discover a hidden pattern in the sun’s chaotic magnetic field

The solar wind's magnetic field twists one way at one scale and the other way at a smaller one, and the pattern drifts outward.

Stir milk into coffee and the swirls that follow have no plan. The stream of charged particles flowing from the sun is turbulent, too, with magnetic fields twisting through the chaos.

Scientists have long struggled to find order in these turbulent magnetic fields.

The twist has a pattern. In measurements from NASA’s Parker Solar Probe, the field turns one way at one size of ripple and the opposite way at ripples twice as small.

The pair of opposite twists sits right where the gas stops behaving like a fluid and starts behaving like a crowd of separate particles.

Masatomi Iizawa of TU Braunschweig led the analysis with Nobumitsu Yokoi of the University of Tokyo and colleagues in ten countries. Among them is Stuart Bale of UC Berkeley, who leads the instrument that took the readings.

“We see a clear structure in the spectrum, even though the turbulence represents unstructured motions,” said Iizawa, the paper’s first author.

A magnetic field in moving gas points somewhere, and it also turns.

As a ripple passes a detector, the field direction rotates, either clockwise or counterclockwise with respect to the gas’s direction of travel.

Physicists call that sense of rotation magnetic helicity. In the big, slow ripples of the solar wind, it has looked like nothing but noise since the 1980s.

Clockwise and counterclockwise turned up in roughly equal measure, which is what randomness looks like.

Sharp peaks near the smallest ripples have shown up before, in data from earlier spacecraft.

Following one as the gas traveled was the part no one could do, because older missions sampled too slowly to catch ripples that fast.

Parker Solar Probe samples fast enough. The team used its magnetometer readings from late September to late November 2021, an hour at a time.

Over those weeks the spacecraft swung between 0.1 and 0.78 times the Earth-sun distance.

Close to the sun, at a tenth of that distance, the spectrum held two spikes rather than noise.

One spike sat at 10 ripples a second and carried the twist one way. The other sat at 20 ripples a second and carried it the other way.

The two peaks revealed an organized pattern that random fluctuations alone could not readily explain.

Two opposite twists sitting side by side is what plasma physicists call a bihelical structure, and until now it was something theory predicted and data rarely showed.

Comparing measurements at different distances from the sun, the researchers found that both peaks shifted toward slower frequencies, corresponding to larger structures.

The drift held from 0.1 out to about 0.4 of the Earth-sun distance.

Gas expands as it travels, so some drift was expected. Simple expansion predicts a particular shape to it, with the frequency falling in step with distance.

The measured drift fell off exponentially instead, far faster than expansion accounts for.

The researchers then checked the other obvious explanation. If the twists were made and maintained by local conditions, their position should track the local scales set by protons in the gas.

Scaled against those, the peaks slid right past them.

The team calls that behavior nonlocal. The findings suggest that interactions across different scales, rather than local plasma conditions alone, may be driving the changes.

Turbulence normally hands energy down a ladder, from big swirls to small ones, until the smallest turn into heat. The same ladder turns the tiny vortices seen on the sun’s own surface.

One recent theory holds that at the boundary between fluid behavior and particle behavior, the twist itself jams that ladder and forces energy back up to larger scales.

A pile-up of magnetic twist at scales bigger than the local proton scales is exactly what the jam would produce.

The team’s observation fits that prediction, and it arrives as a measurement rather than a simulation.

Yokoi said the result matters for plasma physics and astrophysics alike.

Understanding this turbulence could eventually help scientists improve models of the solar wind and its effects on Earth’s magnetic environment.

Past roughly half the Earth-sun distance, the two spikes faded out.

The probe’s orbit stays within a few degrees of the plane the planets share, and around there it keeps crossing the current sheet dividing the sun’s magnetic field in two.

Crossing that sheet may scramble the structure, or the fade may just be where the spacecraft happened to be.

One spacecraft measures one point, so the twist it records is a slice of the full three-dimensional quantity.

Turning ripple timings into ripple sizes rests on an assumption about how fast the gas carries them past. The team puts the possible error there at a factor of about 2.5.

Nobody could watch the energy move, either. That would take readings of the gas’s speed as fast as the magnetic ones, and particle instruments can’t scan that quickly in gas this thin.

No one has caught these structures forming, or followed one outward in a single parcel of gas.

Iizawa’s team suggests Europe’s Solar Orbiter, which flies above and below the planets’ plane, could settle whether the fade is real or an accident of one orbit.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

#6411. The 7 Best Car Battery Chargers for Roadside Emergencies

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Maintain your car battery—or bring a dead one back to life.

The 12-volt battery is one of the least complex components in modern vehicles but one of the most crucial. If it’s not in good condition, the engine won’t start, and none of the vehicle’s fancy systems will work. Car batteries have a limited lifecycle and deteriorate with time. This can happen for many reasons, including extended inactivity, extreme temperatures, or even something as simple as accidentally leaving the lights on after you turn off the engine.

That’s why it’s handy to have an external car battery charger so your engine is ready to go when you need it. A charger can also help extend your battery's life, for instance, in a vehicle you don't drive often—a weekend getaway camper or an old classic cruiser. Some chargers also have a jumpstart feature, eliminating the need for jumper cables (and the inconvenience of a required second vehicle).

You might be surprised to hear that electric vehicles use the same 12-volt car batteries as their internal combustion counterparts. Regardless, modern vehicles rely on this ancillary battery to power lights and onboard electronics when the ignition is off. Here, we’ve compiled the best chargers for cars and motorcycles, including everything from a solar-powered charger to a model that can revive several vehicles at once.

Noco’s Genius 10, the brand’s flagship single-vehicle charger, offers many cool features, including the ability to “force charge” a battery so dead it won't generate any voltage when you hook it up. (Most modern chargers won’t do this.) Maintenance and “desulfation” modes extend your battery's useful life while keeping it ready to go.

Unlike smaller, less ambitious chargers, the Genius 10 charges a vehicle battery to full power in the shortest safe time. It can even charge the new generation of lithium-ion car batteries, like the complex, expensive units fitted to many newer BMWs.

All the basic features are here at a very low price, including protection from reverse clamping and a “float mode” for fully charged batteries.

The included set of bolt-on leads lets you quickly connect and disconnect the charger. Operation couldn’t be simpler: a green light shows the Motopower is on, and a red light indicates charging status. With 1.5 amps of power, it charges slightly faster than most competitors in the low-price bracket.

Think of this 15-amp charger as a miniature version of the shop-grade Schumacher. It’s also the form and function that will be most familiar to older or experienced users. The included clamps are high-quality and should fit most cars. Just clamp on, plug in, and select one of three modes.

The 15-amp rapid charge is slightly more than the competition can manage, and a carrying handle makes it easy to place where you want it.

This charger is compact, light, easy to operate, and almost bombproof. It delivers a 3-amp charge, then automatically switches to float mode to maintain proper voltage and prevent overcharging.

A two-color LED indicates charging status, and if the battery voltage drops below a certain level, it resumes full charging output in adaptive mode. It’s compatible with most automotive batteries and can switch between 6- and 12-volt batteries with the push of a button. Its battery clamps are spark-proof, and the Battery Tender 3-Amp will automatically detect reverse polarity. It comes with a 5-year warranty and lifetime customer service.

Dealerships and race shops that used to scatter CTEK individual chargers throughout the building are now switching to the multi-vehicle Noco 2x4 model. It weighs just under 8 pounds, mounts to a wall, and can handle four vehicles at the same time, each in a different mode.

Want to float charge one car, recondition another, and bring two other dead batteries back to life in force-charge mode? Not a problem.

If you own a vehicle you only drive occasionally, an under-the-hood charger saves the hassle of disconnecting it from the battery and storing it each time you want to go for a cruise.

The compact Schumacher SC1300 mounts under the hood to supply up to 1.5 amps, while a built-in microprocessor automatically adjusts the charging rate to maintain an ideal charge state. Float mode delivers a small current when needed.

Reverse hook-up protection prevents the charger from working if the battery clamps are installed in reverse polarity, and the Schumacher automatically detects 6-volt or 12-volt batteries.

If an electrical outlet isn’t available or if you just want to use the sun to keep your battery topped off, the Sun Energize solar-powered charger is a reliable option. It trickle-charges a variety of automotive batteries, as well as some lithium batteries.

A built-in charge controller prevents overcharging; charging stops when a battery is topped off and automatically resumes when it drains.

An LED indicator shows charge and battery conditions. The 20.1 x 13.8 x 0.7-inch solar panel is larger than the other chargers here, but it’s built to handle high winds and heavy loads and is IP65 waterproof.

We tested some external battery chargers under varying weather conditions, while others were chosen based on feedback from car enthusiast friends. The selections represent a wide variety of chargers with different capabilities to match a broad range of use cases. We have years of experience traveling the country with these chargers and know their performance very well.

If you store a vehicle for long periods, you’ll want a charger to keep the battery from fully dying and turning into a paperweight. (It’s also nice to know it will start without jumper cables.) But a battery charger can make a difference in plenty of other situations.

If you regularly experience below-freezing temperatures at night, a charger with a maintenance function can significantly extend your battery's life. If you rarely drive more than a few miles at a time, a charger can prevent your battery from discharging too far—leaving you with a no-start condition. Last but not least, older vehicles often struggle to recharge slightly depleted batteries on the move, so starting the day with a fully charged battery can also extend the life of your alternator and charging system.

Charging power is traditionally measured in amps. Think of amps as the amount of juice that can be put back into the battery at any given time; for example, a 10-amp charger puts twice as much charge into the battery as a 5-amp one. A quick stroll through a listing of battery chargers can be confounding, though. Some have 40 amps, and some have 0.75 amps, and yet they do the same thing. In reality, the difference is easy to understand. The more power a charger has, the more quickly it can bring a dead battery back to life. The tradeoff is cost, size, and weight.

If you’re charging a small motorcycle battery or maintaining a good-condition battery in a cherished collector car, then a 0.75-amp charger will do just fine. If you’re worried that your pickup won’t start in the winter, 2 to 10 amps is a better bet. Any capability above that is mostly for mechanics who need to quickly charge or recondition batteries in the shop.

Every charger here can “maintain” a charged battery, keeping it from slowly discharging between uses. Most chargers can also bring a depleted battery back up to full power. A few chargers offer specialized modes like “desulfation,” which helps a battery regain its chemical balance through carefully timed charge-and-discharge cycles. A “quick charge” can very rapidly (but safely) prepare a battery for use. A few battery chargers also offer a “jump start mode” that can start a car or motorcycle with a dead battery, but this is rare, and most of the time you’ll need a separate jump starter for that task.

Most chargers in this roundup are designed for conventional lead-acid (flooded cell) or Absorbent Glass Mat (AGM) batteries, which you’ll find in newer vehicles. If you have a vehicle with a lithium-ion battery, like some new BMWs, or a customized car with ultra-compact batteries from manufacturers like Braille, you’ll need a charger with that capability—different battery chemistries require specific charging protocols.

If you are dealing with a cramped garage, or travel between storage spaces throughout the seasons, consider a “wall wart” or direct-mount charger. The former keeps all the charging mechanisms in a large plug that some people might compare to model-train transformer plugs. The latter bolts into your car and plugs directly into the wall.

Not anymore. Today's smart chargers, like the ones in our article, won't overcharge a battery or give it more than it can handle. And choosing a more powerful charger won't shorten your battery's lifespan; quite the opposite, in fact!

It's usually as simple as removing the bolt from both battery clamps, slipping the thin copper loops between the bolt and washer, and reinstalling. Then you can coil the quick-disconnect cord in a convenient place, like inside a motorcycle fairing or under a car hood. The cables can melt when exposed to serious heat, so don't let them touch an exhaust pipe.

Yes, if the batteries are in reasonably decent condition. Any charger rated at 2 Amps or more should be able to rotate between multiple vehicles. If you have more than three or four, consider buying multiple chargers.

#6410. A bandicoot skull given to a museum by a widow in 1920 belongs to a species that went extinct before it had a name

A bandicoot skull donated in 1920 belongs to the little brown bandicoot, a new extinct species, in a study of 800 specimens that lists 7 Isoodon species.

Mrs. Symonds Clark lost her husband on July 10, 1920. In October she handed one of his bandicoot skulls to the South Australian Museum in Adelaide. It went into the drawers as “SAMA M1981, skull only, sex unknown,” and was later labeled as a golden bandicoot.

The ear capsules on it were far too small for that.

Kenny Travouillon of the Western Australian Museum and eight co-authors have now made SAMA M1981 the type of a new species, the little brown bandicoot, Isoodon microtis.

It most likely came from Eyre Peninsula and was gone before anyone noticed. Three skulls and some jaw fragments are all that is left of it.

The paper lists the Adelaide skull as probably female, going by its smaller canines. Two more skulls turned up at Museums Victoria in Melbourne under the label Isoodon sp., with no data except that they came from a Mr. Waterhouse.

DNA was tried on all three and none came back usable. So the species stands on skull and tooth characters. In the team’s combined analysis it lands next to the southern brown bandicoot, even though it shared Eyre Peninsula with a quenda.

Microtis is Greek for “small ear.” It is the smallest Isoodon in overall size. Its bullae are also smaller relative to the skull than in any other member of the genus.

Symonds Clark kept birds and studied them, and he sometimes collected mammal skulls for the museum. The team dated his skull to between 1876, his last logged donation, and 1914. That is the last entry in his diary, now at the State Library of South Australia.

None of the bandicoots in the diary could be matched to it for sure. His only trip out of Adelaide in those years was to Eyre Peninsula.

The Melbourne pair goes back to Frederick George Waterhouse, the museum’s first curator from 1861 until he resigned in February 1882.

His reports mention two bandicoots shipped to Melbourne between November 1866 and January 1867, which puts their collection between 1862 and 1866.

In those years the catalogue shows five bandicoot donations, from a stuffed one given by a Mr. L. Clark in July 1864 to two skins from a Mr. Andrews, and the localities were not always recorded.

The place came instead from subfossil jaws in Adelaide, three lower and two upper, from at least three animals. They were dug at the South Block Site near Edillilie, about 5 miles (8 kilometers) east of Coulta, in an area not cleared for agriculture.

Travouillon has said the work started in 2016, with visits to bandicoot collections in Europe and the United States.

The paper credits the Winston Churchill Memorial Trust and the Australian Biological Resources Study (ABRS) for funding his access to specimens. Steven Cooper and Terry Bertozzi of the South Australian Museum and Adelaide University came in later.

In the end the team examined more than 800 specimens in 11 Australian collections and in London, Paris, Genoa, Munich, Washington and New York. Every available type specimen of Isoodon was examined and sampled for DNA, according to the paper.

DNA came from 83 fresh tissue samples and 75 historical ones. Pieces of dried skin were soaked overnight before extraction. That work ran in a trace DNA lab at the Australian National University, set apart from the main lab to keep modern DNA out.

The Oz Mammals Genomics Initiative did the sequencing. After filtering, 2,050 gene regions were left, about 1.14 million DNA letters, and the specimen list is posted on Dryad.

Eleven Isoodon species have been described over time. The 1990s revisions brought that down to three, and studies in 2012 and 2018 raised it to five. Now it is seven.

The other new one is the New Guinea brown bandicoot, Isoodon moresbyensis, named from Port Moresby in 1877 and later lumped in with the northern brown bandicoot. Its DNA is deeply split from that species and its skull is much smaller.

The Kimberley golden bandicoot is now I. auratus bundilarri, from the Uunguu word for the animal on Wunambal Gaambera Country, and its type is a young male from the Mitchell Falls campground.

A south coast quenda, I. fusciventer halae, honors Marie Hale, the first person to pick it out. The rest come from Daw Island, St Francis Island, Marchinbar Island, Cape York and the Adelaide Hills.

Measurements and genes recently split Sydney’s funnel-web spider into three species. Old specimens also made up much of the 2025 haul of new species from museum cabinets.

The quenda, Isoodon fusciventer, used to be a Western Australian species. Bandicoots from the Mount Lofty Ranges, Kangaroo Island and the Nuyts Archipelago now belong to it as well. The western and South Australian groups separated around 800,000 years ago, the team estimated.

The mainland South Australian quenda is I. f. terrenus, Latin for “earthly,” since it is not an island form. Its type, SAMA M25880, is an adult male taken 6.7 miles (10.8 kilometers) west-southwest of Mount Barker.

The subspecies once ran from the Murray River to coastal Eyre Peninsula but is now down to the Mount Lofty Ranges, Fleurieu Peninsula and Kangaroo Island.

That shrinks the southern brown bandicoot, Isoodon obesulus obesulus, to the coast from Sydney to southeast South Australia. It is already listed as endangered federally, and the authors call for an urgent review of its status.

Australia has lost 42 mammal species since European colonization, and nearly 20 percent were bandicoots and bilbies, the paper notes.

Foxes, cats, land clearing and changes to traditional fire practices are blamed. DNA testing has also shown that feral cats kill more native animals than expected.

There is no date for the extinction. The last of the skulls was in the museum by October 1920. Land clearing for farms was well under way on Eyre Peninsula in the late 1800s.

If the species lasted until foxes arrived, the authors wrote, “it is very likely that foxes would have played a role in its extinction.”

Marchinbar Island’s golden bandicoot is known from just two specimens, and no genetic samples exist for the Cape York northern brown bandicoots. The IUCN Red List was last updated for Australian mammals in 2016.

The authors suggest that I. f. terrenus, which shared Eyre Peninsula with the little brown bandicoot, could be reintroduced there, though “it would be difficult to find an ecological analogue to replace it.”

Craig Moritz and an anonymous referee reviewed the paper, which went in on December 17, 2025, and came out on October 14, 2026. SAMA M1981 is still in Adelaide, now as the type of its own species.

The full study was published in the journal Australian Journal of Taxonomy.

#6409. Where to Stay in Big Sky, Montana, When You’re Dreaming of the Wild West

I’ve visited Big Sky, Montana, a handful of times over the past six years, and I’m still completely smitten. This corner of the Rockies, roughly 45 miles south of Bozeman, is a choose-your-own-adventure kind of city. Winter ski days beneath the hulking silhouette of Lone Peak give way to summer rafting trips and fly-fishing on the Gallatin River, while fall brings horseback rides that sprawl across open ranchlands, and spring offers hikes through wildflower-strewn meadows. The iconic Yellowstone National Park is about an hour south too, putting geysers, steaming hot springs, and roaming bison within day-tripping distance.

The city itself is a quaint yet buzzy collection of restaurants, shops, and watering holes, all adding a welcome dose of small-town charm to all that wilderness. And lately, the destination’s hospitality scene has been booming, with a new wave of stylish hotels and mountain retreats bringing some fresh takes to the city’s rugged Western roots. From luxe resorts with front-row views of the towering peaks to authentic dude ranches and design-forward Airbnbs with cozy fireplaces, there’s an accommodation for every style of Big Sky getaway on the list below. Read on for the best places to stay in Montana’s sweet mountain hub.

A peek at Big Sky's small but mighty town center, where the mountains and Main Street look great together.

Stay at Lone Mountain Ranch, just five minutes from the town center, for a dreamy dude ranch retreat.

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: Mountain access, gorgeous standalone cabins, private hot tubs, spa and wellness facilities (with indoor-outdoor lap pool, heated onsen soaking tub, cold plunge, steam room, and sauna)

Famed for its sumptuous yet tasteful resorts in far-flung destinations like Mauritius, Rwanda, and Malaysia, One&Only’s 2025 Moonlight Basin opening was the brand's American debut, as well as its first foray into the outdoor adventure space. A luxury alpine retreat like this requires a specialized type of hospitality, and the team here—a crew who can do everything from book your activities to whisk you between buildings on a side-by-side ATV—knows exactly what they’re doing. Guests get a direct line to the slopes via the One&Only gondola, as well as access to plush locker rooms, tuning equipment, and gear rentals that will impress even members of Yellowstone Club (the famously tiny private ski community next door).

Moonlight Basin is worth visiting outside of ski season too. Situated on 240 secluded acres within the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, the resort links two sections of protected wilderness in southwestern Montana’s Rocky Mountains, providing critical migration routes for species like moose and bobcats, which means you're in for some exceptional wildlife sightings. Add fly-fishing, stargazing at the on-site observatory, and unwinding at the 17,000-square-foot spa, and even the most discerning ski bums will find themselves spoiled rotten. —Hannah Towey

Neighborhood: Moonlight BasinThings to do nearby: Lone Peak, Madison River Valley, Big Sky Mountain, Madison Base Area

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: White-glove service, buzzy après bar, full spa, on-site activity center, ski-in/ski-out location

Montage Big Sky has always been more rugged than refined, but the buzz around this slopeside resort has Aspen and Jackson Hole loyalists rethinking their next ski vacation. The first five-star resort in Big Sky ushered in a whole new era of luxury for this mountain destination, with an 11,000-square-foot spa (the first true spa in the region), a buzzy bar scene, and stellar restaurants.

Most of the 139 rooms, suites, and residences have terraces and balconies with mountain views, and gas fireplaces turn on with a flip of a switch. Head to Beartooth Pub & Rec for a menu of comfort foods, like Wagyu nachos and oversized hot pretzels served alongside cold-smoked beer-cheese dip. —Jen Murphy

Neighborhood: Spanish PeaksThings to do nearby: Big Sky Resort, Ousel Falls Trail, Lone Peak, Beehive Basin Trail, Gallatin and Madison Rivers

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: True dude ranch experience, tasteful cabin design, horseback riding experiences for all levels, easy access to town

Lone Mountain Ranch, one of Montana’s longest-standing dude ranches, has plenty going for it: a wonderfully attentive staff, character-filled cabins, and a calendar of special events that draw in both longtime regulars and first-time horseback riders. The on-site wranglers are happy to work with riders of all levels one-on-one, even if that means helping you get past a few preexisting fears before climbing into the saddle. The ranch’s roots reach back to the early days of Yellowstone, with its owners involved in conversations around Big Sky’s formation and the region’s ranching, logging, and wilderness preservation. Yet unlike many of Montana’s more remote ranches, it’s conveniently less than a 10-minute drive from town.

You may still find little reason to leave: Set among towering aspens, the 150-acre guest ranch has 25 restored historic cabins, each with its own Wild West–inspired name and one to six bedrooms. And then there are the signature experiences, including Cowgirl Up, a weeklong retreat that brings women from around the world together to experience ranch life and release their inner cowgirl.

Neighborhood: Lone MountainThings to do nearby: Big Sky Town Center, Ousel Falls Trail, Moonlight Basin, Gallatin River, Big Sky Resort

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski-out access, hot tub, gas fireplace, mountain views, outdoor seating on the patio

There’s something pretty splendid about staying at 8,300 feet, especially when the mountains are quite literally at your doorstep. This standalone cabin in Big Sky’s (iconically named) Cowboy Heaven neighborhood is a haven for folks who wish to spend their days outside, whether that means skiing straight from the deck in the winter or taking advantage of the area’s hiking and wildlife spotting in the warmer months. It’s especially ideal for couples, small families, or friend groups, with one caveat for your crew: The second bedroom has a queen-over-twin bunk, so five adults looking for equal amounts of space may want to look elsewhere. A big plus? The town center is less than a 10-minute drive away.

Neighborhood: Cowboy HeavenThings to do nearby: Big Sky Resort, Lone Mountain, Moonlight Lodge, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Private hot tub, in-unit washer and dryer, indoor wood-burning fireplace, fully equipped kitchen, patio with outdoor furniture, longer stays allowed

With three floors and two separate living areas, this Big Sky rental gives small groups room to spread out between outings. And there’s plenty to get out for: Big Sky Resort is about 1.2 miles away, Beehive Basin Trailhead is roughly 2.6 miles, and Ousel Falls Park is another nearby option for low-key but scenic walks.

Inside the light-filled abode, fun Western touches are everywhere. In true Big Sky fashion, you’ll find everything from hanging longhorns and antlers to framed photographs of bison and horses. Through a wall of windows, you can look past the cozy fireplace into the hilly woods—the towering trees are gorgeous year-round. Do note this base might be best for four, rather than six, despite what the listing says. There are two generously sized bedrooms, but two sofa beds in the living room.

Neighborhood: Moonlight BasinThings to do nearby: Big Sky Resort, Beehive Basin Trailhead, Gallatin River, Lone Mountain, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, firepit, spacious design, game room, fully equipped kitchen, patio space with seating and grill, proximity to Yellowstone National Park

For a fun departure from the usual cabin-in-the-woods vibe, this modern mountain retreat sleeps up to eight and puts you in a handy spot for mountain treks, foodie-forward itineraries, and all the trips in between. It’s incredibly spacious, with a large patio for grilling local ingredients, warming up around the fire, and stargazing. In winter, take advantage of the trails practically right next to the property for snowmobiling; you're also in a prime position for skiing at Moonlight Basin, Big Ski Resort, or Bridger Bowl ski area (a bit further north). According to the listing, a sauna is set to open on the property—check in with the hosts to see if it will be set up by the time you visit.

It’s worth noting that this is the closest Airbnb to Yellowstone on this list. You can drive to the West Yellowstone entrance in around 45 minutes.

Neighborhood: Gallatin ValleyThings to do nearby: Gallatin River, West Yellowstone, Lone Indian Peak, Buck Ridge Trailhead, Crown Butte, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: Private hot tub, shared firepits and sauna, board games and books, kid-friendly amenities

This gem of a rental is high on my Big Sky bucket list for more reasons than one. To start, the tastefully designed home is all about panoramic views of misty, moody Ramshorn Ridge. With heaps of walking paths and a mountain-facing hot tub under string lights, guests will be almost poetically connected to Montana’s wide-open landscape. But you won’t be too far from the mountain town’s buzz: This home is part of Aspects, a 10-home village set in a ryegrass field in the Gallatin Valley, meaning you’ll have access to the community’s saunas and two firepits, which you can share with like-minded travelers.

Downtown Big Sky is just a five-minute drive away, while hiking trails branching from Yellowstone are within 15 minutes of the home. Along with its great location, I’m personally captivated by this home’s aesthetic design touches—from the light wood walls that warmly envelop the dining space to the vibrant art that brings fun, unexpected pops of color throughout the home.

Neighborhood: Gallatin ValleyThings to do nearby: The Riverhouse BBQ, West Yellowstone, Downtown Big Sky, Cinnamon Mountain, Gallatin River

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Unique design, minutes from Big Sky Resort, sauna, private walking/biking trail from the property

A little off-grid, a bit otherworldly, and just a couple of miles from Big Sky Resort, this Earthship Airbnb is a unique kind of Montana hideaway. Set on 20 private acres in Michener Meadows, the solar-powered house is designed to bring the outdoors in, with its own potable spring water and a private walking and biking trail winding around the property.

Neighborhood: Michener MeadowsThings to do nearby: Ousel Falls Park, Dudley Creek Trailhead, Table Mountain, Horn and Cantle, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Walkable to Big Sky Town Center; patio with grill; indoor fireplace; fully equipped kitchen; shared access to indoor pool, hot tub, and sauna

For those in search of an easy, breezy Big Sky stay, this convenient condo is a boon. Tucked just outside of the city’s small but mighty town center, you’ll be within walking distance of cozy cafés, outdoor gear and gift shops, and hyper-local pubs and restaurants. Back at “home,” your launchpad is as design-friendly as it is inviting. There’s a snug living room with an electric fireplace, a raised patio with a barbecue, string lights, and a table for enjoying meals made in your fully equipped kitchenette. It’s pretty spacious for a condo—each of the bedrooms boasts a king bed, and there’s a bathroom for each duo.

You’ll also be a short drive to the ski resort and practically right next to Big Sky Golf Course, where you can enjoy an award-winning 18-hole expanse and Nordic skiing, depending on the season. A plus for those chasing the snow? There’s an in-unit washer and dryer for all your ski gear, so it’ll be clean and dry for more mountain fun the next day.

Neighborhood: Meadow VillageThings to do nearby: Big Sky Golf Course, Big Sky Resort, Big Sky Town Center, Lone Mountain Trail, Blue Moon Bakery, Historic Crail Ranch, The Reflector Trail Loop

#6408. Comets probably didn’t deliver life’s building blocks to Earth

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The speed and angle of impact would have destroyed most organic compounds from comets

Comet McNaught shines over Australia a safe distance from Earth in this photo taken in 2007. Most comets that collided with the early Earth would have been moving too fast and at too steep an angle for prebiotic molecules to survive the collision and kick off chemical processes that gave rise to life, a new study suggests.

The chemical building blocks that gave rise to life on Earth probably didn’t come from comets.

Most comets would have been traveling too fast and at too steep an angle to Earth for prebiotic compounds to survive impact with the planet, researchers contend October 28 in Scientific Reports. While the study doesn’t completely rule out the possibility that comets brought these molecules to Earth, it contradicts the long-standing idea that comets seeded Earth with the chemicals necessary for life to arise.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“Even though we see that comets contain all of these molecules in really high concentrations, it’s not straightforward to go from there to saying we’re going to have all of these available for prebiotic chemistry on the surface of the Earth,” says Richard Anslow, a planetary scientist at the Met Office, the national meteorological service for the United Kingdom in Exeter.

Comets carry carbon- and nitrogen-containing molecules left over from early in the solar system’s formation. These molecules can react to form biologically important compounds like sugars and DNA. Scientists have long thought that comets could have delivered these building blocks to Earth when they collided with the planet during its first billion years.

But it’s important to revisit these ideas as our understanding of both comets and the early solar system improves, says Nicolle Zellner, a physicist at Albion College in Michigan who was not involved in the study.

In the new work, Anslow and colleagues used computer simulations to predict the likelihood that a chemical called hydrogen cyanide would survive a comet’s journey through Earth’s present atmosphere and its impact with the planet’s surface. The early Earth’s atmosphere was probably much denser, so would have been even more destructive.

The strong chemical bond between the carbon and nitrogen atoms in hydrogen cyanide can release energy that drives later chemical reactions necessary for life. It also makes the molecule particularly stable compared to other carbon-based chemicals.

“It’s probably one of the more robust molecules to surviving impacts,” Anslow says. “So if things look bad for hydrogen cyanide, then we think it’s going to be much harder for other, more complicated molecules that are more likely to be broken down during these impacts.”

Based on the simulations, a comet impact that kept hydrogen cyanide intact would be extremely unlikely, the team found. On average, the simulations suggest that only one impact would have been able to deliver a meaningful amount of hydrogen cyanide to the planet’s surface over more than a billion years. For hydrogen cyanide to survive the crash, the comet would have to be larger than 100 meters across, slow moving and traveling at an oblique angle to Earth.

A comet that met those narrow criteria would also have had to crash into land, rather than an ocean, to kick off any biologically useful chemistry. If the comet landed in the ocean, any hydrogen cyanide that survived would be diluted too quickly to trigger those reactions.

While still improbable, comets may have been more likely to deliver carbon-based molecules to Mars than to Earth, the simulations showed. Mars’ thinner atmosphere and smaller size meant that comets would impact at lower speeds. That could mean that more compounds could survive the collision.

If Earth’s carbon-based chemicals didn’t come from comets, they may have come from carbon-rich asteroids called carbonaceous chondrites, says Gordon Osinski, a planetary geologist at Western University in London, Canada, who was not involved in the study. Other sources might have included volcanoes and hydrothermal vents.

The study “definitely will make people think twice about comets being the originator for the delivery of organics,” Osinski says. “I hope other people will try to reproduce these results [and] then potentially try something similar with carbonaceous chondrites as well.”

Archaeologists have unearthed a human-shaped funeral offering that may represent an ancient Japanese priestess.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have discovered a ghostly human-shaped artifact at a fifth-century burial mound in Japan. The clay figurine's appearance suggests it represents a female shaman who once guarded a tomb.

The artifact was unearthed at the archaeological site of Nishikaminomiya, northwest of Tokyo, according to a translated statement from Japan's Gunma prefectural government. At the site, archaeologists found nearly a dozen burial mounds known as "kofun" dated to the fifth and sixth centuries.

This time period in Japanese history, which lasted from about A.D. 300 to 710, is called the Kofun period. Many tombs in this period had cylindrical clay sculptures called "haniwa" that were used as offerings to the dead and were often thought to contain the souls of the deceased.

The newly unearthed haniwa is about 16 inches (40 centimeters) tall; but only the head and torso remain, so it would have originally been a lot larger. The figurine was discovered in a moat around an enormous burial mound that measured about 145 feet (45 meters) in diameter. It's likely that the haniwa was originally placed near a boat-shaped sarcophagus archaeologists discovered in the mound and that it slipped down the hill over time to land in the moat, according to the statement.

An aerial view of the tomb where archaeologists found the shrine maiden statuette.

Experts think the haniwa represents a female shaman known as a "miko," or "shrine maiden." These priestesses bridge the gap between the human and spiritual realms in the Shinto religion. During the Kofun period, miko would have performed important funeral rituals and offered spiritual guidance.

The haniwa figurine has a traditional Japanese topknot hairstyle called a "shimada," which indicates that the haniwa represents a miko, according to the statement. Both of the figurine's wrists have bracelets made from clay and red pigment. The haniwa's fingers have been carefully molded, and the figurine has a prominent nose. In addition, she wears a red sash painted on her torso and holds a rod-shaped ritual implement in her left hand.

"These details suggest that considerable care was taken in making the figure, even in features that would not be visible from a distance," representatives of the Gunma prefectural government said in the statement.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Archaeologists discovered the haniwa this year during excavations of the main burial mound at Nishikaminomiya, but they have been working at the site since 2020.

The haniwa is currently on display at the Gunma Prefectural Archaeological Research Center's Excavation Information Museum in the city of Shibukawa.

#6405. Why do flamingos dance while they eat? This scientist found out

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Erin Garcia de Jesús, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

On a family trip to Atlanta, Víctor Ortega Jiménez spent time taking pictures and videos of flamingos as they fed in their pond. It wasn’t to admire their long legs or flamboyant pink color. Instead, he noticed the “beautiful” ripples spreading across the water as the birds ate under the surface. But he didn’t know why the waves were happening.

It took “more than four years to answer that question,” says Ortega Jiménez, of the University of California, Berkeley. “But I think the answer was fascinating.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Ortega Jiménez’s focus is biomechanics, or the study of how mechanics applies to animal movement and structure. His goal is to understand how animal behaviors might lead to human-made engineering feats.

He discovered that, by retracting their heads, flamingos produce vortexlike traps with water to scoop up algae. They stomp around — or dance, if you will — amplifying the vortex. The series of motions brings the food to their crooked beaks. The beaks then filter in food, releasing silt and mud.

The impressive process can weed out particles the size of a single cell. This kind of self-cleaning filter for extremely small particles can be applied to remove microplastics and so-called forever chemicals called PFAS from water, Ortega Jiménez says.

“Nature is always full of secrets,” he says. “And I think that’s the riddle that keeps me going, trying to understand nature. That’s my way to see science: by observation and trying to be inspired and trying to solve a problem.”

#6404. Planning Your First Trip to New Zealand? Here's Where to Go

Living in Sydney, I’m guilty of thinking of New Zealand as somewhere I can always go next month. It’s close enough for a skiing trip, which is usually my first excuse to book. I love Queenstown for that, but what I’ve particularly enjoyed discovering on my travels is how naturally New Zealand brings together its spectacular outdoors and a tradition of luxury hospitality, in every season.

Aotearoa is easy to admire from a car window, but I’ve found that the places I remember most are those where I’ve stopped and spent a little more time. Wellington is overdue for another visit, and Fiordland is somewhere I'd like to explore properly. Then there are the lodges, each with its own character and reasons to return: Huka Lodge for its history, Cabot Lodgefor its working-farm roots, and many others worth discovering.

Below are the five places I’d build a trip around, leaving enough room in the itinerary to linger a little longer wherever I find myself wanting to stay.

I’d start with Queenstown if you’re coming for the mountains, with time allotted for Arrowtown and a few days in Fiordland National Park. For the North Island, Auckland is a useful starting point before heading towards Rotorua for its geothermal landscapes and Māori culture, then Lake Taupō. If food is your priority, I’d make Wellington part of the trip. My main advice is to choose a few places you’re interested in and give each at least a few days.

It can be, although a luxury lodge and a helicopter aren’t compulsory parts of an itinerary. I’d spend on a stay I really wanted, then balance it with somewhere simpler, ideally with a kitchen so you can cook some of your own meals. Skiing and guided activities can take a sizable bite out of the budget, so decide which matter most before booking everything else. If you’re considering a camper van, compare the total hire cost, including fuel and campsite fees, with a car and accommodation. I’d also leave room on the budget for eating out and wine tasting.

Seven days is sufficient for a trip, but I wouldn’t try to cover both islands in that time. On the South Island, you could spend the week around Queenstown and Arrowtown, adding Te Anau if Milford Sound is a priority. Or drive from Christchurch to Lake Tekapo and spend time in the Mackenzie region. On the North Island, Rotorua and Taupō work well together.

I always prefer to spend an extra night somewhere than keep repacking. Leave some flexibility, too: if you’ve come for stargazing and the sky clouds over, you’ll appreciate having another evening available.

Arrowtown, 20 minutes from Queenstown, is an idyllic place to visit.

Queenstown is great for the skiing, but I’d make time for nearby Arrowtown even if it meant losing a day on the slopes. I love the old cottages and shopfronts, and how much of its gold-mining history is still visible. The partially restored Chinese miners’ settlement beside Bush Creek is worth walking through before lunch.

Food is another reason to stay. At Aosta, northern Italian cooking makes good use of Central Otago produce. Nearby Ayrburn occupies a former 150-acre farm, with restaurants spread across its restored buildings. Billy’s, in the original homestead, serves modern Chinese food. I’ve visited both Arrowtown and Ayrburn, and would happily organize another Queenstown trip around eating here, with some skiing fitted in.

Where to stay: Arrowtown House is a small boutique hotel in town, making walking to dinner easy. Millbrook Resort, nearby, has more of a resort feel, with apartments as well as rooms and a spa for sore ski legs.

I still think about the water outside Huka Lodge. The Waikato River is this extraordinary emerald color, and I could have spent much of my stay watching it. Huka also got me interested in New Zealand’s lodge history: it began as a fishermen’s camp in 1924. There’s something appealing about discovering that a place has been welcoming people for the same reason for more than a century.

You don’t have to stay there to spend time beside the river. Follow the riverside walks towards Huka Falls, where the water forces its way through a narrow rock channel. I’d also get out on Lake Taupō, with a boat or kayak trip to the Ngātoroirangi Mine Bay Māori rock carvings. Created by Matahi Whakataka-Brightwell and his team, they’re a striking example of contemporary Māori art.

Where to stay: Huka Lodge has a certain stateliness, with its manicured grounds beside the Waikato River and a history of royal guests. I have dreams of running away to Poronui Safari Camp, in the wider Taupō region. Its two canvas tents sit beside the Mohaka River, with hot showers and food supplied by the kitchen. It’s booked exclusively for up to four people.

The Cairns Alpine Resort’s Alpine Lodges on crystalline Lake Tekapo

I visited Dark Sky Project while reporting on quiet destinations for Traveler and loved having someone explain what I was looking at. The indoor experience brings Māori astronomy and science together, and houses an enormous restored 19th-century telescope. It gives you a way into the subject even if your astronomical knowledge is limited. For nighttime stargazing, book the Summit Experience at Mount John Observatory, within the Aoraki Mackenzie International Dark Sky Reserve. I’d arrange it early in the stay, leaving another night available if the weather doesn’t cooperate.

There’s plenty to look at during the day, too. Lake Tekapo gets its milky turquoise color from fine glacial rock flour floating in the water. It’s a good place to spend a few days on a South Island drive from Christchurch, with time for the Southern Alps and a separate excursion into Aoraki/Mount Cook National Park.

Where to stay: The Cairns Alpine Resort’s Alpine Lodges take their inspiration from musterers’ huts. Inside, there are two bedrooms and a kitchen, with timber-lined rooms and a wood-burning fireplace. After a late night stargazing on Mount John, you can have a lie-in and cook breakfast whenever you’re ready.

The city of Wellington, a great place to visit for good eating and galleries.

New Zealand received its first Michelin restaurant selection in 2026, although you hardly need the guide to eat well here. For me, Wellington would be a few days of galleries and restaurant bookings, with enough time between them to walk around and see what’s changed since my last visit some years ago City Gallery’s reopening has moved it up my list and is the sort of thing I’d build a weekend around. I’d leave plenty of time for eating, though.

Puffin is on my list for a glass of natural wine. I’m also keeping an eye on Rita, a small restaurant in an Aro Valley cottage known for its changing set dinners. The team is also opening a daytime deli called Super Rita, expected to open in early next year.

Where to stay: The Intrepid Hotel is the one I’d book: 18 rooms in Te Aro, near Cuba Street, with Puffin downstairs. I like the idea of a nightcap in a locals-filled wine bar and a short walk upstairs to bed.

The Cabot Lodge, a working farm, is an intriguing stay in Fiordland

Milford Sound and Doubtful Sound are still on my list, and I’d like to give Fiordland a trip of its own. I’d stay around Te Anau rather than make the long journey out and back from Queenstown. There are glowworm caves across Lake Te Anau, while nearby Manapouri is the starting point for the most direct land-and-water route to Doubtful Sound: a boat across Lake Manapouri, followed by a coach over Wilmot Pass to the fjord.

I also have a shopping recommendation for the journey. At The Key, on the approach to Te Anau, Davaar sells knitwear (that has a cult following) made from wool grown on the family’s working sheep station, Davaar Station. Founder Kate Macdonald is the fifth generation, and her sister Anna runs the food caravan next door. I bought a jumper a few years ago when she had a pop-up in Arrowtown that I still love. It’s exactly the sort of place I want to find when traveling: a homegrown product with a family story; make the best souvenirs.

Where to stay: Cabot Lodge interests me because it’s on a working farm overlooking Lake Manapouri, and near Doubtful Sound departures. For a night at Milford itself, Milford Sound Lodge has chalets overlooking the river and rainforest. I’d decide which sound I wanted to spend more time exploring before choosing where to stay.
