#6403. Can a Power Station Cut Down Your Electric Bill? Yes, Based on Your Rates and Setup.

Time-of-use mode found in some power stations utilizes an integrated battery backup to reduce the time your appliances spend on the grid when rates are highest.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Can a power station help me save money on my electric bill? I reviewed enough units to know the opportunity is there if the station has a time-of-use mode (TOU, for short). Stations with this feature utilize integrated battery backups to reduce time spent on the grid when rates are highest. That sounds pretty cool, but I’ve often wondered just how much money it can actually save.

I discovered it depends on a number of factors. For your best chance to save the most money, you need to live in an area where variable electric rates are available. You also need to primarily use portable power for a whole-home backup system or on appliances that are always running, like a refrigerator, to get the most out of TOU mode. That’s because the cost of electricity is typically lowest in a variable-rate system when demand is at its lowest, during the middle of the night, for example.

Below is everything I’ve learned about setting up TOU mode on a portable power station and how to find out how much money this feature can save you over time.

Power stations with TOU mode tend to be large or designed for home backup, such as whole-home battery-based systems or models designed to back up one or two appliances, like refrigerators. But some smaller portable power stations offer this mode. Jackery’s HomePower series, including the 1000 Plus v2, for example, offers this mode within its mobile app.

If you’re someone who primarily uses portable power for camping trips and other activities, it’s worth noting that TOU mode may not be very useful to you. To effectively switch back and forth between peak and non-peak hours, the station must be consistently connected to grid power and the devices you want to run from it. It makes more sense to plan a TOU-based setup with a more dedicated type of power station, or a portable one that you don’t plan to move around very often.

First, you need to know if variable rates are available in your region and how they operate. Electrical utilities are not regulated at the federal level in the U.S., so this varies from state to state. Utilities in states that regulate their electric utilities may offer variable rates (sometimes called time-variable pricing), while states that deregulate may have variable-rate options through the various energy providers.

For example, in my home state of Pennsylvania, the primary electric company offers only flat rates. However, Pennsylvania is a deregulated market, so if I opt for a different energy provider, I can select one that offers variable rates. Some states, like Texas, even offer times of the day when rates are free.

In most cases, variable-rate programs require you to sign up in some form or another to activate these rates, so call your local provider to get the details of what is available to you.

Once you have that worked out, setting up your station is fairly straightforward. Choose the device or devices you wish to run partially during the day from battery power and connect them to the power station. Plug the power station into an outlet in the house. From there, everything is set in your power station’s app by selecting the TOU working mode, which can usually be found in the advanced settings.

The app then prompts you to enter the high-rate (peak) hours and the low-rate hours, along with the price for each rate (dollars per kilowatt-hour). This helps the app calculate savings over time, so you don’t have to. Once that is set up, the battery automatically powers your devices during peak hours and returns to the grid during low-rate hours. It also uses the low-rate hours to recharge the battery from the grid, or you can opt to recharge it from a portable solar panel.

If only flat rates are available to you, you could still use TOU mode and choose a set of hours each day to run on battery power; there just won’t be the advantage of opting for cheaper rate times.

The potential for saving money isn’t as simple to figure out. While the apps can generally track savings over time, variable rates can fluctuate (e.g., some utilities change them every few months), so unless you are keeping up with the fluctuation and adjusting the app accordingly, those numbers can be off.

The amount of actual savings is also tricky to predict. Much of it depends on how many devices in your home you plan to run using this mode and how low the rate is during off-peak hours. The latter will have the most effect, and the savings will be harder to realize if you’re only powering one or a few things.

For example, if you’re using Bluetti’s FridgePower to power only a refrigerator in TOU mode, that appliance typically only draws 300 watts on average, so the actual savings by running it from the grid only during off-peak hours might only equate to a few dollars per month, maybe even less. Then again, if you’re powering a lot of stuff in TOU mode using a large-capacity whole-home system, the savings will likely be more significant.

Something else to keep in mind is that the most expensive devices to run in your home are usually the higher-voltage systems such as heating/ventilation/air-conditioning (HVAC) and high-voltage appliances such as ovens and electric dryers. These need to be paired with stations that can handle 220/240-volt output (only the larger ones can) and need a significant amount of battery capacity to operate over several hours. This requires a large system with at least one or two additional batteries (if not more), which can cost several thousand dollars. The cost of chasing the savings enabled by the TOU mode could likely take a few years to actually be recouped.

While the money-saving potential can be a bit hard to estimate or feel significant, especially in the short term, this feature will shave something off your monthly bill, so it’s definitely worth looking into, especially if you have a large system that powers several always-on devices.

It might not be a reason to buy a power station for home backup, but it’s certainly a good feature to have at your disposal. It may not be a huge help, but there’s no real downside either.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. He has over 25 years of experience writing about and reviewing consumer electronics, kitchen appliances, DIY products, outdoor gear, and more. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with new recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

#6402. A New York City Weekend Guide for Design Lovers

The thing that makes visiting (or living in) New York worth every penny is that you don’t have to go out of your way looking for inspiration. You might be struck by a vintage sign advertising color TVs in the East Village; a grandpa on the Upper East Side pairing bright red socks with his loafers; or that never-gets-old view of the Brooklyn Bridge from an elevated subway track. Design is, indeed, everywhere in NYC, but sometimes you need a bit of a roadmap to plot your next moment of awe.

Like many New Yorkers, I derive a lot of joy from looking at pretty things and existing in cool spaces. When I feel like I’m staring at a blank page—or I just want to spend a weekend more intentionally—the places below are the ones I turn to for a creative spark. These spots span boroughs and cover art, architecture, and fashion—from former artist residences and Japanese-inspired stationery stores to restaurants and spas with covetable interiors.

For the aesthetes who have already seen the latest exhibition at MoMA, this weekend guide for design lovers is intended to point you in a few other directions (and no, this does not include that viral room full of dirt in SoHo).

The Cooper Hewitt is the only museum in the United States devoted exclusively to both historical and contemporary design.

For many New Yorkers, to go uptown is to go to the museum. And while the Metropolitan Museum of Art holds down the fort, there are a few other players along Museum Mile that always seem to take me by surprise whenever I visit. The Cooper Hewitt, for instance, showcases “design objects” in the broadest sense that span across centuries—you might find an Egyptian ceramic from 1100 BCE in one room, and a Swedish midcentury-modern lamp in another. It’s also a lovely hangout spot; earlier this year, the museum hosted a Hi-Fi listening room, and when the weather’s nice, visitors can take advantage of the garden (tickets are not required and Wi-Fi is free), admiring the gorgeous architecture of Andrew Carnegie’s former mansion.

The “Einspänner” at Sabarsky—double espresso with whipped cream.

A short walk away, the Neue Galerie, which specializes in early 20th-century German and Austrian art, is where I go to gush over furniture designed by the likes of Josef Hoffmann and Adolf Loos. The museum is set to reopen on November 12 for its 20th anniversary, but in the meantime, you can visit the stunning Café Sabarsky—the Viennese restaurant located within the museum—and pretend you’re at the helm of the next great intellectual movement with your friends over fancy whipped-cream-topped coffees.

Further downtown, in Midtown East, the Paul Rudolph Institute is a must for anyone who enjoyed The Brutalist. Join the monthly open house at the Rudolph-designed duplex within the iconic Modulightor building, once the headquarters of the lighting company the architect co-founded with his life partner, Ernst Wagner. Docents are on-site to answer any questions as you wind your way through the all-white apartment, with its disjointed staircases and built-in shelving units, though private tours are also available.

When it comes to shopping, I believe one can gain a lot from staring into the windows along Madison Avenue, or even heading inside to get a feel for the luxe fabrics, sans purchase. But for second-hand designer clothing, Upper East Vintage (by appointment only) and Designer Revival (Gentleman’s Resale is also right next door), both on the Upper East Side, are your best bet. I’m also always delighted by what I find at Spellman Gallery, a small showroom owned by an art appraiser with fantastic taste—you can discover all kinds of treasures, from a rare vinyl record to a painting worth a few thousand.

Browsing beautiful items will inevitably stir up an appetite, and for a restaurant that has tables equipped with landlines during live art auction sales, check out Marcel 945 Madison, housed inside the historic Breuer Building that is now the global headquarters of Sotheby’s. While the restaurant serves (very expensive) French bistro fare, it’s all about the rotating art on the walls—including works by Roy Lichtenstein and Willem de Kooning, to name a few past residents—which are also available for purchase.

With its glass blocks, chrome light fixtures, and black leather booths, Bridges in Chinatown is a design-lover's dream.

If you prefer to walk amongst grittier cast-iron buildings or people-watch from plastic stools, then it’s best you head downtown. Start with a trip to the Judd Foundation, where you can book a slot to explore 37 of minimalist Donald Judd’s artworks, each permanently installed in the late artist’s former residence and studio on Spring Street, and get a glimpse of how an artist lived and breathed in SoHo before the luxury flagships arrived. Over in Greenwich Village, the Renee and Chaim Gross Foundation boasts over 12,000 of American artist Chaim Gross’s sculptures, drawings, and prints, as well as his personal collection of global art. The late artist’s personal home, which he shared with his wife Renee, is light-filled and lived-in—an intimate experience that cannot be replicated at a traditional museum.

The Lower East Side, specifically Orchard Street, is where to go to shop independent designers. Browse Colbo—more of a multidisciplinary space than a retail store—for unisex neutrals as you sip an espresso. Adjacent to the shop, Colbo Next Door is a great spot to grab a glass of wine and listen to vinyl. Further along Orchard Street, you’ll find Lara Koleji for vintage Miu Miu, as well as Tumbao, a curation of the very best in Latin American fashion design. On East Broadway, also in the LES, Aeon Bookstore is one of my favorite bookstores in New York, a basement-level shop with a small-but-mighty selection of used titles, whether you’re looking for a coffee table book on the Bauhaus or a beautiful edition of Lolita.

Gem Home on Mott Street saves the day whenever I’m in need of a unique, last-minute gift—say, a stainless steel ice cream bowl or spiral toothbrush holder—and the shop, which is also a café, has recently started hosting dinners in collaboration with French pop-up Mon Petit Canard. Continuing on with the theme of downtown cool, Bridges is a swoon-worthy restaurant space that’s bound to get your interior design wheels turning, and there’s a famous Comté cheese tart that’s a work of art in and of itself.

If you've ever wondered what the subway looked like decades ago, the New York Transit Museum has your answer.

If you’re spending a day in Brooklyn, make sure to pop over to the New York Transit Museum in Downtown Brooklyn—talk about a celebration of design. In addition to touring over 20 different vintage train cars, you’ll view an otherwise quotidian part of New York City life in a new light. Graphic design nerds in particular will geek out over the exhibits dedicated to Massimo Vignelli, who designed the 1972 subway map we love and use today. For a different kind of museum experience, Pioneer Works in Red Hook was born out of a former 1866 red-brick warehouse, and today it’s dedicated to all kinds of arts and science programming. On view right now, for instance, is a multimedia exhibition by Helsinki-based artist Tuomas A. Laitinen, drawing on more than a decade of research on octopus intelligence, sleep, and consciousness.

There’s only one place I trust for buying jeans, and it’s Front General Store's Outpost, which boasts an entire wall of vintage Levi’s and then some—think worn-in Burberry trench coats, military deadstock, and new shoes from Japanese or British brands you might not have heard of. The vintage shopping in Brooklyn, of course, doesn’t stop there: 10 ft Single by Stella Dallas in Williamsburg is a reliable favorite for threadbare T-shirts and Ralph Lauren sweaters, and if you’re on the hunt for a conversation starter of a chair, Dream Fishing Tackle in Greenpoint is part fishing supply center, part midcentury-modern furniture store. If it wasn’t already clear, NYC loves a retail space that’s also something else: Chyelle in Bushwick and Apartment Ra’el in Bed-Stuy both serve up coffee and beautiful homeware. For those obsessed with paper and pens (guilty), Yoseka Stationery in Greenpoint stocks the very best in Japanese stationery design—from Hobonichi journals to Kaweco fountain pens.

In a sea of white-marbled wellness spaces, Spencer’s Spa in Williamsburg proves good design is integral to relaxation. I’ve had excellent facials at both the Brooklyn and SoHo locations, lingering for as long as possible afterwards in the lounge areas, which seem to take inspiration from traditional Japanese, Art Deco, and Scandinavian design (I like to take pictures of all the unique lamps and objects so I can reverse image search them for my apartment later on). But if you’d rather find your zen within New York City’s nightlife scene, James Murphy–owned club Nightmoves in Williamsburg, music venue Public Records in Gowanus, and listening bar Eavesdrop in Greenpoint all boast incredibly impressive custom sound design.

The Noguchi Museum is one of the most peaceful pockets of the city.

Akari Light Sculptures abound at the Noguchi Museum, and you can even bring one home.

A trip to Queens would not be complete without a visit to the Noguchi Museum in Astoria, where you can feel a sense of serenity walking around Isamu Noguchi’s biomorphic sculptures, then buy one of his Akari light sculptures in what is perhaps the best museum gift shop in New York City. While the museum is home to its own sculpture garden, there’s also one practically across the street—make sure you allot some time to strolling Socrates Sculpture Park, where you’ll encounter a whole host of experimental installations (they’re always rotating), with the Manhattan skyline as the backdrop.

In Long Island City, the industrial hub-turned-creative enclave in western Queens, MoMA PS1 is at once nostalgic and of-the-moment, showcasing contemporary art within former elementary school halls—it’s especially fun in the summer when it's running its Warm Up series, when everyone gathers outside for DJ sets and music performances. Also in the neighborhood, Somerset House is a staging and interior design gallery that sells collectible furniture and art—think Pierre Jeanneret armchairs and Poul Henningsen lamps—by appointment only. For something a bit more accessible, Lichen in Ridgewood sells a similar catalog of vintage furniture, plus its own in-house designs ranging from glass coffee tables to futuristic sconces.

This bank-turned-hotel features original vaulted ceilings that rival those of Grand Central Station. Sip a martini at the Swan Room, the property's see-and-be-seen lobby bar.

Situated in NoMad, The Fifth Avenue Hotel gives you access to both Museum Mile and downtown shopping. The 19th-century, Renaissance-style mansion is dressed in maximalism.

Once a barrel factory in the early 1900s, this hip Williamsburg hotel is your gateway to industrial-chic rooms, a cinema with red velvet seats, and the acclaimed Le Crocodile restaurant.

The Mercer is SoHo in a nutshell, with loft-like suites, a neutral color palette, and a buzzy restaurant. Minimalists, this one’s for you.

#6401. Three-quarters of NFL football players may end up with CTE

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

It’s the first population-level estimate for the neurogenerative disease among NFL players

The neurodegenerative disease CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy. The condition has been identified most frequently among American football players.

An estimated three-quarters of NFL players who died in a 16-year period had the devastating neurogenerative disease called CTE.

Back in 2017, researchers reported that an estimated 99 percent of former NFL players developed CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, from an analysis of donated brains. But the families who provided the donations may have done so because their football-playing relatives had symptoms related to CTE, which could skew the results. A new study, which accounts for this potential bias, estimates that nearly 75 percent of former NFL players have CTE at death. It’s the first population-level estimate for NFL players, researchers report October 28 in JAMA Network Open.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The development of CTE is linked to repeated blows to the head over time. The disease can occur in people who play contact sports, experience intimate partner violence or engage in military combat. A study of American football players suggests that the longer the duration of repeated head trauma, the higher the risk of CTE and the more severe the condition. During life, people who are later diagnosed with CTE can experience symptoms including memory issues, difficulty concentrating, depression and poor impulse control.

A brain protein called tau, which usually helps nerve cells communicate and performs other jobs, goes awry in CTE. Brains with the disease are snarled with irregular, damaging clumps of the protein. The condition is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy, and has been identified most frequently among American football players.

The new study, by a Boston University research team, included all previous NFL players who passed away from January 2008 through December 2023. The more than 2,300 players included almost 400 with samples in the university’s UNITE Brain Bank, with the remainder identified from records in the U.S. National Death Index. The research team determined that families of NFL players who had CTE-related symptoms in life were five times more likely to donate their relative’s brain than families whose relative did not experience symptoms. Taking that into consideration, the team landed on a population-level CTE estimate for NFL players of 74.5 percent.

The research team notes that determining the true prevalence of CTE is important to understanding the public health impact of the disease.

How did the universe transition from an impenetrable fog of hydrogen into the bright and starlit cosmos we see today? Astronomers think they're onto the answer.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The mysterious force that cleared the cosmic fog at the dawn of the universe may not be what we thought, a new study suggests. The results hint that astronomers may need to rethink a major aspect of cosmological evolution, which led to the universe we clearly see today.

Around 400,000 years after the Big Bang, the fledgling universe finally cooled enough to form atoms — mostly hydrogen. But these neutral, non-electrically charged hydrogen atoms shrouded the cosmos in a fog that made it opaque to ultraviolet (UV) light.

Then, after the first stars flickered to life and gathered into galaxies, bursts of radiation ionized the neutral hydrogen. This turned the impenetrable fog of atoms into electrically charged protons and electrons, allowing light to pass through interstellar space unimpeded and, eventually, reach our observatories. This cosmic curtain parting is known as the Epoch of Reionization, or what a team of researchers studying it call the "last major phase transition in the universe."

A chart showing the evolution of the universe, from the Big Bang to today. The first stars started to appear from the hydrogen fog a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

"We don't know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved," Cody Carr, an astronomer who focuses on galaxy evolution at the University of Michigan and first author of a new study of the epoch, said in a statement. "We know that it took place, but we don't have complete answers to those questions."

Astrophysicists previously thought that this fog-clearing effect depended on supernovas, the violently explosive deaths of stars around eight to 50 times the mass of the sun.

But in the new study, published Oct. 15 in the journal Nature Astronomy, Carr and colleagues presented evidence that supernovas exerted the opposite effect, trapping the so-called Lyman continuum (LyC) photons of ionizing UV radiation that dispelled the celestial fog instead of scattering them.

"The most interesting thing about our paper is the observation that the strongest LyC emitters do not have fast galactic winds," Carr told Live Science via email. "This challenges the notion that galaxies require fast supernova-driven winds to enable LyC escape."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers used the Hubble Space Telescope to observe an analogue of the ancient universe in the local cosmos: six star-forming, wind-launching galaxies around 3.5 billion light-years away.

These compact starburst galaxies are generally smaller than 6,500 light-years in diameter and form around 10 solar masses' worth of stars per year. That star-birthing rate is several times higher than that of the Milky Way, which is up to 20 times larger.

The galaxies' spectra, or light-based fingerprints, revealed the origin, chemical composition, speed and direction of their stellar winds, which were whipped up by the radiation from their newly formed stars.

The researchers also described how these processes changed as the massive young stars evolved and died in energetic supernovas several billion years later, with the resultant galactic winds overpowering the stellar winds.

These nearby galaxies highlighted a counterintuitive two-phase process.

In the initial phase, which occurred during the first 3 million years of star formation, the newly formed massive stars' stellar winds carved through their galaxies' neutral gas and dust at nearly 2,000 miles per second (3,000 kilometers per second). This allowed LyC light to escape the galaxy and ionize the neutral gas and dust in intergalactic space.

The second phase, which emerged around 3 million years after star formation, seemed to reverse this process. As O-type stars — the hottest, bluest and most massive stars in the cosmos — lived fast and died young, their expelled stellar guts added to the opaque galactic gas and dust, churning it and loading it with mass, which created a trap for LyC light.

The oldest galaxies in this study ‪—‬ and, therefore, the ones with the fastest supernova-generated galactic winds ‪—‬ allowed the least amount of ionizing radiation to escape their environs.

"In general, our results are in disagreement with most cosmological simulations, which typically show the LyC escape fraction peaking after the launch of supernova-driven winds," Carr explained via email. In other words, supernovas didn't drive the Epoch of Reionization, but they may have dampened it. The intense light of newborn stars now seems like the most viable source of reionization.

Future research could aim to obtain additional galactic samples and higher-resolution observations across other wavelengths.

Carr, C., Cen, R., McCandliss, S., Ford, J., Saldana-Lopez, A., Scarlata, C., Huberty, M. S., Jaskot, A., Flury, S., Oey, M. S., Amorín, R. O., Borthakur, S., Haye, M., Heckman, T., Ji, Z., Komarova, L., Reste, A. L., Leclercq, F., Marques-Chaves, R., . . . Xu, X. (2026). Lyman continuum escape during the onset of galactic winds in compact starbursts. Nature Astronomy. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-026-02999-z

#6398. Sleep Under the Stars at These Incredible Igloo-Like Airbnbs Around the World

Few travel experiences are as otherworldly as watching the night sky from the cozy cocoon of a glass-topped igloo. In the far north, that might mean watching the aurora borealis shimmer overhead, surrounded by pine forests and frozen lakes. But you don't have to travel to the Arctic Circle to experience an igloo-like stay. From snow-covered mountain landscapes in Germany to peaceful corners of Spain, these unusual stays can be found in some unexpected places across Europe and beyond.

The impressive northern lights in Finnish Lapland

Many interiors lean into a Nordic theme—think Scandi-style decor, underfloor heating, faux-fur throws, and panoramic windows designed to maximise stargazing. In Nordic destinations, many of these igloos give you the chance to enjoy classic experiences nearby, such as husky and reindeer sledding, cold-water swimming, or a spell in a geothermal spa. Elsewhere, the appeal might be waking up to mountain views, exploring the surrounding countryside, or simply enjoying the novelty of sleeping inside a transparent dome.

Wrap up, pour a hot chocolate, and settle in—here are the best igloos to bed down in for a memorable night under the stars.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Pet-friendly, private deck, hot tub

Set within 45 acres of secluded private woodland, this spacious dome is a cozy base for exploring the surrounding walking trails by day and stargazing after dark, thanks to the area's limited light pollution. Inside, there's a king-size bed, two fold-out single beds, armchairs, and a dining area, as well as a private bathroom with a hot shower and a small kitchenette equipped with a microwave, kettle, toaster, and fridge. Outside, the deck has plenty of seating and a barbecue, while a covered Scandinavian wood-fired hot tub overlooking the surrounding countryside can be used for an extra charge. Dogs are welcome too, making this a good option if you don't want to leave four-legged family members behind.

Location: Shropshire, United KingdomThings to do nearby: Ludlow Castle, Tenbury Museum, Mortimer Forest

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Lake views, fireplace, air-conditioning, hot tub

Perched on a hillside above Lake Superior, this geodesic dome combines the feel of camping with all the comforts of home. Designed to be enjoyed year-round, it has a gas fireplace and heating for chilly Minnesota winters, as well as air-conditioning for warmer summer days. There's room for up to four guests, with a queen bed and a second lofted bed, plus a fully equipped kitchen and bathroom with a walk-in shower. The highlight, though, is the large private deck, where a hot tub overlooks the lake and can be used throughout the year. The town of Two Harbors is also just a short drive away, with cafés, restaurants, shops and a local brewery.

Location: Two Harbors, MinnesotaThings to do nearby: Two Harbors town, Pierre the Voyager, Two Harbors Pierhead Light, Rock Beach

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: Studio, shared bathWhy we love it: Fjord views, secluded location, terrace

Perched on rocky terrain above Trondheim Fjord, Dome Smiberget makes the most of its spectacular waterfront setting. The geodesic dome feels wonderfully secluded, surrounded by trees with little between you and the water below. Inside, a wall of honeycomb-shaped windows wraps around the bed and seating area, framing sweeping views across the fjord and letting you watch the sky change without stepping outside. Come evening, you can stargaze from bed, while a small private terrace overlooking the water makes an idyllic spot to sit out when the weather plays along.

Location: Indre Fosen, NorwayThings to do nearby: Ulvestøtta monument, Sukkertoppen mountain hikes

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Outdoor grill, swimming pond, boules court

Drive through the scenic Dresden Elbe meadows to reach this rüdehof, which serves as both the headquarters of a family distillery and a tranquil countryside retreat—best enjoyed under a layer of icing-sugar snow in winter. The igloo is more like a hobbit house, with all you need to shelter from the cold, including a double bed, compact kitchen, shower room, and a dining area with panoramic, bucolic views. You're secluded as can be, around 90 minutes from Hamburg within a two-hectare wild and rugged estate, now yours to explore at your leisure. Stoke the fire and grill outdoors at suppertime, then settle in for some stargazing. If you're feeling brave, there's a swimming pond; then warm up in the hot tub afterwards. A boules court is available for a few leisurely games before supper.

Location: Amt Neuhaus, Niedersachsen, GermanyThings to do nearby: Stixer Wanderdüne hiking paths, Alte Eiche Forsthaus grüner Jäger momumental oak tree, Hamburg

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Fireplace, sledding, northern lights viewing

This is glamping, but not as most know it. On the cusp of Rovaniemi's thick pine forests, this igloo is furnished in true Nordic style with thick down blankets, plenty of wool rugs, cozy bedding, and a crackling log fireplace to huddle around in the evenings. Wrap up and head into the garden for wintry fun, including sledding—or simply huddle under the duvet to watch as frost forms and snow falls gently behind the windows.

Location: Rovaniemi, FinlandThings to do nearby: Ounasvaara Ski Oy ski resort, Ounasvaara Winter Trail, Forestry Museum of Lapland

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Panoramic views, breakfast included, kitchenette station

Spain isn't the first place you'd think of for igloo adventures, but this Airbnb might just change your mind. Deep in Spain's Selva de Irati forest, this immersive retreat pairs stylish design with wild beauty, perched on a hilltop overlooking the lush Aezkoa Valley. Interiors are simple and sparse, leaving space to focus on the comfortable silence and the nature that surrounds—there are dreamy panoramic views over the mountains from every angle. Previous guests have loved this experience, saying the sunsets from here are especially lovely. For something a little different, it's hard to beat.

Location: Orbaizeta, SpainThings to do nearby: Mirador de Zamariain viewpoint, Museo de Roncesvalles, Irati Forest

#6397. November 2026: What’s in the sky this month?

Saturn is already visible as darkness falls; some challenging transits of its moons occur this month. Neptune is a binocular object close to Saturn, while Uranus is an easy target in Taurus. A Full Moon courses in front of the Pleiades in late November. Mars and Jupiter dominate the early-morning sky, and in the hour before dawn, look also for Venus and Mercury.

Neptune and Saturn are well placed for observation after sunset. They’re about 7° apart all month, with Neptune in southern Pisces and Saturn just across the border in Cetus. Only Saturn is visible to the naked eye, shining at magnitude 0.5. Neptune, at magnitude 7.7, requires binoculars to spot.

Swing 7×50 binoculars one field of view west of Saturn and look for a parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars: 27, 29, 30, and 33 Piscium. Neptune is within 3° northeast of 29 Psc all month. A waning gibbous Moon hangs 5° northwest of Neptune’s location on the 19th. The following night, Saturn is 6° south of the Moon.

As the month opens, Saturn is 24° high in the east an hour after sunset, reaching 50° by 9 p.m. local time following its opposition last month. It’s observable overnight and by the end of November sets by 2 a.m. local time. The rings are angled 6° to our line of sight and reveal their southern side. The planet spans 19″ through a telescope and the disk exhibits a pale yellowish hue. Atmospheric details are tricky to spot unless you have very good conditions.

Titan, Saturn’s brightest moon (magnitude 8.3), sits closest to the planet Nov. 8 and 24 (north), and Nov. 16 (south). Tenth-magnitude Tethys, Dione, and Rhea orbit closer in. Dione and Tethys transit Saturn’s disk this month. These transits and shadow transits are extremely challenging. They’re good targets for advanced observers with video imaging experience. Visit Astronomy.com for more details on the timing of their transits if you’d like to try for them.

Iapetus reaches greatest eastern elongation Nov. 10, when it stands 9.4′ east of Saturn. The moon’s darker face is turned earthward, dimming it to magnitude 11.9. It’s hard to find but as the month progresses, Iapetus brightens nearly a magnitude by the time it reaches inferior conjunction early on the 30th, 1.7′ due north of Saturn.

Uranus remains midway between Aldebaran and the Pleiades (M45). This position makes the planet easier to find than in previous years. It reaches opposition Nov. 25, visible from dusk to dawn. From 1.71 billion miles away, its disk spans 4″. Uranus shines at magnitude 5.6, within easy range of binoculars and potentially visible to the unaided eye from the darkest skies.

To find Uranus, look between Aldebaran and M45 for two stars: 37 and 39 Tauri (4.5° southeast of M45). Brighter 37 Tau glows at magnitude 4.4. On Nov. 1, Uranus is 1.6° southeast of 37 Tau, and by the end of November stands 1.5° due south of this star. Another star, some 2.7° southeast of 37 Tau, shines at magnitude 5.5. This is 43 Tau; in mid-November, Uranus is halfway between the two stars.

The Full Moon crosses the Pleiades early on Nov. 24, setting up a series of occultations of the northern part of the cluster just before dawn across the western half of the U.S. You’ll need a telescope — plan for higher magnification so you can place the brilliant Moon largely out of your field of view. Fifth-magnitude Celaeno is the first of the cluster’s brighter stars to be occulted, around 6 a.m. CST. Both visibility and timing heavily depend on your location, so set up at least 30 minutes before the event starts. You can download timings for the brightest occultations from 40 major North American cities from the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

Mars and Jupiter rise close together in Leo. They meet in a conjunction midmonth not far from Leo’s brightest star, Regulus. Mars rises first, soon after midnight on the 1st, followed by Jupiter about 30 minutes later. Jupiter shines at magnitude –2.0 and Mars at 0.8. They’re hard to miss.

On Nov. 1, Jupiter stands midway between Mars and Regulus, each just over 5° from its neighbor. A waning gibbous Moon sits in Cancer only a few degrees west of M44, the Beehive star cluster. On the 2nd, Mars and the Moon are 1.5° apart, and by the 3rd the Moon lies less than 2° from Regulus as they rise in the Midwest. Mars and Jupiter close in on each other, and by the 15th Mars is 1.2° due north of Jupiter.

Mars continues eastward, reaching a point 1.7° due north of Regulus on the 25th. By the 30th, Mars is just over 2° northeast of Regulus and is rejoined by the waning gibbous Moon, just southwest of Regulus. Through a telescope at the end of November, Mars has reached 8″ in diameter and its magnitude has increased to 0.4.

Home to the most visibly dynamic atmosphere in the solar system, Jupiter has a lot to offer through a telescope. The planet shows off a 36″-wide disk on the 1st, which grows to 39″ by the 30th. The hour before dawn can hold remarkable views if there is steady seeing. Look for the occasional appearance of the Great Red Spot.

Jupiter’s moons and their shadows often transit the planet or are eclipsed by it. Nov. 8 finds Io and Callisto transiting Jupiter’s disk along with Io’s shadow. Soon after, Europa exits from an occultation. East Coast observers will see the whole event; the Pacific Coast, only the latter half. It begins as Io’s shadow appears on the planet’s eastern limb at 1:29 a.m. EST, followed 24 minutes later by the reappearance of Europa from behind Jupiter. Callisto’s transit begins at 2:07 a.m. EST. Io approaches the eastern limb, passing due north of Europa at 2:23 a.m. EST and beginning its transit 19 minutes later. Because of Io’s faster orbital speed compared with Callisto, it overtakes the larger moon within half an hour. Io’s shadow exits the disk at 3:45 a.m. EST, and Io itself ends its transit 74 minutes later. Callisto’s transit ends at 5:51 a.m. CST, as the sky is growing light in the Midwest.

Ganymede’s huge shadow crosses Jupiter’s face Nov. 11. The start of the transit at 12:27 a.m. EST is visible from the Eastern time zone; it ends at 4:03 a.m. EST, visible across the U.S. Ganymede begins to transit at 5:29 a.m. EST.

Ganymede, Europa, and Io orbit in resonance, so similar events recur, although they are not always observable. On Nov. 15, Io’s shadow begins a transit at 3:22 a.m. EST. Europa reappears at 4:27 a.m. EST, with Io close to the limb. They pass north-south just seven minutes later. Io’s transit begins at 4:36 a.m. EST. Its shadow leaves at 5:38 a.m. EST, and Io departs at 5:52 a.m. CST (in daylight for EST). Ganymede’s shadow transits again three days later, Nov. 18, from 4:25 a.m. EST to 6:01 a.m. MST (note the time zone change).

On Nov. 22, Io and its shadow are already transiting by the time Europa reappears. Io’s shadow transit starts at 5:15 a.m. EST; Io follows at 5:29 a.m. CST, with the sky very bright along the East Coast. Europa reappears at Jupiter’s eastern limb at 6:00 a.m. CST, as twilight begins in the Midwest and visible in darkness farther west.

To cap off the month, watch Ganymede reappear from behind Jupiter Nov. 29 at 5:53 a.m. CST (minutes before sunrise in EST), followed by Io’s shadow transit starting a few minutes later, at 6:08 a.m. CST. Io is due north of Ganymede at 6:49 a.m. CST, seen in twilight in the Midwest.

Mercury is at inferior conjunction Nov. 4, then moves into the morning sky. Northern Hemisphere observers gain good views in the second half of the month. Look for it Nov. 13, when it’s magnitude 0.5. An hour before sunrise, it is 4° high in the eastern sky, nearly 13° to the lower left of Venus. Swing binoculars toward Mercury to spot 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis 0.9° north of the planet.

Mercury reaches its greatest western elongation 20° from the Sun late on Nov. 20. The next morning, it shines at magnitude –0.5 and stands 7° high an hour before sunrise, easy to spot with a clear eastern horizon. Mercury displays a 62%-lit globe when viewed with a telescope, though it spans only 7″, so you’ll need steady air to see the phase. That phase grows to 84% by Nov. 30.

On Nov. 4, look for Venus 2° south of 1st-magnitude Spica, Virgo’s brightest star. A 25-day-old crescent Moon stands high above the pair. Three days later, on Nov. 7, Venus, Spica, and the Moon lie close together in the morning sky. Venus is 1.3° from Spica, with the waning crescent Moon about 2° below Venus, a stunning view in the brightening twilight. Venus rises about 100 minutes before the Sun and the trio is 11° high at 6 a.m. local time.

Venus reaches a stationary point Nov. 11. From the 10th to the 12th, Venus appears not to move in right ascension relative to Spica, as the planet slides due north to stand 1.2° due west of Spica on the 10th.

Check out Venus with a telescope. The bright planet becomes easier on the eyes as twilight grows, reducing the contrast. It’s already dazzling at magnitude –4.2 on the 1st, when its disk is 3% lit. By Nov. 15 it is 14% lit and magnitude –4.8, and reaches its greatest illuminated extent Nov. 29 at magnitude –4.9 and 27% lit. If you’re under Bortle 1 or 2 skies, can you see your shadow? Venus rises more than three hours before the Sun, so you’ll have a dark sky for an hour or so to check.

Much of the Moon’s history is encapsulated in one feature: the crater Schickard, way down in the lunar southwest. Protective measures are necessary to comfortably carry out this observation. Screw in a dark filter, mask off part of your scope’s aperture, or pump up the magnification to reduce the glare of an almost full lunar disk.

Start on the evening of the 21st, when the rays of sunlight strike the flooded crater at a glancing angle, highlighting the differences in height of the smaller features. This is an old crater, its rounded rim pounded down across the ages. The splatter of smaller craters across the smooth floor sport the classic sharp edges of relative youth. The western wall, steep at the instant of formation, slumped abruptly down into terraces that remain visible to this day. Shadows disappear over the next two evenings as the climbing Sun almost erases these features.

During the following nights, Schickard transforms into a two-faced striped crater, an unusual swath of lighter gray painted across the middle of this time-worn feature. The 130-mile-wide depression was carved out some 4 billion years ago as bombardment was ending. Lava soon welled up and covered its central peaks. Then the giant Orientale impact event to the west sprayed the whole region with lighter-hued material. A final surge of lava managed to cover the northern and southern portions, but did not rise enough to erase the lighter stripe.

This year’s annual Leonid meteor shower is active from Nov. 6 to 30 and peaks Nov. 17/18. A nine-day-old gibbous Moon sets right around midnight on this night, favoring the best time for meteor observing, which is after midnight. That’s when we’re on the leading hemisphere as Earth plows into the meteoroid stream.

Leo is also rising around local midnight and the radiant, located in the Sickle asterism, climbs to more than 60° in altitude by dawn. But don’t look at the radiant — meteors come head-on from that direction. Longer trails occur 40° to 60° away from Leo.

Rates are predicted to be 15 meteors per hour if the radiant were overhead. If you get more than a half-dozen per hour, you’re doing well. If you want a change, spend some time with Jupiter (also in Leo) through a telescope — Ganymede’s shadow is transiting the morning of the 18th.

The Leonids are known to be swift and some leave glowing, persistent trains, which are fascinating to experience. The shower is associated with Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which last reached perihelion in 1998.

Comet 10P/Tempel is floating halfway between Fomalhaut and Beta (β) Ceti. It’s about 10th magnitude, but historically has had post-perihelion outbursts, which could help it shine through the thicker air near the ground.

Meanwhile, Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS is higher and in a more interesting sky as darkness settles.

The Moon-free window closes after the 14th but reopens on the 27th. To see this 10th-magnitude fuzzy, a site well away from city lights is needed. Despite Earth’s increasing distance, the comet is sunward bound for perihelion Nov. 27, so its magnitude is fairly constant.

The short, broad fan should sport a circular green coma that looks great on images as it floats across the rich Milky Way north of Altair. At month’s end, Hartley-IRAS lies within 3° of the Coathanger asterism. Visually, a 4-inch scope can pull it in, but a larger one will show more detail, especially the sharp south flank where the solar wind pushes away the expelled dust in a bow shock.

Discovered in 1983, the comet returns every 21.5 years. Next month will be our last chance for a good look until two revolutions down the road, in 2069.

With five minutes of dark adapting, it’s easy to follow a main-belt asteroid along a retrograde curve. Saturn leads the way to 4 Vesta in the midevening sky — just drop down 9°, two binocular fields, to 25 Ceti, a magnitude 5.4 candle compared to the other nearby 8th- to 9th-magnitude stellar points. None of those will get confused with the brighter asteroid.

Use 25 Ceti and the more northerly 20 Ceti (closer to Saturn) to anchor a sketch or your memory. Watch a simple hockey stick pattern morph every three nights or so into a golf club, and then become a vertical line.

Spanning about 320 miles, Vesta is the second-largest body in the main belt. It was initially thought to be a chunk of the “missing” world astronomers expected between Mars and Jupiter. We now know it is an unfinished building block left over from the formation of the solar system, a rocky mantle surrounding an iron core.

The map below portrays the sky as seen near 35° north latitude. Located inside the border are the cardinal directions and their intermediate points. To find stars, hold the map overhead and orient it so one of the labels matches the direction you’re facing. The stars above the map’s horizon now match what’s in the sky.

The all-sky map shows how the sky looks at:

9 p.m. November 18 p.m. November 157 p.m. November 30

#6395. A striking Mars cloud may be born from surprising physics

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud might not need dust to kick-start its formation

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud emerges every day during spring and summer on Mars, a long wispy ribbon downwind of the Arsia Mons volcano. This image of the cloud was captured by a camera aboard the European Space Agency’s Mars Express mission.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

One of Mars’ strangest clouds may rely on unusual physics to emerge.

The Red Planet’s ribbonlike cloud — which stretches as long as four Grand Canyons laid end-to-end — may form without a speck of starting material to seed it, researchers report October 7 in Nature Geoscience. This manner of forming clouds, called homogenous nucleation, was thought to be possible on paper but not to occur naturally.

Tiny particles such as dust or salt floating in the air seed typical clouds on Earth. But that cloud physics doesn’t seem to apply to the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud. Beyond its impressive length, this wisp of water ice is remarkably consistent, forming daily in the same spot roughly 45 kilometers high on the slope of a Martian volcano for several months each year.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The team tried and tried but couldn’t reproduce the cloud’s formation, including its lengthy tail and consistent cycle, with computer models employing standard cloud physics, says François Forget, an astrophysicist at the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique, or LMD, in Paris.

There’s no shortage of dust on Mars. The trouble is that high up in a thin Martian atmosphere, few cloud-forming dust particles stay suspended. Instead, they probably clump together and eventually fall, says planetary physicist Jorge Hernández-Bernal, who did the work at LMD. This left cloud formation without seeds as the most convincing explanation, he says.

Every day during some seasons on Mars, a long wispy cloud emerges along the flanks of the Arsia Mons volcano, as seen in the observations video spanning three Martian hours. How that cloud forms has been a mystery. A new simulation, bottom, included unusual physics, in which clouds form without starting material. That approach replicated the shape and timing of Mars’ Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud for the first time.

The team’s model suggests that the eye-catching plume originates when air flowing across the volcano triggers a rapid lifting of a moist parcel of air. The decrease in pressure at that altitude lets the air parcel expand, rapidly cooling it.

The newly cooled air now has 100,000 times more moisture than it can hold, the team’s model suggests. This excess moisture undergoes homogenous nucleation, rapidly forming more stable ice crystals. Winds sweep the forming cloud outward, creating the cloud’s distinctive long shape.

While the model doesn’t perfectly match satellite observations, it does capture how the phenomenon that leads to the cold air pocket reoccurs day after day, just like the real cloud does.

The study was surprising because “homogeneous nucleation is generally treated in our field as this theoretical concept,” says Samuel Atwood, an atmospheric and planetary scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., who was not associated with the study.

“It’s a pretty compelling story that they’re telling with the model, but it’s only one view or one perspective on it,” Atwood says, adding that future measurements supporting the team’s finding will provide more certainty. Hernández-Bernal says that he plans to validate the study by testing alternative explanations.

Even beyond Mars, the study provides food for thought. Previous studies have suggested that on Earth, meteor smoke provides particles for cloud formation in an upper layer of the atmosphere called the mesosphere, though a few studies have suggested homogenous nucleation could be responsible. Now that scientists are proposing homogenous nucleation on Mars, Hernández-Bernal says, “maybe there will be an increased interest in investigating this on Earth.”

D.E. Siskind et al. Understanding the effects of polar mesospheric clouds on the environment of the upper mesosphere and lower thermosphere. Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres. 2018. doi: 10.1029/2018JD028830

#6394. The Sky Today on Sunday, November 1: The Moon in Cancer

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

October 31: Glimpse the ghostly Phantom Galaxy

Daylight saving time ends at 2 A.M. local daylight time this morning, when clocks fall back one hour to 1 A.M. local standard time.

Early this morning, the waning gibbous Moon is in Cancer, just west of the naked-eye Beehive Cluster (M44). The cluster might be hard to catch today without optical aid due to the nearby light of our satellite, but should show up nicely in binoculars or even your telescope’s finder scope. Its stars are spread so widely — across nearly 100’ of sky — that observing them through a telescope at higher magnification only shows the cluster’s central regions.

East of the Moon, Mars and Jupiter shine brightly in western Leo, to the upper right of the bright star Regulus. Brighter Jupiter should be particularly easy to spot, located halfway between the Red Planet and the blue-white star.

The Moon will reach Last Quarter phase this afternoon at 3:28 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 6:29 A.M.Sunset: 4:57 P.M.Moonrise: 11:23 P.M.Moonset: 1:11 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (47%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

By 5 A.M. local time on November 2, western Leo is more than 50° high in the southeast. The Moon lies just to Mars’ upper right, roughly 1.5° southwest of the Red Planet’s position and 6.3° west-northwest of Jupiter. The gas giant is by far the brightest light here, shining at magnitude –2.0. This morning it lies halfway between the Moon and Regulus to its lower left (east), Leo’s alpha star and the base of the Sickle asterism.

This view offers a great opportunity to see just how far the Moon travels through our sky in a day. By tomorrow morning at the same time, Luna will have moved some 14° to the east, passing close to Regulus and standing southeast of the star in the early-morning sky at the same time. Make sure to check out the view tomorrow for comparison.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6393. The 15 Most Haunted Places in the World and How to Visit Them

The most haunted places in the world may seem like something out of a fable that defies all logic. They're places where UFOs hover over Transylvanian forests, headless queens roam through castle corridors, and ghosts take shape of bears, children, and any other creature imaginable. No matter where you’re traveling, you’re sure to find some sort of haunted landmark, hotel, even landmark-turned-hotel—and usually a ghost tour to go along with it.

You might be guided more by scholarly than ghastly pursuits, though these locations are still worth your time. Spectral hauntings often come with spectacular history, architecture, and artwork, not to mention proximity to incredible cities and natural beauty. Whether you’re scheming up a Halloween trip or simply want to entertain the chills with a dash of the macabre, explore 15 of the most haunted places in the world below, if you dare.

Over the span of nearly one millennium, the Tower of London has served as an armory, prison, menagerie, and palace. Though best known today for its housing of the Crown Jewels, the UNESCO World Heritage Site also falls among the most haunted places in the United Kingdom. It's not uncommon to hear strange noises echo through the White Tower, while over a dozen ghosts—with backstories that range from ridiculous to outright tragic—are said to lurk in its limestone hallways.

The most infamous apparition is that of Anne Boleyn, Henry VIII's second wife, who was executed in the tower in 1536 for being found guilty for treason and adultery. Today, some visitors may encounter her headless body roaming about, head in hand. Other specters include two young princes who were mysteriously murdered in the 1400s and even multiple accounts of a phantom bear, who made multiple appearances in the 1800s and was said to leave any witness dead.

There are two long-running explanations for the curses that plague this 16th-century fort in Rajasthan. The first is that a religious ascetic had destroyed the fort and nearby towns after its height surpassed that of his own home, casting Bhangarh in perpetual shadow. The second, equally melodramatic, is that a black magic priest fell in love with a princess and was crushed to death by a boulder after she rejected him; right before he passed, however, he condemned the premises to a fate of destruction.

Today, the scene at the fort is quite serene, and visitors can wander throughout royal palace ruins, Hindu temples such as Gopinath and Hanuman, as well as old marketplaces and townhouses like Nartakiyon Ki Haveli. The fort is open each day from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., as no visitors—those living, at least—can legally stay after sunset.

Built by lumber magnate Carl Beck for his family in the late 1800s, this house in Penetanguishene is one of Ontario's most troublesome. Legend goes that after Beck's wife passed away, his eldest daughter Mary was put in charge of raising her younger siblings. Years later, when Carl died, he inexplicably left Mary $1 in his will. Today, an angry female ghost—presumably Mary—is said to appear in the upstairs windows (you’d probably haunt the house too if your dad gave you a $1 inheritance). For any travelers curious about Victorian architecture with a side of paranormality, consider renting the Carl Beck House on Airbnb.

What's far scarier than a haunted graveyard? A haunted graveyard 50 feet underwater. Micronesia’s Chuuk Lagoon (formerly Truk Lagoon) served as a fortified base for the Japanese Navy during World War II and was attacked by American forces during a three-day air strike in 1944. Dozens of warships, planes, tanks, and railroad cars sank to the bottom of the lagoon, where they still remain in what is known as the “Ghost Fleet of Truk Lagoon.”

The ship graveyard is immensely popular amongst scuba divers, with PADI dubbing it “one of the best wreck diving destinations on the planet.” Underwater explorers can swim up close to the wartime vessels, which are littered with weapons, gas masks, and, according to some superstitious divers, a few waterlogged ghosts.

This Victorian-era prison in Belfast is often referred to as Europe’s Alcatraz and for good reason. During its 150 years of operation, the jail contained some 25,000 inmates (men, women, and children), publicly hung many prisoners, and buried their bodies within the prison walls. The institution officially shut its doors in 1996, but the ghosts of deceased inmates are said to still roam the iron walkways today.

If this sounds like the sort of place you want to spend time in, you’re in luck—Crumlin Road Gaol offers daily tours, live concerts, and reasonably priced meals at its in-house (in-prison?) restaurant. It even serves as a venue for conferences and, believe it or not, weddings.

Though travelers have been coming to Estes Park since 1909 to enjoy The Stanley Hotel’s stately Georgian architecture and world-renowned whiskey bar, its reputation took a dark turn on October 30, 1974, when Stephen King and his wife, Tabitha, checked in. The hotel was about to close for the season, and the couple were the only guests there. King was particularly struck by the endless empty corridors that he walked through after dinner, and the property as a whole ended up serving as inspiration for The Shining’s Overlook Hotel.

Of the eerie stay, King said, “[The hotel] seemed the perfect—maybe the archetypical—setting for a ghost story. That night I dreamed of my three-year-old son running through the corridors, looking back over his shoulder, eyes wide, screaming. He was being chased by a fire-hose. I woke up with a tremendous jerk, sweating all over, within an inch of falling out of bed.” In the years since, the hotel has leaned into the reputation King bestowed upon it with ghost tours and a resident psychic.

Named after a shepherd who, along with his flock of 200 sheep, vanished without a trace in the forest, Hoia-Baciu hit it big in 1968 when a military technician photographed a supposed UFO hovering over the trees. Some believe it to be a portal capable of transporting visitors to places unknown. Those who pass through (and live to tell the tale) have reported rashes, nausea, and anxiety. The curved, spindly trees that make up the forest are particularly conducive to a twisted feeling, as is the location in Transylvania—a real nexus point of abnormal activity.

The St. Augustine Lighthouse is visited by over 200,000 people annually, though it's just as well-known for its otherworldly guests. Several tragic events that occurred at the now-historic site have contributed to the alleged paranormal activity. The ghost of a lighthouse keeper who fell to his death while painting the tower has been spotted watching over the grounds. Ever since the horrific death of three young girls, who drowned when the cart they were playing in broke and fell into the ocean, visitors have claimed to hear the sounds of children playing in and around the lighthouse.

Less than half a mile from the canals of Venice, Poveglia Island has served as a quarantine zone for bubonic plague victims, storage space for Napoleon’s weapons, and the site of an early 20th-century psychiatric hospital. The latter played host to horrific medical experiments and finally closed for good in 1968 after a doctor threw himself off the institution’s bell tower. Locals still claim to hear echoing chimes from the island—even though the bell was removed decades ago. Though it's illegal to visit Poveglia, you can see the island and decaying hospital at a safe distance from the beaches of nearby Lido or by hiring your own boat charter to pass a little closer (do not disembark onto the island).

Himeji Castle dates to 1333 and is regarded as one of the greatest remaining examples of Japanese castle architecture. It also has some rather eerie folklore associated with it—most notably the story of Okiku, a palace servant who was falsely accused of losing valuable dishes and thrown to her death in the castle’s well as punishment. Her ghost now sulks in the castle at night, counting dishes in a mournful tone; she reaches nine before shrieking and returning to the well’s depths. A visit to Himeji Castle is best done as a day trip from Osaka, about two hours away by train.

On the northern edge of Ireland's Wicklow Mountains, at the summit of Montpelier Hill, the ruins of a lone building remain. As many tales begin, the hill was originally site to an ancient grave, which wealthy Irishman William Conolly disregarded (even taking stones from) while building a hunting lodge in the 1720s. It's no surprise that terror ensued, and after Conolly's death, private club Hell Fire Club occupied the space, where they were said to engage in black masses, ritual murder, and other occultish happenings. At one such meeting, an unfamiliar guest with horse hooves as feet disappeared as mysteriously as they arrived. A curious farmer who had witnessed another night unfold was apparently left so terrified he no longer remembered his own name. Today, an enormous black cat with striking eyes is said to haunt Montpelier, which, beyond its murky past, offers forest trails and guided paths that make for an otherwise pleasant walk (before dusk).

Hidden among the canals of Xochimilco, Isla de las Muñecas (“Island of the Dolls”) is something of an internet legend and dark tourism mecca. The backstory centers on a man named Julian Santa Barrera, who reportedly encountered the body of a girl floating in the channels. Shortly thereafter, he found a discarded doll in the same canals, and he hung it from a tree on an artificial island in her honor—and to ward off evil spirits. So he continued, adding more and more dolls to appease the ghost of the young girl.

After Barrera passed away in 2001, his family opened the island to the public, and travelers have been seeking it out ever since. As if the mere idea of the island isn’t unnerving enough, there have also been reports of the dolls whispering to each other and moving their eyes.

Often considered the “king of Czech castles,” this early Gothic fortress in South Bohemia has undergone sieges and assaults from the 1400s onward, though, today, the source of its terrors is an impish creature called Rarášek, who is said to trip and poke at any unassuming visitor. A ghastly woman, known only as “the White Lady,” also resides here, while hellhounds allegedly guard a secret passage to the castle tombs.

Beyond the paranormal, visitors can enjoy self-guided tours through Zvíkov's cellars, courtyards, and rooms—be sure to stop and take a look at St. Wenceslas Chapel's frescoes.

The entire city of Savannah is essentially one giant ghost story, due in large part to the mysterious tunnels that run below the town’s streets. The underground structures play a major role in many of Savannah's most haunted locations, including Forsyth Park, the fountained green space you probably recognize from a postcard or two.

According to Savannah Magazine, doctors at the adjacent Candler Hospital (now the Savannah Law School) performed autopsies in the tunnels below. Maria Pinheiro, a historian and spokesperson with Ghost City Tours, says these below-the-surface rumblings make Forsyth Park particularly ripe for sightings of shadowy shapes that, even if unclear, it's certain they are not of this world.

We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.
