#6341. The 9 Best Binoculars, According to Our Tests and Research

See the world in greater detail with one of these recommended models.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Despite ubiquitous satellite imagery, incredible smartphone cameras, and a video doorbell on almost every house, there’s still incredible power in witnessing something with your own eyes. Unfortunately, despite eyesight being our dominant sense, our optics have some real limitations. Binoculars are considered relatively old technology, but they’re still recognized as the best tool to reach for when identifying a far-off animal or examining details on a backyard bird.

Hunters use binoculars to spot and pick out details on their quarry thousands of yards away, birders confirm species they’re identifying, and stargazers zoom in on constellations. They’re also just handy to keep in your house or even your vehicle for those moments when you just want to “see for yourself.”

You can extend your vision with telescopes, spotting scopes, and even zoom camera lenses, but the comfort and ease of use are why binoculars have such enduring appeal. Monocular devices—spotting scopes, for instance—can put strain on your eyes after only a few minutes, while binoculars offer a much more natural extension of normal vision, making them more comfortable for long sessions and easier for beginners to use. Binoculars are also lighter than those similar devices, which makes them packable and portable for trips into nature where they offer a more intimate look at shy creatures.

The challenge in shopping for a pair of binoculars is the sheer number and diversity of options from big, high-powered zooms that require a tripod to pocket-sized budget versions and everything in between. To help you narrow your search, we dive into how to select a pair that fits within your price range and how you intend to use them. We also share our favorites from years of testing in the field.

I’m a lifelong hunter and wildlife enthusiast who uses binoculars year-round for hunting as well as volunteer wildlife surveys for bighorn sheep and goats. Long hours behind glass, as well as more than a decade of testing dozens of pairs of binoculars in the field for editorial reviews, have informed my picks, along with conversations with brand representatives and optics dealers. For this update of my long-running guide, I tested six new pairs of binoculars that are new releases from established optics brands. Not all of them made the cut here, but several did, including the Nikon Trailblazer II 10x25, the first time I enjoyed a microcompact binocular enough to include it.

The new Leupold BX-3 Alpine HD binoculars deliver premium-enough outdoor optics while maintaining a price point almost everyone can stomach. The BX-2 Alpine HD, which occupied that exact niche for years, did it well enough that it became my favorite binocular in the midrange category and my everyday hunting optic.

This is a compact, lightweight binocular with good clarity and low-light performance, which makes it a solid choice for basically everyone from birders to stargazers, even though Leupold tends to market mostly to hunters and target shooters. While not the cheapest bino on the market, it’s worth the upgrade over the lowest-tier optics and, like any Leupold optic, comes with a lifetime warranty, meaning it could conceivably be the last pair you’ll ever buy.

The BX-3 doesn’t reinvent anything, but Leupold subtly refined the binos, updating coatings, tweaking ergonomics, and adding a few quality-of-life improvements while keeping the same general form factor, magnification options, and modest price point that made the BX-2 so successful in the first place.

The price jumped up slightly with the release of the BX-3, so while I’d buy the BX-3 for the improvements if you’re paying full price, retailers appear to be deeply discounting the existing stock of BX-2s, so it’s worth considering the older model if there’s a great price on it, at least until retailers run out of the now-discontinued model.

Read the Full Review of the Leupold BX-3 Here

Zeiss is synonymous with good glass in consumer camera lenses and sport optics, so the mid-tier-priced Terra ED 10x42 binoculars are somewhat of a surprise in the manufacturer’s lineup. I’ve tested several higher-end Zeiss binoculars, which were unsurprisingly great given their price tags, but finding nearly as good clarity and color in this $500 pair was unexpected.

While $500 isn’t cheap for most casual binocular buyers, I’d argue getting Zeiss quality at this price presents a serious value if you’re looking for good glass but aren’t ready to put down a mortgage payment to get it.

The 10x42 Terra ED uses ED glass and Zeiss's hydrophobic multicoating to produce a bright, high-contrast image that will feel like a serious upgrade to budget options. It's not going to match the edge-to-edge perfection or low-light performance of Zeiss's flagship binoculars, but it delivers enough optical quality to be an obvious jump in clarity for the investment.

The 10x42 configuration is a versatile middle ground for hunting, hiking, birding, and general wildlife observation. The Terra ED has a 330-foot field of view at 1,000 yards and a 5.3-foot close focus, so it is adequate for birding, casual stargazing, and wildlife watching. At 25.6 ounces, it's also light enough to carry comfortably in a chest harness (not included) for long stretches without pulling on your neck.

The fiberglass-reinforced housing is waterproof and nitrogen-filled to minimize fog and condensation outdoors. The hydrophobic coating helps keep moisture from becoming a major distraction when you're using the binoculars in wet weather or going between temperature extremes. The large focus wheel is also easy to find and operate quickly.

The Terra ED isn't the cheapest 10x42 on the market, but that's not really the point. It's a relatively affordable way into a serious optics brand, and the difference is visible when you use them side by side with cheaper binos.

Most hunters don't need the biggest or most expensive binoculars they can buy, but many with the budget and obsession with the sport will spend thousands hoping expensive optics can buy success. While $3,000 binoculars are overkill for most, hunters do ask a lot of their optics. Early morning and late evening light and long distances expose the weaknesses of lower-quality glass, so many hunters get the advice to buy the best glass they can afford.

While the top-tier binoculars are undoubtedly better, there’s a mid-tier sweet spot that gives you most of the performance of those four-figure binos at a fraction of the price. The Vortex Viper HD 10x42 binoculars are squarely there. Vortex’s Triumph binoculars are our Best Budget pick above for the value they provide at $100, but dedicated hunters who get up early and stay out late will eventually want to upgrade.

The Viper HD 10x42s have a list price around $729, but can be found at most retailers for closer to $500, a good value for the upgrade. Still, that’s $400 more than the Triumph, so you’ll want to be sure you value the improvements. The benefits over cheaper options are better light transmission and reduced distortions such as chromatic aberrations. If you’ve used cheaper binos, you’ve seen off colors such as purple fringes on trees. In broad daylight, this isn’t a problem you can’t adjust your eyes to, but in low light and longer distances it can result in straining and struggling to tell a stump from a bear or deer.

A relatively low 24.9-ounce weight and compact form factor enabled by the roof prism design make these comfortable to carry in a chest harness over long days in the field or a tree stand. The rubber housing offers satisfactory grip and I notably appreciated the underside thumb grooves, though they don’t look as high-end as magnesium housings. The included chest harness is capable enough, but will be a throwaway for hunters who already own a specialized hunting chest rig.

Turned off by cheap compact binoculars in the past? These are worth it. They offer quality optics with powerful-enough magnification for bird-watching, hunting, and a range of everyday uses. In addition, they’re sealed, so they're waterproof and fogproof, and there is a lifetime warranty on the optical parts so you won’t need to replace them if you drop these binos even once.

Nikon’s Trailblazer II 10x25 compact binoculars make some compromises on field of view and low-light performance, but on the plus side, they’re small enough to fit in your pocket. These are binoculars you can toss in a daypack for when you want them, rather than committing to positioning them on you, front and center, and dealing with the weight.

The trade-off, however, is the 25mm objective lens. There's simply less glass available to gather light than you'll get with a 42mm binocular, and the field of view isn’t bad but feels cramped if you’re used to bigger binos. The 10mm eye relief also isn't particularly generous for eyeglass wearers. But for quick looks during daylight, the compact size makes these much easier to have on you when you need them.

Bigger is typically better when it comes to optical performance in binoculars, but there is always a give-and-take. With standard 10x42 or larger binoculars, you get better performance, but usually at least a pound of weight and a bulky item. Bird-watchers and hunters use chest harnesses to distribute the weight and keep them accessible, but that’s a commitment you don’t always want for a casual hike.

The Trailblazer II has a more palatable price at $130 than you’ll find with larger binos with similar optical quality, making these a no-brainer if you’re shopping for casual use.

Like Leupold, Vortex has a great reputation, in large part due to its accommodating lifetime warranty program—a comfort to those of us who are hard on our gear. One challenge with Vortex is the sheer number of lines and models, but the newer Triumph line is easy to understand: it’s the brand’s cheapest pair of binoculars in the 10x42 build and arguably its best value at $100. While the optical clarity and quality aren’t on par with that of the more expensive lines, the Triumph does surprisingly well, especially in daylight.

Like most cheaper binos, the clarity falls off the closer you get to the edges of the field of view, but is sharp and color-true in the center. Yes, you can spend less, but I wouldn’t recommend it, having tried a lot of $25 to $50 binoculars over the years. Despite the attractive price, the Triumph ships with a case, harness, and neck strap as well.

Full Vortex Triumph 10x42 Binoculars Review

Nikon is best known for its cameras and lenses, but this Japanese optics brand makes a wide range of excellent binoculars as well. I’ve tested several models over the years, but the Monarch M7 stands out for the optical clarity it delivers at a mid-tier price point.

Nearly any pair of binoculars will work for birding, but for most species, you’ll be in trees and fairly close quarters where higher magnifications can make it harder to spot and track birds with the more zoomed-in view. Even when you spot a bird, even the slightly tighter 10x magnification can make it harder to follow flight.

The 8x42 version of the Monarch M7 binos gives you enough magnification to confirm details without spooking wildlife, but the wide field makes it easier to track them. The M5 series is also good and about $200 cheaper, but it has a narrow field of view even in the 8x42 configuration.

Like most binoculars, they’re nitrogen-purged and O-ring sealed, which just means they’re waterproof and fogproof. (Note: Fogproof only means there won’t be interior fog. You can still steam up the glass if, for example, your face is warm and the air or binos are cold.)

More money can, of course, get you even better glass from Nikon and other companies, but this is one of the best mid-tier options that delivers a clear and comfortable birding experience. Less money will downgrade your clarity, but cheaper and smaller options that weigh and cost much less abound if those are your priorities. (The entry-level Nocs Provisions Standard Issue 8x25 binos, for example, weigh about half as much.)

There are times when 10x binoculars simply aren't enough—and that’s especially true in Western hunting country where the animal you're looking for might be thousands of yards across a canyon. A 15x binocular like Maven's C.4 gives you considerably more reach while retaining the depth perception and comfort of looking through both eyes.

Extra reach is the reason to buy these. At 15x, details that can be frustratingly ambiguous through a conventional 10x42 become much easier to pick apart. I've found high-power binoculars particularly useful for searching large expanses of terrain where the ability to use both eyes makes extended glassing considerably more comfortable than squinting through a spotting scope. At distances of a mile or more, you’ll still want a spotter that’s 20x and up, but the 15x is a meaningful middle ground that’s wide enough to use in a forest, but reaches far enough for big mountain hunting.

The C.4 combines 15x magnification with large 56mm objective lenses, giving it a 215-foot field of view at 1,000 yards. This is noticeably tighter than, for example, the 342-foot field of view of the Leupold BX-3 10x42s, but that’s by design and the trade-off for 50 percent more zoom.

The other big trade-off is the weight and size. At 45 ounces, they’re still lighter than a spotting scope, but you’ll likely also be carrying a tripod, which adds several pounds to your pack. Compare this to 10x42s, which are usually 1 to 2 pounds total, and it’s a big difference. Still, if you’re using binoculars to cover big mountain distances and need the clarity and zoom to identify animals precisely, it’s likely a weight penalty you’ll be willing to pay.

The ED glass and phase-corrected, dielectric-coated prisms produce a surprisingly sharp image, and the 92 percent light transmission is key around dawn and dusk—impressive for the price. Most high-quality, high-power binoculars are at least four figures, but Maven delivers the C.4 for $550. Unlike the rest of its line that uses Japanese and Chinese components that are assembled in Wyoming, the C.4 is produced entirely in China. Despite this difference, I didn’t notice a sharp drop-off in build or optical quality from other Maven binos I’ve tested.

There's a catch: These aren't really handheld binoculars. At 45.1 ounces, the C.4 is almost twice the weight of many conventional 10x42s, and 15x magnification makes even small hand movements obvious. I used the C.4 handheld fine for short periods, but the size and weight wear on your stability much faster than lightweight hunting binos. Once mounted, however, the extra weight only affects your pack and the C.4 becomes a remarkably capable long-distance optic.

Any decent pair of binoculars can enhance casual stargazing, but if you’re closer to “astrophile” than “occasional noticer of the night sky,” you’ll want a somewhat specialized pair and the best low-light performance you can afford. As binoculars go up in price, into the thousands, the returns are diminishing, giving you small increments of improved clarity and edge-case benefits, but they are better.

Celestron is a budget binocular brand, but its SkyMaster series is astro-focused and worth a look if you’re focused on stars. The massive objective lenses, high magnification, and Porro prism combine for a heavy build, but one that’s designed for night use at the distance of light-years.

The 25x magnification won’t be much good for backyard bird-watching or any handheld use, but they’re designed for tripod mounting, and for use as a stationary sky-watching setup that’s more comfortable for longer sessions than telescopes.

Going with binoculars for sky watching, especially ones as zoomed-in as these, adds a layer of dimensionality that’s lost looking with the naked eye (or with one eye as with telescopes). Unlike cheap Amazon optics brands, Celestron has friendly price points but still gives you a lifetime warranty. If your stargazing habit sticks, you may eventually want to upgrade to a higher-end model, but this pair will show you what you’ve been missing for a few hundred bucks.

Any decent pair of binoculars can enhance casual stargazing, but if you’re closer to “astrophile” than “occasional noticer of the night sky,” you’ll want a somewhat specialized pair and the best low-light performance you can afford. As binoculars go up in price, into the thousands, the returns are diminishing, giving you small increments of improved clarity and edge-case benefits, but they are better.

Celestron is a budget binocular brand, but its SkyMaster series is astro-focused and worth a look if you’re focused on stars. The massive objective lenses, high magnification, and Porro prism combine for a heavy build, but one that’s designed for night use at the distance of light-years.

The 25x magnification won’t be much good for backyard bird-watching or any handheld use, but they’re designed for tripod mounting, and for use as a stationary sky-watching setup that’s more comfortable for longer sessions than telescopes.

Going with binoculars for sky watching, especially ones as zoomed-in as these, adds a layer of dimensionality that’s lost looking with the naked eye (or with one eye as with telescopes). Unlike cheap Amazon optics brands, Celestron has friendly price points but still gives you a lifetime warranty. If your stargazing habit sticks, you may eventually want to upgrade to a higher-end model, but this pair will show you what you’ve been missing for a few hundred bucks.

Yes, this is an article about binoculars, but I humbly present the little-known monocular as a better tool for certain jobs. Like spotting scopes, monoculars aren’t as natural to use since you have to close one eye and miss out on the depth of a stereo picture. However, there are times when the weight and bulk of binos mean you leave them at home even though you might want them in the field.

I personally carry this Nocs Field Tube monocular every time I go backcountry skiing and find it quite literally worth its weight for scouting potential approach and descent lines, using it to pick out details about snow quality, avalanches, and terrain that my naked eye regularly misses. It’s also easy to throw in a pack or pocket for casual hikes or pre-hunting season scouting walks where I never know when I might want a closer look at something but am not motivated enough to harness up with my binoculars.

There aren’t a lot of companies making monoculars, but Nocs has several options. I love the 8x32 size of the Field Tube, but you can get a 10x32 version that offers a bit more zoom but a slightly narrower field of view in the same size package. There’s also the newer 8x32 Zoom Tube that’s significantly cheaper and slightly lighter and smaller but isn’t fully waterproof.

Not everything we test or like ends up in our buying guide, but some are products that still warrant a mention. Here are a few.

Vortex Crossfire HD 10x42: These budget binos fall between the Triumph and Viper models we recommend above. They’re solid optics for the cost, but in a no-man’s-land for the price. If you’re on a tight budget, the Triumph 10x42s are less than half the price and nearly as good. And if you’re looking to upgrade to the mid-tier, it’s worth saving up for the Vipers or the Zeiss Terra ED 10x42s for a more noticeable jump in quality in a compact all-arounder.Nocs Field Issue 10x42: Give us some fun colors and a grippy, overmolded texture like on these 10x42s. But similar to the Vortex Crossfire, they’re not enough of an improvement on our best budget pick to justify double the cost. If you like the design that stands out from a crowd of bland black options, you won’t be disappointed, but we prefer to pay for performance.Zeiss SFL 12x50: These are awesome high-end binoculars that pack a little extra zoom as well as a large, 50mm objective lens that pulls in extra light for early and late. They also are incredibly compact and light despite their specs. The problem is the $2,000 price tag that puts them out of reach of most casual users. They’re really good, just not 10 times as good as a solid $200 pair from our list above.

The magnifications of most consumer binoculars are fixed (i.e., not zoomable), making it one of the most important decisions for buyers. More isn't always better and can feel claustrophobic in tight quarters such as trying to track a small bird in dense forest, while wider-angle, lower-power lenses can feel underpowered if you're trying to see across longer distances.

Most binos range between 7x and 18x. Much less than 7x isn’t enough of an effect to bother with for most applications, while 15x and up becomes difficult to use without a tripod. In general, lower-power binoculars are a better fit if you’re mostly glassing shorter distances, such as in forests, and don’t need precise detail. Higher-power binoculars make sense if you’re looking to avoid also carrying a spotting scope and glassing longer distances up to a mile or need precise detail for identifying wildlife.

Objective lens diameter is the size of the lens farthest from your eyes and impacts the field of vision you get, as well as how bright the image is since, generally, bigger lenses capture more light. Jeremy Bentham, senior manager of SRO Sales & Operations for Nikon, explains the trade-offs associated with objective lens size.

“One of the key things that needs to be decided is brightness versus weight,” he says. “Larger objective lenses allow more light into the optic but are also heavier to pack and carry with you.”

Objective lens sizes in binoculars range anywhere from 20 mm to 100 mm, but the common sizes are mostly in the 30 mm to 60 mm range. I find ultracompact binoculars of less than about 30 mm annoying to use for more than a quick look at something nearby since the field of view is small and it can be harder to keep in position on your eyes. On the other end of the spectrum, most binoculars larger than about 55 mm become heavy and unwieldy if used without a tripod.

Binoculars are listed by size spec, where the first number is magnification and the second is objective lens diameter. Probably the most common size is 10x42, which permits a big enough field of view and magnification for viewing things as near as 15 feet but still allows you to spot larger objects such as wildlife as far as a mile away.

For backcountry hunters and hikers, weight is one of the most important considerations in a binocular. You need to balance the desire for a larger, brighter optic with your ability and interest to carry it around your neck over long distances. For me, anything heavier than about 35 ounces is too much to carry in a chest harness when actively hunting and covering several miles a day. If you’re a hunter or hiker who doesn’t need ready access to your binoculars and can keep them in a pack until you need them at specific spots, you may be able to tolerate heavier options.

Even folks who mostly use binoculars at home or from a vehicle need to consider weight. Heavier binoculars are harder to use for longer periods of time since your arms and shoulders do eventually fatigue and become shaky. If you’re mostly using binoculars on a tripod (a must for higher-magnification binos), you may want to prize optical quality over weight savings.

Aside from range-finding binoculars, most have surprisingly little tech as we usually think of it in terms of electronics and connectivity. What makes great binoculars hasn’t changed much over the years and still boils down to quality glass and craftsmanship.

Where tech does show up is in the glass quality and the coatings used. High-tech coatings are used to make colors true, enhance brightness, and protect your expensive lenses. Coatings and glass often use nonstandardized terms such as ED, HD, and UHD glass, or proprietary branding such as LotuTec or Swarobright, making it hard to compare apples to apples when talking about something as subjective as optical quality. What you can look for is whether lenses are “fully multi-coated,” meaning that all glass surfaces have multiple coatings for durability and performance, whatever the branding.

Jamie, Senior Reviews Editor, joined the Hearst Enthusiast Group in 2021. She has written about, tested, and reviewed everything from turkey fryers to high-definition TVs. Her byline has appeared in TWICE, Sound & Vision, Consumer Reports, and many others. #6340. Can You Pack Power Banks in Checked Luggage? 2026 Airline Battery Rules Travellers Need to Know

Most travellers now fly with several battery-powered items: a phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones, smartwatch, portable charger or vape. But packing one of them in the wrong bag can cause real problems at the airport.

In 2026, aviation safety authorities are warning travellers to pay closer attention to lithium batteries after reports that millions of batteries are still being packed incorrectly. The biggest mistake is simple: power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not go in checked luggage.

They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat, smoke or catch fire. This matters even more when your carry-on gets taken away at the gate and sent underneath the plane.

No. Power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not be packed in checked luggage. They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat.The same goes for loose camera batteries, spare laptop batteries, rechargeable battery packs, vape devices and phone battery charging cases. If your carry-on bag is taken away at the gate and checked underneath the plane, remove all power banks and spare batteries before handing it over.Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras with batteries installed are treated differently from spare batteries, but the safest habit is still to keep valuable battery-powered electronics in the cabin whenever possible. If an airline allows a device to be checked, it should be completely powered off, protected from damage and prevented from turning on accidentally.

The safest habit is simple: power banks, spare batteries and removable batteries stay with you. Valuable electronics are usually better in the cabin too.

Power banks are not allowed in checked luggage because they contain lithium batteries that can overheat if damaged, poorly packed, overcharged, exposed to heat or affected by a defect.

In rare cases, lithium batteries can enter thermal runaway. That means the battery heats faster than it can cool itself down. It may swell, smoke, burn or ignite.

If that happens in the cabin, passengers and crew can spot the problem quickly. Cabin crews are trained to respond to battery incidents. If the battery is hidden inside a suitcase in the cargo hold, it is much harder to access.

That is why this rule is not just airport red tape. A small charger in the wrong bag can become a serious safety issue.

Before you check a suitcase, look for anything with a loose, spare or removable lithium battery.

These items should stay in your carry-on or personal item:

You should also think carefully before checking valuable electronics with installed batteries, including:

Some airlines may allow certain devices with batteries installed in checked luggage if they are completely powered off and protected from damage. But for most travellers, the smarter choice is to keep electronics in the cabin.

Checked bags get dropped, delayed, searched and occasionally sent on their own little vacation. Your laptop does not need that character-building experience.

This is where the rules confuse a lot of travellers.

A spare battery is any battery that is not installed inside the device it powers. A power bank also counts because it is an external battery used to charge other devices.

A battery installed in a device is different. This includes the battery built into your phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones or smartwatch.

If the battery is loose, removable or used to charge something else, do not check it. The FAA’s lithium battery guidance says power banks and spare lithium batteries must travel in carry-on baggage, not checked luggage.

Gate-checking is one of the easiest ways to accidentally break the battery rule.

You may pack your power bank correctly in your carry-on at home. Then you reach the gate, the overhead bins are full and the agent tags your carry-on to go underneath the plane.

At that moment, your carry-on has become checked luggage.

The easiest system is to keep all power banks and spare batteries in one small pouch inside your personal item. If your roller bag gets gate-checked, you can remove the pouch in seconds instead of digging through your suitcase while the boarding line gives you the collective death stare.

Airlines measure lithium-ion battery size in watt-hours, written as Wh.

Most standard phone power banks are under 100 Wh and are usually allowed in carry-on baggage. Larger batteries may require airline approval, and very large batteries are generally not allowed in normal passenger baggage.

The 100 Wh rule matters most for large laptop power banks, professional camera gear, video equipment and drone batteries.

A typical 10,000 mAh power bank is often around 37 Wh. A 20,000 mAh power bank is often around 74 Wh. Larger power banks can get close to the limit, so check before you pack.

According to CATSA’s battery packing guidelines, travellers should keep batteries and electronic devices containing batteries in their carry-on baggage, avoid damaged or recalled batteries, and protect spare batteries from short-circuiting.

Look for the Wh rating printed on the back, bottom or side of the power bank. Newer batteries often show this number clearly.

If the label only shows mAh and volts, you can calculate watt-hours with this formula:

Since 1,000 mAh equals 1 Ah, a 20,000 mAh power bank is 20 Ah.

That would usually fall under the 100 Wh carry-on limit.

If the label has rubbed off and the airline cannot confirm the battery rating, the item may be refused. Do not rely on guessing at the airport.

Laptops, phones and tablets have batteries installed inside the device, so they are not treated the same way as loose spare batteries or power banks.

However, airline rules vary. If an airline allows these devices in checked luggage, they should be completely powered off, protected from damage and packed so they cannot accidentally turn on.

That means fully powered off, not sleeping, hibernating or sitting there quietly planning to wake up mid-flight.

In practice, keep phones, laptops and tablets in the cabin whenever possible. They are valuable, easy to damage and often essential if your checked bag is delayed.

No. Vapes and e-cigarettes should not be packed in checked luggage because they contain batteries. They should travel in the cabin and must not be used or charged during the flight.

Rules for vaping products also vary by destination, and some countries restrict or ban them. If an adult is legally travelling with one, it still needs to follow airline battery rules.

If you are packing for someone else, check for these before closing a checked suitcase. A vape tossed into checked luggage can create the same battery issue as other lithium-powered devices.

Smart luggage can usually be checked only if the battery can be removed.

A smart bag is luggage with built-in charging, tracking or other battery-powered features. If the bag is going into the cabin and meets carry-on size limits, it may be accepted as a carry-on. If it has to be checked, the battery must usually be removed and brought into the cabin.

If the battery cannot be removed, the airline may refuse to accept the bag as checked luggage.

Before travelling with smart luggage, find the battery compartment at home. Do not wait until the check-in counter to discover that the “removable” battery requires a tiny screwdriver, a prayer and the patience of a saint.

The drone or camera body may be allowed in checked luggage by some airlines, but spare lithium batteries should be removed and carried in the cabin.

Spare camera batteries and drone batteries should be individually protected so the terminals cannot touch metal or each other. Use the original packaging, a battery case, a protective pouch or tape over exposed terminals.

If you travel with several batteries for photography or video work, check your airline’s quantity limits before you fly. Battery rules can be stricter for professional video gear and larger drone batteries.

Loose batteries should never be thrown into a bag with coins, keys, jewellery, cables or other metal objects. Battery terminals can short-circuit if they touch metal.

This is especially important for camera batteries, drone batteries and loose rechargeable cells.

Do not travel with a battery that is swollen, cracked, leaking, unusually hot, damaged or recalled.

A swollen power bank is not “probably fine.” It is a damaged battery and should be taken to an appropriate recycling or disposal location.

Before flying with an older power bank, check the model number and look for current recall notices from the manufacturer or your government recall site. Some recalled power banks may be prohibited onboard entirely.

If a battery looks questionable, leave it at home. Replacing a charger is cheaper than dealing with a safety incident at the airport.

If a battery or device becomes hot, starts swelling, smokes, sparks or smells strange during a flight, tell the cabin crew immediately.

Do not put it in the overhead bin. Do not hide it in a bag. Do not take it to the washroom. Cabin crew are trained to respond to battery incidents, but they need to know right away.

The goal is not to handle the problem yourself. The goal is to alert the people trained to deal with it.

Before leaving for the airport, do this quick check:

This takes less than two minutes and can prevent a pulled bag, confiscated item or airport delay.

Before you check a suitcase or hand over a carry-on at the gate, make sure:

Before you check any bag, open it and look for batteries.

Power banks, portable chargers, spare batteries and removable lithium batteries stay with you in the cabin. Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras are usually safer in your carry-on. If your carry-on gets taken at the gate, remove your battery pouch before the bag goes underneath the plane.

The goal is not to stop travelling with electronics. The goal is to stop packing them on autopilot.

A two-minute battery check before every flight can save your bag, your gear and possibly your travel day.

NASA's Swift Observatory is about to make a fiery reentry through Earth's atmosphere after a private mission to save it failed. Most of the spacecraft will burn up in orbit.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: The latest estimates from the Aerospace Corporation predict Swift will reenter the atmosphere at 5:19 a.m. EST on Wednesday (Nov. 4), plus or minus two hours. The earliest window for reentry opens around 3 a.m. Wednesday. NASA has not changed its estimates as of yet. This article was updated at 6 p.m. EST on Tuesday (Nov. 3).NASA's decades-old Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is rapidly falling out of orbit and could tumble back to Earth as early as tonight (Nov. 3), the space agency says.

According to NASA's latest estimates, shared yesterday (Nov. 2), the roughly 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) spacecraft will likely reenter Earth's atmosphere around 3:30 a.m. EST Wednesday (Nov. 4), with an uncertainty of plus or minus 11 hours — meaning the defunct observatory could plunge down as early as this evening.

An independent analysis from the private nonprofit Aerospace Corporation, which tracks thousands of objects in orbit, similarly estimates that the telescope will reenter the atmosphere at 5:12 a.m. EST Wednesday, give or take eight hours. Both estimates suggest the Swift spacecraft may be no more by Wednesday morning.

As with all spacecraft reentries, the risk to humans is minimal. Most of the Swift telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere, according to NASA. Any surviving fragments will likely fall somewhere between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude — a range that includes parts of Mexico, the Caribbean, Central and South America, the Arabian Peninsula, India, Africa and Oceania, but also a lot of ocean.

NASA predicts that the chances of Swift debris falling over a populated area are approximately 1 in 2,100. For comparison, the odds of a person being struck by lightning in their lifetime are 1 in 15,300, according to the National Weather Service.

NASA will continue to update their predictions as the reentry window draws closer.

Swift has detected thousands of deep-space explosions, including sudden flares from neutron stars (illustrated here).

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is a multiwavelength optical, ultraviolet and X-ray telescope that launched in November 2004 on a mission to study the most powerful explosions in space. Initially designed for a two-year primary mission, the telescope ultimately spent more than 10 times that duration hunting for supernovas, gamma-ray bursts and black-hole-induced eruptions around the universe.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Swift has been rapidly losing altitude for more than a year, after rampant solar activity increased the drag on the aging spacecraft. This past August, a costly mission to boost Swift's orbit with a private spacecraft failed shortly after launch, hammering the final nail in Swift's coffin.

Engineers on the Swift team officially shut down the observatory's science operations on Oct. 20, after the spacecraft fell too low in orbit to continue taking steady observations of the sky.

As Swift goes out with a fiery bang, it leaves behind a trove of scientific data, including contributions to more than 7,000 scientific papers so far, according to NASA. This number will only increase as Swift's final observations are processed.

#6338. I Rarely Recommend Gas Pressure Washers to Homeowners. This Westinghouse Is the Exception.

It gives you the performance of gas and the convenience of electric at an accessible price.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

I’ve often said that gas pressure washers are the best choice for professional job sites, while electric pressure washers are a better fit for DIY projects and home maintenance. The Westinghouse WPX3400 pressure washer has prompted me to reconsider that advice. Here’s why: It delivers true gas power at an affordable price while minimizing the drawbacks of a gas engine.

Gas pressure washers traditionally deliver the most powerful cleaning, but come with a higher purchase price and recurring maintenance responsibilities. I’ve spent lots of time on job sites while workers huddled around a pressure washer, yanking on the pull cord and trying to troubleshoot a malfunctioning engine—not to mention the noise, weight, and fumes that come with a gas engine. But the WPX3400 is quieter, lighter, and more reliable than any of the other gas pressure washers I’ve used. It’s robust enough that it’s made me rethink my default recommendations for most homeowners.

If you’re a DIYer who wants maximum power and performance, and you aren’t deterred by working with a gas engine, this pressure washer will more than deliver.

The Westinghouse WPX3400 delivers powerful performance while minimizing the downsides of a gas-powered tool. Rated at 3,400 psi and 2.6 gallons per minute (GPM), it’s the most powerful pressure washer we’ve tested, both in terms of water pressure and volume.

I used the Westinghouse WPX3400 to clean concrete sidewalks, vinyl siding, and brick walls, as well as to refresh an earthenware chiminea and wash my truck (with a third-party foam cannon). The Westinghouse excelled on each of these surfaces. It had the power to clean stained and dirt-caked sidewalks, while its even spray and high GPM made car washing straightforward and hassle-free. Cleaning the chiminea and brick wall was effortless because the Westinghouse offers consistent psi. If pressure fluctuates up and down, it’s possible to damage surfaces such as brick or mortar.

So what about the downsides? This pressure washer has a gas engine, so it produces exhaust, and I certainly wouldn’t call it quiet, registering 89 decibels when idle. Still, that’s not overly loud in terms of gas-powered pressure washers, many of which can register well over 90 decibels. I expected the hard plastic wheels on the WPX3400 to make it louder and rattle-prone, but this issue seems to be counterbalanced by the soft rubber front foot. That same rubber foot seemed to help it withstand my durability tests, as well. The wheels did struggle some when moving across uneven surfaces and muddy terrain.

The Westinghouse pressure washer also went through evaluation for several months by Test Editor Paul Smith. “I spent the better part of the summer putting the Westinghouse WPX3400 to work on vinyl siding, a driveway, patio, and fence,” he said. “This thing is a workhorse. It has serious cleaning power, knocking all of that stubborn algae off the siding portion of my house that lives in the shade, my fencing, and all of my pressure-treated landscape timbers. There’s a lot of satisfaction in watching all of that green disappear with each pass of the wand and seeing the original surface restored.”

Smith found the WPX3400 to be relatively quiet compared to other gas-powered models he has used—benefiting both him and his neighbors. “If I have one gripe, it’s that I found the hose between the machine and the wand to be a bit short, which required a few extra moves of the machine,” he shared. “Beyond that, it’s a pressure washer perfectly suited to homeowners who want to wash a bit more—and faster—than they might with an electric model.”

One of the reasons that gas-powered pressure washers are popular on professional job sites is that they can take a lot of abuse. The WPX3400 stood up to everything I threw at it and kept running without a hitch.

I tried to find failure points by attempting to kink the hose and running it on an uneven surface, but the Westinghouse sailed through those tests. Next, I dropped it onto a concrete pad from a foot up. The rubber foot that also served as a drop buffer absorbed and distributed the fall impact.

I intentionally ran it out of gas, and I pushed it by using it with low oil. In all instances, it came back to life once I refilled the fluids. At the end of the testing, I winterized it—a straightforward if somewhat messy process of loosening a single bolt to drain gasoline from the float bowl (rather than the entire tank) and stocking the pump with antifreeze. It’s more winterization work than an electric model requires, but not much more. When I break it out next year for the buying guide refresh, I’ll get to find out how well it comes back to life.

If you need true power to deal with intense dirt and debris or if you have large jobs that would take hours with a less powerful washer, then this is a smart choice. And the user-friendliness of the WPX3400 minimizes the additional work of a gas engine. I have found small engines can be finicky to get started, and many require tinkering to keep them running. Not with the WPX3400, which has started easily every single time I used it.

If you dislike dealing with standard engine maintenance, or you need to store your pressure washer in your home over the winter, this machine may not be the way to go. And (just like any gas-powered option), it’s definitely not for anyone who plans to use their pressure washer indoors or in an area with poor ventilation.

Throughout my testing, the WPX3400’s power, durability, and ease of use impressed me at every turn. It’s my top recommendation for DIYers who are looking to make a pressure washer purchase.

Shop the Westinghouse WPX3400 Pressure Washer

At 3,000 psi and 2.0 GPM, the Greenworks Pro GPW3002A tackles tough jobs, making it comparable to many gas-powered models, minus fumes and maintenance costs. Its low center of gravity makes it stable and easier to move around on uneven terrain. Even after substantial rain, though, its 10-inch wheels never got bogged down in the mud.

Battery-powered pressure washers offer freedom from a power cord, and the HPW3204-2 even comes with a siphon hose to allow feeding water from a bucket, a well, or other water source. The Power+ HPW3204-2 offers three power settings, typically providing about 60 minutes, 45 minutes, and 20 minutes, in ECO, High, and Turbo modes, respectively.

If your cleaning tasks will be entirely in or around your property, there’s no need to worry about how mobile a pressure washer might be. I found the 100-foot hose could reach about 95 percent of my home and yard—simply by walking with the wand, with no need to wheel a cumbersome mounted washer.

A former residential remodeler and maintenance manager, Dan Stout has worked in nearly every part of the construction and DIY industry, from project planning and permitting to plumbing, drywall, carpentry, and more. He loves to write about the weird history of everyday objects, and to help readers make informed decisions about their homes.

Jamie, Senior Reviews Editor, joined the Hearst Enthusiast Group in 2021. A recent rat study hinted that cosmic radiation could pose health risks for future Mars explorers. Live Science asks its readers whether they'd take the journey anyway.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A crewed mission to Mars could be one of humanity's greatest achievements, but getting there may come with serious health risks. Beyond the challenges of surviving in space for months at a time, astronauts would face prolonged exposure to cosmic radiation ‪—‬ high-energy particles in space that can penetrate the human body and potentially damage vital organs.

A new study suggested that cosmic radiation could pose a particular threat to heart health. Researchers found evidence that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what human astronauts might encounter during a mission to Mars and back developed more scar tissue around the small vessels in their hearts compared with rats that weren't exposed to space radiation.

Although the findings haven't been confirmed in humans yet, they add to the growing concerns about the long-term health effects of sending astronauts on long-duration space missions.

NASA and other space agencies are working on ways to eventually send humans to Mars and beyond. Given these latest findings, would you travel to Mars? Vote in the poll below, and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

#6335. Plywood Isn’t Cheap. That’s Why I Appreciate the Accuracy of Bosch’s ProFactor Circular Saw.

I put it to work on a cabinet project and came away impressed by its accuracy, well-designed adjustments, and easy handling.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It isn’t too often that things in the world of circular saws tend to catch me by surprise. I’ve been around them and used them in my daily life long enough that, for the most part, my expectations are fairly straightforward. I want:

Everything else is gravy, but once in a while, I get my hands on a tool that’s such a pleasure to use, I’m reminded that I guess I like a lot of gravy.

I recently put Bosch’s GKS18V-25GN ProFactor 7-1/4-inch cordless circular saw—our choice for best circular saw for finished plywood—to work, ripping through multiple sheets of sanded cabinet-grade plywood for a project I’m building in the Popular Mechanics shop. It’s the kind of work where making precise cuts matters. Plywood isn’t cheap, particularly the good stuff, and there’s nothing quite as frustrating as watching a cut wander off course midway through a full 8-foot sheet.

The Bosch GKS18V-25GN made the entire process incredibly easy. And the more I used it, the more I appreciated all of the thought that went into its design.

The first thing I noticed when using the GKS18V-25GN was how comfortable it felt in my hands. It’s light and well-balanced and has excellent grip ergonomics. With some saws, I find myself shifting my weight for better placement or battling the heft of the saw just to keep my running cut on track. This saw feels natural to operate, which makes a big difference when you’re making long cuts across large sheets of material.

Power was never an issue, either. The saw moved through plywood smoothly. It never bogged down or made me feel like I needed to slow my feed rate to accommodate the motor. More importantly, the cuts were clean and consistent—exactly what I wanted for a project where finished edges matter.

I also appreciated how easy it was to make basic adjustments while I cut. The depth-of-cut control is intuitive—a thumb-driven red button atop the handle releases the shoe—and becomes totally natural after a bit of use. The bevel adjustments are accessible and straightforward. None of this is very glamorous (although the depth adjustment is pretty cool), but when you’re switching quickly between material depths or working with angled cuts, these refinements make a big difference.

The GKS18V-25GN offers six speed settings, along with an Eco mode designed to extend battery runtime. When I first saw that, I had my doubts. I’ve never been very keen on the idea of turning a circular saw into an electronic gadget, and I doubted the validity of that particular feature. I’ve always been of the mind that a saw should do its job, simply put, and the trigger should pretty much take care of the rest.

But after making a bunch of cuts, I started experimenting with those lower settings. I figured that if I didn’t need the maximum blade speed to get through 3/4-inch plywood, why use it? As it turns out, I didn’t. Even at reduced speed, the saw delivered a smooth cut through the material without sounding like it wanted to quit. Being able to dial down the blade speed without losing cutting performance was a welcome surprise.

Eco mode takes that idea a step further, giving battery runtime priority over the saw’s maximum cutting speed. While I didn’t conduct an exhaustive battery-runtime test, I did appreciate having the option to conserve power when the material doesn’t necessarily demand all that this saw has to offer. I went from dismissing these electronic features as unnecessary to quickly recognizing their overall worth. My takeaway is that it all makes good energy-saving sense.

Circular saws have a habit of throwing sawdust where you don’t want it, which tends to obscure the line you’re trying to follow. For many brands, proper dust exhaust seems like an afterthought in the design phase. How many times have we all bent to the material, breathed deep, and blown the excess dust away while cutting? I certainly have.

But Bosch’s dust port arrangement—specifically its orientation at the rear of the blade guard and its ability to pivot when connected to a shop vac hose—keeps debris away from the cutting area. Throughout all the cuts I made with the GKS18V-25GN, I had an excellent view of where the blade was headed. Maybe that sounds like a minor convenience, but when you’re cutting plywood, maintaining a clear sightline makes for a more accurate and confident cut.

For all its impressive performance, I think the GKS18V-25GN does its best work when paired with the company’s guide track—in the case of my testing, the 63-inch FSN 1600. There’s a big difference between cutting plywood freehand and running a saw along a properly positioned track. The latter takes much of the guesswork out of the process, particularly when you’re making long rip cuts or breaking down full sheets into more manageable pieces.

With this saw riding on a track, the cuts were laser straight. I wasn’t worried about drifting away from my layout marks or compensating for a slightly wandering blade. It was so simple to position the track, secure the workpiece, and make the cut. For cabinetry, built-ins, furniture projects, or any woodworking that demands accurate sheet-good cuts, this simplicity and reliability become true time-savers.

There is one distinction I’d make about this saw. Although it’s certainly capable of handling general construction work, I wouldn’t approach it as a rough-and-tumble job-site tool. To me, this is a precision-oriented circular saw that deserves to be treated accordingly. Its carefully designed adjustments, electronic controls, and track compatibility are all features that reward some deliberate TLC in your approach to how you use it.

That’s hardly a criticism. In fact, it’s part of what I like about it. I’d much rather have a saw that excels at the kind of detailed work I’m doing than one designed primarily to survive being tossed around in the back of my truck.

The Bosch GKS18V-25GN impressed me with its cutting power, comfortable handling, thoughtful adjustments, and genuinely useful speed settings. But its performance on the guide track is the main reason I’ll keep coming back to this saw in the future.

If you plan on taking on projects that include a bit of breaking down sanded plywood for cabinets, shelves, or furniture where that precision really matters, this is an exceptional saw that’s easy and actually fun to use.

Shop the Bosch ProFactor 18V Cordless Circular Saw

#6334. Sea to Sky Highway Named One of the Best EV Road Trips in the World

Most people know the Sea to Sky Highway as one of Canada’s most beautiful drives. It winds from the edge of Vancouver along Howe Sound, climbs past waterfalls and mountain viewpoints, and continues toward Whistler and Pemberton.

Now, it has another reason to be on your road trip list: it has been named one of the best EV road trips in the world.

According to a study by iSelect, British Columbia’s Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally among the world’s most EV-friendly road trips. The study analyzed 48 iconic road trips across six continents and scored each route based on factors such as charging infrastructure, distance, estimated charging cost, and traveller reviews.

For Canadian travellers, that is a big deal. EV road trips are no longer just about whether you can make it from one charger to the next. The best routes now combine scenery, reliable charging access, reasonable costs, and places you actually want to stop along the way.

Yes. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of the best EV road trips in Canada because it is relatively short, scenic, well-travelled, and supported by charging options along the route. iSelect ranked it seventh in the world for EV road trips, with 49 chargers available across its 121-mile route and a road trip score of 88.15 out of 100.

The route is ideal for electric vehicle drivers because it connects major destinations like Vancouver, Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton without requiring a long, remote drive through charging gaps.

Electric vehicles are becoming a bigger part of travel planning. The International Energy Agency expects global electric car sales to reach 23 million in 2026, representing 28% of total car sales. That means more travellers are thinking about charging stops the same way they used to think about gas stations, rest areas, and coffee breaks.

Charging infrastructure is also expanding. The IEA reported that the worldwide stock of public charging points reached more than 7 million at the end of 2025, with nearly 1.8 million public chargers added in 2025 alone.

That shift matters for road trips. A few years ago, EV travel could feel like a math problem with scenery attached. Now, on the right routes, it can feel much closer to a normal road trip — as long as you plan ahead.

The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally in iSelect’s study. The route stretches from Horseshoe Bay toward Pemberton, passing through some of British Columbia’s most famous scenery, including Howe Sound, Squamish, Whistler, and the Coast Mountains.

Chart idea: create a simple horizontal bar chart titled Top 10 EV Road Trips in the World, using the Road Trip Score column. This would work well just below the table.

One of the most interesting parts of the ranking is that Canada appears twice in the global top 10.

The Kootenay Highway ranked second in the world, with a score of 99.24 out of 100. The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh, with a score of 88.15. That gives Canada two of the highest-rated EV road trip routes in the world according to iSelect’s index.

That should not be surprising to anyone who has road-tripped through British Columbia. Canada’s western mountain routes already offer some of the best scenery in the world. The difference now is that EV infrastructure is starting to make those drives more accessible for electric vehicle owners.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not a long cross-country endurance test. That is part of what makes it such a good EV route.

The drive from Vancouver to Whistler is short enough for many modern EVs to handle comfortably, but scenic enough that you will want to stop anyway. Instead of treating charging as an inconvenience, you can build it into the trip.

Stops like Squamish, Shannon Falls, Brandywine Falls, Whistler Village, and Pemberton give travellers natural breaks along the way. For EV drivers, that means charging can happen while you eat, hike, shop, or take photos instead of sitting around watching a battery percentage crawl upward.

Horseshoe Bay is a great place to start if you are coming from Vancouver. It has waterfront views, ferry traffic, cafes, and a relaxed village feel before the highway begins climbing toward Squamish.

Shannon Falls is one of the easiest scenic stops on the Sea to Sky Highway. The short walk to the waterfall makes it a perfect break on the way to Squamish or Whistler.

Squamish is one of the best stops on the route. It has food, coffee, outdoor shops, hiking access, and views of the Stawamus Chief. It is also a practical place to stop, stretch your legs, and check your charge before continuing north.

The Sea to Sky Gondola is one of the most popular attractions along the route. It offers sweeping views over Howe Sound and the surrounding mountains, making it an easy way to turn the drive into a full day trip.

Brandywine Falls is another easy stop between Squamish and Whistler. The walk is short, the waterfall is impressive, and it is a good reminder that the Sea to Sky Highway is not just about getting to Whistler.

Whistler is the main destination for many Sea to Sky road trips. In summer, it is great for hiking, biking, patios, lakes, and mountain views. In winter, it becomes one of North America’s most famous ski destinations.

Pemberton is a quieter extension of the trip beyond Whistler. It offers mountain scenery, farmland, and a slower pace for travellers who want to continue past the busiest part of the route.

Even on EV-friendly routes, it is still smart to plan your charging stops ahead of time. Check charger locations, charging speeds, plug types, and whether stations are available or out of service before you start driving.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not the place to play battery roulette. Mountain roads, weather, traffic, and detours can all affect range. Keep a buffer so you are not stressed if a charger is busy or unavailable.

EV range can drop in cold weather, heavy rain, strong winds, or mountain driving. The Sea to Sky Highway includes elevation changes, so it is better to plan conservatively.

The best EV road trips are the ones where charging fits naturally into the route. Stop for lunch in Squamish, explore Whistler Village, or take a scenic break while the car charges.

Do not wait until you are in a parking lot with weak signal to download a charging app. Set up your accounts, payment methods, and route planning tools before you leave home.

For an EV road trip, we would use a mix of navigation, charging, and general travel apps.

For more trip-planning tools, see our guide to the best travel apps for 2026.

Absolutely. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of Canada’s great scenic drives whether you are driving an electric vehicle, hybrid, or gas-powered car.

The EV ranking simply shows that the route is becoming more accessible for modern travellers. The scenery was already there. The charging infrastructure is what makes it easier for EV drivers to enjoy the route with more confidence.

The Sea to Sky Highway’s global ranking is part of a bigger shift in travel. Sustainable travel is no longer just about choosing trains over planes or staying in eco-lodges. For many travellers, it now includes how they drive, where they charge, and whether road trips can be done with lower emissions.

Canada has the scenery. The challenge has always been distance. As charging infrastructure improves, more Canadian road trips will become realistic for EV drivers.

That is good news for travellers, but it is also good news for smaller communities along the way. EV road trips encourage people to stop longer, spend locally, and build their route around towns, restaurants, viewpoints, parks, and overnight stays.

Before driving the Sea to Sky Highway in an electric vehicle, make sure to:

The Sea to Sky Highway has always been one of Canada’s most spectacular drives. Now it is also being recognized as one of the best EV road trips in the world.

That combination makes sense. The route is scenic, manageable, practical, and packed with places worth stopping. For EV drivers, that is exactly what makes a great road trip. You do not want to plan your entire day around charging. You want charging to fit into a journey you already wanted to take.

From Vancouver to Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton, the Sea to Sky Highway proves that EV travel does not have to mean giving up adventure. It just means planning the route a little smarter.

And honestly, if your charging stop comes with mountain views and a coffee in Squamish, that is not exactly a hardship.

#6333. Best Things to Do in Hamilton, Ontario

A trip to Hamilton always feels a little like coming home for us. Dave’s dad was born and raised in Hamilton, and Dave spent much of his childhood visiting family in the city. We’ve watched “The Hammer” change from the Steeltown we knew as kids into one of Ontario’s most interesting places to visit.

Hamilton has always had history, grit, and character, albeit today, it also has waterfalls, hiking trails, waterfront parks, museums, restaurants, art galleries, street festivals, and one of the best food scenes in Southern Ontario.

Now that we have friends in the area, we visit often and are always discovering something new therefore this guide brings together the classic Hamilton attractions we’ve loved for years with the newer energy that makes the city so fun to explore today.

The best things to do in Hamilton, Ontario, include visiting Dundurn Castle, chasing waterfalls at Webster’s Falls and Tews Falls, hiking the Dundas Valley, exploring the Royal Botanical Gardens, walking the Waterfront Trail, visiting the Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum, attending James Street Art Crawl, and eating at local favourites like Born & Raised on James Street North.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines history, nature, food, art, and outdoor adventure in one easy-to-reach city.

Hamilton has a deep industrial, military, and political history. These museums and historic sites help explain how the city shaped Ontario and Canada.

Dundurn Castle is one of the top attractions in Hamilton and a great place to start if this is your first visit as this grand 1830s villa was once home to Sir Allan Napier MacNab, who served as Premier of the United Canadas.

The house has been restored to show what life looked like in the 19th century, with guided tours and period rooms that make the history easy to understand. Admission to Dundurn Castle is by guided tour only, and the City of Hamilton notes that admission includes access to the Hamilton Military Museum on the same property.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Leave time to walk the grounds and kitchen garden however even if you are not a big museum person, the views over the bay and the historic setting make this one of Hamilton’s must-see stops.

Tickets cost $16.75 for adults and $10 for children, with children under 5 allowed in for free.

Located beside Hamilton International Airport, the Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum is a must for aviation and history lovers. It houses a major collection of Canadian military aircraft, including vintage planes connected to Canada’s wartime history.

The highlight is the Avro Lancaster, one of the museum’s most famous aircraft and if you time your visit right, you may even see vintage aircraft taking off.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Check the museum schedule before you go as seeing one of these historic aircraft in motion is far more memorable than only viewing it on the floor.

HMCS Haida is one of Hamilton’s most unique attractions. This floating museum sits on the waterfront and lets visitors explore a former Royal Canadian Navy destroyer.

Known as “Canada’s most fightingest ship,” HMCS Haida served during the Second World War, the Korean War, and the Cold War. Walking through the ship gives you a real sense of how tight, loud, and intense life at sea must have been for the crew.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Wear good shoes. You’ll be climbing steep ladders and moving through narrow spaces, which is part of what makes the experience feel so real.

When staying in Hamilton, a great choice is the Holiday Inn Express on Upper James Street it’s a 15 minute walk to TD Coliseum and near some of the best dining and nightlife in Hamilton.

Housed in the restorThe Hamilton Museum of Steam & Technology is housed in a restored 1859 waterworks building and tells the story of steam power and industrial innovation in Canada.

The massive steam engines are the star of the visit. They once helped supply water to the growing city and remain an impressive reminder of Hamilton’s industrial roots.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Try to visit during a live demonstration. Seeing the machinery in action makes the museum much more interesting.

The Battle of Stoney Creek was a key moment in the War of 1812, and the site preserves that history through Battlefield House Museum and the Battlefield Monument.

The house, grounds, and monument help visitors understand how important the area was during the conflict between British, Canadian, and American forces.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Climb the monument if it is open during your visit. The view helps you understand why this location mattered strategically.

The Erland Lee Museum in Stoney Creek is a meaningful stop for anyone interested in Canadian history and women’s history. This 19th-century farmhouse is connected to the founding of the Women’s Institutes, an organization that began locally and later spread around the world.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: This is one of Hamilton’s quieter historic sites, but the story is important. It is especially worth visiting if you like places with a strong local connection.

Hamilton sits along the Niagara Escarpment, giving the city one of the best natural settings in Southern Ontario. This is where Hamilton really surprises people.

Hamilton is often called the Waterfall Capital of the World, and chasing waterfalls is one of the best things to do in the city. The region is known for having more than 100 waterfalls, many of them tucked into forested escarpment trails and conservation areas. Tourism Hamilton highlights the city’s waterfalls as one of its major outdoor draws.

Some of the most popular waterfalls include:

Webster’s Falls is one of the most famous, while Tews Falls is one of the tallest. Albion Falls is another classic stop, with water cascading over wide rock shelves.

Important Tip: Access rules, parking, shuttle systems, and reservations can change, especially at popular waterfalls. Always check the Hamilton Conservation Authority before you go.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t only chase the famous waterfalls. Tiffany Falls is beautiful and easy to reach, making it a great stop if you want a short walk without committing to a long hike.

Spencer Gorge Conservation Area is one of the best places in Hamilton for scenery. It is home to Tews Falls, Webster’s Falls, and access to the Dundas Peak viewpoint.

Dundas Peak is especially popular in autumn when the valley turns colour. The view over Dundas and the surrounding forest is one of the best in Southern Ontario.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go on a weekday if you can. This is one of Hamilton’s most popular outdoor areas, and it can get very busy on weekends.

The Royal Botanical Gardens, often called the RBG, is one of the top attractions in the Hamilton area. It is Canada’s largest botanical garden and includes formal gardens, nature sanctuaries, walking trails, and seasonal blooms.

The RBG is huge, so it is best to pick one or two areas instead of trying to see everything in a single visit.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you only have time for one section, start with Hendrie Park or the Rock Garden. Both are beautiful and easy to enjoy without feeling rushed.

Hamilton is a great hiking city because the Bruce Trail passes right through the area. The Dundas Valley Conservation Area also has more than enough trails for a full day outside.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Start at the Dundas Valley Trail Centre if you want an easy introduction. From there, you can connect to several trails without overcomplicating the day.

Hamilton’s waterfront has changed dramatically over the years. What was once mostly industrial has become one of the city’s best recreation areas.

Bayfront Park is one of the best places in Hamilton for a relaxed afternoon. It has walking paths, harbour views, green space, a playground, and room for families to spread out.

It is also a great place to start if you want to walk or bike along the waterfront.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Bring a picnic or grab food nearby and spend some time watching the boats in the harbour.

The Hamilton Waterfront Trail connects parks, lookout points, and harbourfront paths. It is flat, scenic, and easy to enjoy whether you are walking, cycling, or visiting with kids.

This is one of the best low-effort ways to experience Hamilton outdoors.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Rent bikes if the weather is nice. The trail is easy, and stopping for ice cream along the way is part of the fun.

A harbour cruise gives you a different view of Hamilton. You’ll see the city’s industrial history, waterfront redevelopment, and working harbour from the water.

This is a good choice for visitors who want to understand the city beyond the usual attractions.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: The narrated sightseeing cruise is more interesting than you might expect also Hamilton’s harbour tells a big part of the city’s story.

ThGage Park is one of Hamilton’s classic city parks. It has gardens, walking paths, open green space, a tropical greenhouse, and seasonal events.

The Tropical Greenhouse is especially nice in winter when you want a warm escape without leaving the city especially on a cold day, the greenhouse feels like a mini vacation. It is a great stop if you are visiting Hamilton outside of waterfall season.

Hutch’s is a Hamilton-area classic. This old-school spot near the waterfront has been serving fish and chips, burgers, ice cream, and milkshakes for generations.

We have a soft spot for Hutch’s because Dave used to come here as a kid because he lived just down the road in Burlington, and her dad would take the family there as a Sunday treat.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Expect a lineup on a sunny day and order the fish and chips, but don’t skip the milkshake.

Hamilton’s arts scene is one of the biggest reasons the city feels so different today since the city still has its industrial edge, but it now mixes that with galleries, music, theatre, sports, restaurants, and street festivals.

James Street Art Crawl is one of the best things to do in Hamilton if you want to feel the city’s creative energy.

Held on the second Friday of every month, Art Crawl transforms James Street North into a street festival with galleries, shops, restaurants, artists, vendors, music, and food. The event runs from around 5 p.m. until late, and from May to October, part of James Street North becomes pedestrian-only during the event.

This is the kind of event that shows how much Hamilton has changed. It feels local, creative, casual, and welcoming. You can browse galleries, listen to live music, grab food, shop from local makers, and make a full evening of it.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Plan your visit around the second Friday of the month if you can. Start with Art Crawl, then book dinner on James Street North so you don’t have to move the car or rush across town.

The Art Gallery of Hamilton is the oldest and largest art museum in Southern Ontario. Its collection includes historical and contemporary Canadian art, with works connected to some of the country’s most important artists.

It is a great indoor activity and a strong cultural stop if you are spending time downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Give yourself at least a couple of hours. The Canadian collection is the highlight. Please verify the current admission structure on their official website.

Hamilton is a football city, and seeing the Tiger-Cats play at Tim Hortons Field is one of the most local experiences you can have.

The CFL season usually runs from summer into fall, and the atmosphere at a Ticats game is loud, loyal, and very Hamilton.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Wear black and gold and join the “Oskee Wee Wee” chants, besides, even if you are not a huge football fan, the energy is infectious.

Located at Tim Hortons Field, the Canadian Football Hall of Fame celebrates the history of Canadian football and the CFL conversely it is a good add-on if you are already going to a game or visiting the stadium.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Pair this with a Ticats game for the full experience.

Hess Village is one of Hamilton’s classic nightlife areas. The pedestrian-friendly cobblestone street is lined with bars, patios, restaurants, and live music spots and it is liveliest in summer when the patios are full.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Hess is great for drinks and nightlife, but for dinner we’d also look at James Street North or King William Street.

Theatre Aquarius is Hamilton’s main professional theatre company and a great option for a night out downtown.

The productions are polished, and it is a nice alternative to heading into Toronto for live theatre.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Check the schedule before your visit because a show here makes an easy culture-and-dinner evening.

Hamilton’s food scene has grown into one of the best in Ontario. You’ll find old-school classics, farmers’ market eats, pizza, cocktails, patios, and chef-driven restaurants.

Hamilton Farmers’ Market has been part of the city since 1837 and remains one of the best places to eat downtown.

You can find fresh produce, cheese, meat, baked goods, prepared foods, coffee, and international food stalls, plus it is a great lunch stop, especially if you are visiting the Art Gallery of Hamilton or exploring downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t just shop. Plan to eat here. It is one of the easiest ways to sample Hamilton’s food scene in one place.

Born & Raised is one of the best restaurants to pair with a visit to James Street North, as it is located right in the Art Crawl district, it is surrounded by galleries, shops, cafes, and the creative energy that makes this part of Hamilton so fun.

The restaurant was created by chef Vittorio Colacitti and focuses on bold flavours, Italian-inspired dishes, pizza, and a lively neighbourhood atmosphere. It is a great choice for dinner after Art Crawl or a night out downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you are visiting during James Street Art Crawl, make a reservation if possible because the street gets busy, and this is exactly the kind of place you’ll want to settle into after walking the galleries.

King William Street has become one of Hamilton’s best dining areas, with restaurants, patios, and cocktail spots packed into a walkable downtown strip especially if you want a more polished dinner, this is a good area to explore.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: King William is a great choice if you want to turn a Hamilton day trip into an evening out.

Hamilton is a great family day trip because many attractions are easy to combine. therefore good family-friendly stops include:

The key with kids is not to overpack the day. Pick one museum, one outdoor stop, and one easy food stop.

Hamilton can be a budget-friendly day trip if you plan it well.

Always check parking and reservation requirements before visiting waterfalls or conservation areas.

Yes, Hamilton is worth visiting because it combines waterfalls, hiking trails, museums, waterfront parks, restaurants, art galleries, and local culture in one easy day trip or weekend getaway. It has the outdoor appeal of the Niagara Escarpment, the history of an old industrial city, and the food and arts scene of a place that has reinvented itself without losing its character.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it is close enough for a full-day visit but different enough to feel like a real change of scenery. You can tour Dundurn Castle, hike to waterfalls, walk the waterfront, visit the Art Gallery of Hamilton, and end the day with dinner on James Street North.

Hamilton is best known for its industrial history, waterfalls, hiking trails, the Niagara Escarpment, arts scene, food scene, and waterfront. It is still called “Steeltown,” but today it is just as well known for outdoor adventure, creative neighbourhoods, and one of Ontario’s most underrated city breaks.

Spring, summer, and fall are the best times to visit Hamilton for waterfalls, hiking, gardens, patios, festivals, and James Street Art Crawl. Fall is especially beautiful in the Dundas Valley, while winter is better for museums, restaurants, theatre, the Royal Botanical Gardens, and indoor attractions.

A car is useful in Hamilton, especially if you want to visit waterfalls, conservation areas, Dundas, Stoney Creek, the Royal Botanical Gardens, or attractions outside downtown. Once you are downtown, areas like James Street North, King William Street, the farmers’ market, and the Art Gallery of Hamilton are much easier to explore on foot.
