#6291. Frontier Airlines Warns Of Scam Emails With Real Booking Codes And Fake Refunds

A fraudulent airline email is easier to dismiss when it gets your trip details wrong. What happens when it includes your actual flight information and confirmation number? Frontier Airlines passengers are reporting precisely that, with scammers using real reservation details to solicit credit card information. Frontier has confirmed an active phishing campaign, and the obvious question is how the scammers obtained the data.

View From The Wing highlights a concerning report that Frontier customers have received fraudulent emails offering refunds or claiming an existing reservation has a payment problem.

The troubling part is that passengers say the messages contain genuine confirmation numbers and flight details. Some report entering their credit card information into the linked websites.

One version promises a refund after the passenger verifies the card used for the booking. Another creates urgency by suggesting payment for an upcoming trip has not gone through.

The latter is a scammer’s dream: someone expecting to travel soon may be particularly inclined to resolve what appears to be a ticketing problem.

Frontier has published a warning on its website, acknowledging an active email phishing campaign targeting customers.

The airline says it will not email passengers asking them to revalidate a reservation, reconfirm credit card information, or provide payment details to obtain a refund.

The critical point is that a correct confirmation number does not make an email legitimate.

If the passenger reports are accurate, someone has obtained information that should not be available to a random scammer. That raises the possibility of unauthorized access to a reservation-related system, compromised credentials, or misuse by someone with legitimate access.

An inside job is one possibility. A breach at the airline or a service provider is another. Compromised passenger email accounts could also expose booking confirmations, though it seems too coincidental if this has been happening on a larger scale and only with Frontier.

We do not yet have enough evidence to identify the source, establish how broadly information was exposed, or conclude that the access happened recently. Older stolen data can still be used in a new scam campaign.

There is, however, a relevant disclosure. In an October 2, 2026 notification, Frontier described a security incident involving its customer care database and information submitted through its customer care form. The airline said it updated the database configuration and improved monitoring in response.

That disclosure does not establish that this phishing campaign is linked to that incident, but it makes the question of where these reservation details originated even harder to ignore.

Warning passengers is necessary…but it would be nice if Frontier was a bit more transparent about the source of the leak.

I recently questioned Lufthansa Group’s decision to require a Travel ID account for online check-in. My objection was to making passengers create an account to complete a basic task after buying a ticket.

This Frontier story gives me reason to consider the security side more closely.

A booking reference and surname are convenient credentials, but they can be copied from a confirmation email or exposed elsewhere. Requiring additional authentication before allowing access to sensitive reservation information could offer passengers protection, even if it still strikes me as a bit heavy-handed like the incessant two-factor-authorization to log into Air Canada Aeroplan or United MileagePlus.

I’m not convinced Lufthansa introduced its requirement for this reason, or that its particular implementation would prevent the Frontier scam. Still, I would be more receptive to an account requirement accompanied by a clear explanation of what it protects and why the existing process is inadequate. Communication goes a long way in just about everything…

Frontier has confirmed a phishing campaign, while passengers report that fraudulent messages include their real booking details. For now, verify any supposed payment problem or refund through the airline’s official website or app. Do not trust a message merely because it contains your personal details.

But the burden should not fall entirely on passengers to spot convincing fraud. Frontier needs to explain, to the extent its investigation can establish, how scammers obtained the information that makes these messages so believable.

Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Yeah, this is on the airline. Not passengers. Of course, exercise good digital hygiene, but, c’mon…

#6290. 15 of the Coolest Marathon Courses Around the Globe, From the Arctic Circle to the Great Wall of China

The TCS New York City Marathon is consistently one of the best days of the year in the city—it's emotional, it's inspiring, and it shows off the best of humanity. If you're a runner or a spectator who got the itch for more this past weekend, you're in luck: There are tons of incredible courses around the world, and while they may not traverse NYC's five boroughs, they will take you to world wonders, through safari lands, and across borders.

As someone who regularly travels for halfs, I spend a lot of my time researching and bookmarking races. For me, running through a new place one of the best ways to get to know a destination—you get the lay of the land, see what the community is like, and notice things you might not see from a car or public transportation. And as destination races grow in popularity, the courses offered are getting even more spectacular. The races on this list—halfs, fulls, 10Ks, and more—prove it. Below, I’ve rounded up 15 of the most spectacular races happening in the next year or so, all of which are well worth traveling for.

Date: March 13, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Half marathon, 10K, 3.5K

What to know: If you haven't run a Rock ‘n’ Roll marathon yet, you're missing out on a good time. As the name suggests, these music-centric runs make for an extremely lively course—bands and DJs fill the roads and the after party. Locations change each year, and in 2027, the series is going to Taitung on Taiwan's east coast; runners will move between the mountains and the Pacific Ocean on a flat, smooth route. After the race, be sure to check out the area's night markets, hot springs, and endless good eats.

Where to stay: Luxury hotels near the starting line include the Sheraton Taitung Hotel, which has an outdoor swimming pool, and Formosan Naruwan Hotel, with a spa and saltwater pool.

Date: April 25, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, 21-miler, 11-miler, 12K, 5K

What to know: With a cliffside, oceanview course running from Big Sur to Carmel along California’s iconic Highway 1, it doesn’t get much more scenic than this. It’s a Boston qualifier race and has a six-hour time limit, along with several course length options, making it a good one to run with a group, even if your ideal mileage differs.

Where to stay: Room blocks are available at a few different properties in Monterey, closer to the finish line. Of course, there is no shortage of luxury hotels in the area—Alila Ventana Big Sur, Post Ranch Inn, and Carmel Beach Hotel are a few Traveler favorites.

Date: April 4, 2027Registration: The 2027 lottery entry has taken place; check back in May for the 2028 race; charity bibs are still availableDistances included: Half-marathon

What to know: As the name suggests, the course runs past several London landmarks, including Big Ben, the Tower of London, the London Eye, and Somerset House. It’s a lively course—musical performances, DJs, dancers, and themed cheer stations can be expected—and even better, it's a flat one, with 238 feet of total elevation gain.

Where to stay: In 2026, Blue Orchid Hospitality and the Clermont Hotel Group offered discounts for race weekend stays at properties like The Wellington Hotel, The Tower Hotel, and Thistle Trafalgar. We’ll update that list once 2027 partners are announced. For luxury stays near the starting line, consider Raffles London at the OWO or the Corinthia London.

Date: April 04, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, half marathon, 10K

What to know: Okay, I'll get the cons over with first (for most, I'd presume): This is a cold and snowy course. Once you've got that fact out of the way, you can weigh the very unique pros. This Finnish Lapland course kicks off in Santa Claus Village square (!) in Rovaniemi, starting exactly on the line of the Arctic Circle. It's put together as part of a five-day running program with log cabin lodging, each with a private sauna, as well as activities like husky sledding, Northern Lights excursions, and an Ice Pool Experience. It all wraps up at a trophy dinner with—wait for it—Santa Claus himself. This is peak whimsy, friends.

Where to stay: Lodging is included in the tour package.

Date: May 15, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, half-marathon, 8.5K

What to know: This race lets you run along one of the seven wonders of the world. It’s a strenuous, hilly course, but if the views alone don’t keep you going, the residents in local villages cheering you on along the route just might.

Of note, to register, you must sign up for a tour package; the starting price is $790 and includes race entry plus two nights of accommodations. It’s sponsored by Albatross Adventure Marathons, which also puts on The Big Five Marathon (more details below) and the Iceland Volcano Marathon, among other adventurous runs.

Where to stay: Hotels must be booked along with the packages. For a relaxing post-race stay, check into the Mandarin Oriental Qianmen, Beijing, with its award-winning spa (after a massage, consider the tea meditation too) and standout dining options, from Italian to dim sum.

Date: May 16, 2027Registration: Open now and quite affordable—the most expensive distance is €39 ($44)Distances included: Half-marathon, 10K, 5K (paved course); 17K, 8K (trail)

What to know: Set in Tossa de Mar, a beautiful, historic seaside town on Spain’s Costa Brava, these runs are all about the coastal views. Of course, that does mean a challenging, hilly course for all but the 5K, which boasts a flat route in the town’s center. Of note, the maximum time is on the shorter end: 2 hours 35 minutes for the half, 1 hour 15 for the 10K, and 45 minutes for the 5K.

Where to stay: Zel Costa Brava, about a 10-minute drive from the starting line, was mentioned in our list of the Best Places to Go in Spain and Portugal in 2026. It has a funicular to take guests down to the beach, a huge pool with plenty of lounge chairs to kick back on, and a spa with a thermal circuit, ideal for soothing sore legs.

Date: June 11-12, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Half marathon, 5K

What to know: Running around America's first national park, near sites like the Grand Prismatic Spring, is bound to be a highlight for any outdoor-loving runner. While not inside the bounds of the park, the views from the Custer Gallatin National Forest and the Hebgen Lake Ranger District are still impressive. The half marathon starts bright and early at 6 a.m. and has a four-hour course limit. There are five aid stations along the way, and 552 feet of elevation (of note, there are some technical, rocky sections to contend with).

Where to stay: The Lazy Duck Inn is the most convenient choice, given it's location near the start and finish line. To pad out the rest of your trip, check out our guide to where to stay in and near Yellowstone.

Date: June 19, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Full marathon, half-marathon

What to know: The name says it all: You might just see the big five while you run! The course takes runners through the South African Savannah on the Entabeni Game Reserve. It is a smaller race, with a maximum of 300 participants, in a moderate climate (expected to be in the 60s to 70s this year) along a sand and gravel trail. Past participants rave about this one, calling it “The ONLY marathon I have wanted to run twice!” and “the best adventure ever.” Like the Great Wall course, registration requires selecting a tour package, starting at $3,560 for the seven-day package, which includes accommodation, meals, game drives, bush walks, and more.

Where to stay: At the end of any package, you’ll be transferred to Johannesburg International Airport. Give yourself a night to decompress at the Park Hyatt Johannesburg, where peacocks roam the grounds, rooms overlook serene gardens, and Sunday brunch comes with a side of live music.

Date: June 19, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Marathon, half-marathon, 10K, 5K, kids race

What to know: The Tromsø, Norway, race begins at 8:30 p.m.—but thanks to the midnight sun the event is named after, it’s still light out. One of the northernmost races in the world, with a course surrounded by mountains and fjords, it boasted 9,000 runners from an impressive 88 countries last year. Of note, the maximum time limit is 5 hours and 30 minutes for the marathon and 3 hours and 30 minutes for the half.

Where to stay: Right in Tromsø, St. Elisabeth makes for a lovely stay, especially if you take advantage of the spa’s thermal bath, pool, and saunas. A bit further out (45 minutes or so), the Yggdrasiltunet Farm Hotel offers an even more blissful setting for a post-race escape with its wood-fired barrel sauna, guided ice bathing, hot tub overlooking the sea, and yoga classes.

Date: June 20, 2027Registration: Open now (half marathon is already sold out; sign up for 2028 notifications on the website)Distances included: Half marathon, 10K

What to know: The race website dubs this “the most beautiful run on the planet,” and honestly, that might not be so hyperbolic. Running through Canada's first national park sounds like a dream, especially when the course passes by the Vermilion Lakes, Legacy Trail, and Bow Valley Parkway, with wildlife likely to be spotted along the way. It's not a particularly hilly course, with a total elevation gain of 418 feet, but do note the elevation, which maxes out at 4,620 feet.

Where to stay: The official host partner is Banff Lodging Company, which operates 16 hotels across Banff, Canmore, and Lake Louise, including Hotel Canoe & Suites and Otter Hotel. Guests can receive a 15% discount on these rates. Afterward, consider a wellness-centric stay at the stunning Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise.

Date: July 03, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Full marathon, half-marathon, 10.55k

What to know: Designed for adventure-seekers, this Northern Iceland race explores one of Earth's geological hot spots—you’ll run along the rim of two volcanic craters and over black lava rock, with steaming geysers taking your mind off the miles ahead.

Unless you’re an Icelandic resident, you’ll need to book the six-day tour package, which is around $3,100 and includes accommodation, transportation, meals, a celebratory post-race dinner, and some activities, with add-ons like whale-watching and waterfall chasing available too. Of note, race entrance is not included in that fee ($350 for the half and full, and $223 for the quarter marathon).

Where to stay: Our resident Iceland expert and contributing writer Erika Owen highly recommends one of the tour lodging options, Fosshotel Glacier Lagoon, saying that it “embodies the best of Iceland: seclusion, surrounding nature, and beds topped with Icelandic wool blankets.” On your way out of town, consider a stay at The Retreat at Blue Lagoon; beyond the must-dip-in thermal baths, the tasting menu at Michelin-starred Moss is well worth a splurge.

Date: July 18, 2027Registration: Open nowDistances included: Half-marathon, 5K, The Pairing (both!)

What to know: A 13.1-mile route through Napa and Sonoma’s wine country, this course is surrounded by farms, vineyards, and ranches—yes, there are gently rolling hills, but it’s not an overly challenging course. The real prize for the 3,000-ish participants is at the finish line: At the post-race wine festival, top local vineyards reward you with wine tastings, and your goodie bag includes a commemorative wine glass.

Where to stay: Several hotels partner with the race to offer discounted stays, including the Westin Verasa Napa Hotel, notable for its Hyperice Recover & Recharge Kit available at the front desk. (Heads up for other future runs: Hyperice and Normatec products can be found at most Westins across the US! I swear by the Normatecs and Hypervolt for post-race recovery.) Just across the street from the starting line sits Carneros Resort and Spa, a seven-time Readers’ Choice Award winner; down the street is Stanly Ranch, Auberge Collection, a resort with a gorgeous outdoor pool that’s exactly where I’d want to park myself post-race.

Date: October 15–17, 2027Registration: Opens January 1, 2027Distances included: Marathon, marathon relay, half-marathon, 5K, one miler, kids races

What to know: This is one course that’s absolutely on my running bucket list, and one I hope to tackle in 2027 (which happens to be the event's 50th anniversary!). It’s the only US race I’ve found that crosses borders: After starting in downtown Detroit, runners cross over the Ambassador Bridge into Windsor, Ontario, before returning to the US through the Detroit-Windsor Tunnel (yep, an underwater mile!). Uniquely, this means you will have to carry your passport during the marathon and international half.

Where to stay: The AC Hotel Detroit at the Bonstelle is minutes from the start line, and well-situated to other places of interest (Little Caesar’s Arena, Fox Theater, the Detroit Institute of Arts). For a post-race treat, stop by Warda Pâtisserie. JW Marriott Detroit Water Square, opening in February 2027 near the Riverwalk, is sure to be a lovely place to stay too.

Date: November 2027Registration: Not yet openDistances included: Marathon, 10K, 5K

What to know: History buffs will love this course in Greece, which, according to legend, follows the original marathon route Pheidippides ran way back in 490 B.C. when he brought news of victory from the battlefield of Marathon (it’s also the course used in the 2004 Olympics). The marathon course stays open for eight hours and passes by landmarks like the Athens Concert Hall, Eleftherias Park, the Presidential Palace, and the National Garden. There are packages available if you want transportation, accommodations, and tour options baked into your visit; they’re not required for entry, but individual registration tends to sell out first, so plan accordingly.

Where to stay: The race starts in the town of Marathon, northeast of central Athens. For a stay close to the finish line with an excellent spa and both indoor and outdoor swimming pools, consider Hotel Grande Bretagne, a Luxury Collection Hotel. A bit further south, the seaside One&Only Aesthesis offers a touch of coastal glamour, plus a Guerlain spa.

Date: November 2027Registration: Not yet openDistances included: Marathon, marathon relay, half-marathon, 5K, one miler

What to know: The course begins in downtown Tulsa, weaving through neighborhoods and the University of Tulsa campus. Along the way, you'll encounter lots of support from the community, with block parties hosted along the course to cheer runners on. Of note, this is a Boston Qualifier, and race day temperatures tend to sit around the 50s.

Where to stay: Room blocks are available at several partner hotels, including Brut Hotel, a charming boutique hotel a short drive from the start line with an outdoor pool, rooftop bar, and spa. I’m eyeing the Olympian Massage, designed to “relieve tension and restore mobility by utilizing deep tissue and sports massage techniques.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6289. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

#6288. Eurostar Premier (First Class) Review: Better Than Flying, But Hardly A Luxury Experience

My first Eurostar Premier journey took me from Brussels to Amsterdam Schiphol Airport, where I connected to a KLM flight to Los Angeles. The train itself felt older than I expected, but the quiet carriage and productive journey made it a pleasant alternative to flying.

I sometimes enjoy trying a new travel experience without researching every detail beforehand. There is a certain irony in that, considering how much of this blog is devoted to helping others know what to expect. Eurostar was one of those experiences. I had long wanted to try it, and an award booking provided the opportunity.

I booked Brussels to Los Angeles through Air France/KLM Flying Blue for 60,000 miles in business class (plus $478.13 in taxes and fees). The itinerary included a Eurostar train from Brussels-Midi to Amsterdam Schiphol, followed by KLM World Business Class to Los Angeles. I could have booked a departure from Brussels Airport for the same mileage price, but chose the rail connection to try something different.

The cabin description was confusing. My ticket indicated business class, while KLM’s Air&Rail information referred to a “premium” experience for those connecting in business class. Eurostar’s actual classes are Standard, Plus, and Premier. At check-in, the agent confirmed I was booked into Premier.

Rather than use the actual Eurostar check-in desk, Brussels-Midi has an Air France-KLM ticketing office and rail check-in counter located in the rear of the station.

My train departed at 5:53 am and I showed up at 5:15 am to check-in…where I found a massive line and only one agent on duty. One passenger in the front of the line was traveling on SNCF to Paris but had a ticketing issue which the lone agent was trying to resolve. But time was ticking and the line grew longer.

Finally at 5:30 am I walked to the front of the line to ask for assistance, noting my train departed in 20 minutes. I did not mean to be the ugly American, but it was just what the agent needed to ask the frazzled traveler from Côte d’Ivoire (I noticed her passport) to step aside. Within a few minutes she had cleared the line and I was on my way upstairs to the rail platform.

There was a Eurostar lounge in Brussels, but it did not open until 6:00 am during my visit, so I could not use it…though I would have access to it had my train departed an hour later.  Not that I ended up having a lot of time to spare, but it woudld have been nice to have a cup of coffee there before the train departed.

Stepping onboard, I found my seat in Coach 11, the very last cabin designated as Premier.

Stepping onboard felt more like entering an older TGV first class carriage than the sleek, modern interior I had imagined. Old is, not necessarily a bad thing, but the cabin showed wear. My footrest was broken and the cabin just look tattered and well past its prime.

In the very rear of the cabin was a compartment with seating of four that remained empty throughout the journey.

The bigger advantage on this particular departure was how quiet it was: there was only one other passenger in my carriage and even as we neared Amsterdam there was never more than five in the cabin.

A nearly empty premium cabin is not something you can count in Premier, but it made this an especially pleasant setting to work ahead of a long flight in which I did not want to open my computer.

The lavatories in the Premier cabin were very typical European train toilets with metal toilets, a small sink, but fairly spacious.

We departed on time, and an attendant welcomed us and offered me breakfast menu shortly after pushback, along with a packaged moist towelette.

Sandwich IGP Bayonne ham, AOP Comté cheese, with dill picked cucumbers

Fruit Kampot pepper and verbena apples, gala melon, watermelon

Both were accompanied by yogurt, a croissant, juice, and coffee. I chose the fruit, though I would have liked both (and my request for both was politely declined).

It was a modest meal, but I enjoyed it. The fruit was good and the coffee was decent, as was the croissant.

I preferred this breakfast to the catering KLM serves on its short intra-European flights and the presentation was far nicer. It did not need to be elaborate to be satisfying at that hour and I had a second cup of coffee and some cold pressed berry juice prior to arrival at AMS.

The onboard internet worked well, allowing me to be productive during the ride. For this trip, I valued that more than a particularly luxurious cabin, though I was initially concerned that I would be capped at 500 MB of data.

Thankfully, even though I quickly exceeded the cap the internet continued working…

In-seat power was also available so I arrived in AMS with my devices fully charged.

The attendant’s welcome and breakfast service provided a pleasant start to the morning. Sure, it would have been nice to have the sandwich as well (I was still hungry and the cabin was empty), but she denied my request in a very kind way!

At one point I took a walk through the train to check out the Café Car which offers food and drinks for purchase.

Looking at the menu, I’d say I would have been fine with a falafel wrap and Lavazza coffee had I been booked in coach.

My destination was Schiphol Airport, not Amsterdam Centraa, whcih thankfully meant no backtracking a regional train to the airport.

Next came my KLM lounge visit and onward flight to Los Angeles.

For my itinerary, I was happy to have Premier included in the Flying Blue award.

Whether I would pay a substantial premium for it separately is another question and the answer is probably not. Eurostar lists extra-spacious seating and lounge access among Premier’s benefits, but I could not use the Brussels lounge on this departure.

It is also important to compare the correct route. Eurostar’s class descriptions distinguish between London services and continental routes. For example, the included meal in Premier on a London-route would have included a multi-course hot meal.

For a separate purchase, I would compare the actual fare difference and the benefits available for the particular trip (like the lounge), probably paying no more than €50 for the upgrade on this particular route.

Eurostar Premier was less polished than I expected, but I enjoyed the journey. The worn interior and broken footrest deserved attention, while breakfast and reliable internet helped make the ride worthwhile. For this Brussels–Schiphol connection, I was glad I chose the train. It gave me a quiet, productive start to the trip home and left me interested in trying Eurostar again.

Good option. Between the age of those seats and the fabric, I feel like an antimacassar would not have been out of place.

For some reason, I pictured something more like a modern Japanese or Chinese high speed rail carriage.

The seating is awful – Regiojet, our local carrier, used these same coaches as a lowest (sub-economy) class.

I take all lines of the Eurostar fairly frequently, and for context you took an older model of what was Thalys – the high speed train connecting Belgium to France and the Netherlands. They merged with Eurostar a few years back, but the experience remains quite distinct. Eurostar to/from London requires going through security and passport control, and is in a completely different part of the train station, and a lot more like getting in a flight. Overall. I’d recommend Plus. The price difference is rarely huge with economy, and you get more or less the same as Premium but without the lounge access or meal. Most routes max out at less than 3 hours, so I’d buy something before or after leaving, or as noted get a coffee on the train. I’ve taken Premium a few times and while it’s a nice upgrade, I’d not spend my own money on it, and the two times I’ve chosen it with the option of Plus were because I had urgent work and needed the lounge as a quiet office space. Overall, it’s a good review and reflective of the experience. Fingers crossed the new rolling stock freshens things up when it arrives, and I’m glad you could try things in this part of Europe.
